full.hn-neck:
What's tested
  • Spinal nerve parts, white vs gray rami, and the sympathetic and parasympathetic layout (thoracolumbar vs craniosacral, the four head ganglia)
  • Horner syndrome: the four signs and why each happens
  • Boundaries and contents of the posterior and anterior triangles; CN XI in the posterior triangle; the cervical plexus at the nerve point
  • Suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles and their nerves; ECA branches; carotid sheath, sinus and body
  • Root of the neck: subclavian parts and branches, phrenic and vagus, thoracic duct; thyroid and parathyroid relations and the nerves at risk in thyroid surgery
  • Deep cervical fascia, the retropharyngeal and danger spaces, and how infection reaches the mediastinum

Spinal nerves and the autonomic plan

The dorsal root is sensory (cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion), the ventral root is motor, and the short spinal nerve they form is mixed. It splits into a dorsal ramus (deep back muscles and skin) and a larger ventral ramus (body wall, limbs, and the cervical and brachial plexuses). C1–C7 exit above their vertebra, C8 between C7 and T1, and the rest below. The cord ends at L1–L2 (conus medullaris); the dural sac runs to S2.

  • Sympathetic = thoracolumbar: presynaptic cell bodies in the lateral horn of T1–L2; short presynaptic, long postsynaptic fibers; ganglia in the sympathetic trunk (paravertebral) or around the aorta (prevertebral). White rami (presynaptic, myelinated) exist only at T1–L2; gray rami (postsynaptic) join every spinal nerve.
  • To the head: presynaptic fibers from T1–T2 ascend the trunk and synapse in the superior cervical ganglion; postsynaptic fibers ride the internal and external carotid arteries (periarterial plexuses) to the dilator pupillae, superior tarsal muscle, sweat glands and vessels.
  • Parasympathetic = craniosacral: CN III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4; long presynaptic, short postsynaptic fibers; ganglia near or in the organ. The four head ganglia: ciliary (III), pterygopalatine and submandibular (VII), otic (IX). The vagus uses small ganglia in the organ walls.

Horner syndrome (cervical sympathetic chain cut or compressed, classically by an apical lung, or Pancoast, tumor): ptosis (superior tarsal muscle, so the droop is partial), miosis (unopposed sphincter pupillae, so the pupil is small), anhidrosis and flushing (warm, red skin) on the same side.

Posterior triangle

Bounded by the posterior border of the SCM, the anterior border of the trapezius and the middle third of the clavicle. Roof: investing layer of deep cervical fascia (platysma over it). Floor: prevertebral fascia over splenius capitis, levator scapulae and the scalenes. The inferior belly of the omohyoid splits it into occipital and supraclavicular triangles.

  • CN XI crosses it superficially on the levator scapulae, so a lymph node biopsy here can cut it: the shoulder droops and the patient can't shrug (trapezius). The SCM is often spared because its branch leaves earlier.
  • Cervical plexus (C1–C4 ventral rami) cutaneous branches emerge at the nerve point (Erb's point) at the middle of the SCM's posterior border, the site of a cervical plexus block: lesser occipital (C2), great auricular (C2–C3; skin over the parotid and the angle of the mandible, which is not trigeminal), transverse cervical (C2–C3; front of the neck), supraclavicular (C3–C4).
  • Also: external jugular vein (cut where it pierces the fascia, it can suck in air), phrenic nerve on the anterior scalene, brachial plexus roots and trunks and the third part of the subclavian artery between the anterior and middle scalenes. The subclavian vein passes in front of the anterior scalene.

Anterior triangle

Bounded by the midline, the inferior border of the mandible and the anterior border of the SCM, and divided by the digastric and the superior belly of the omohyoid into submandibular (submandibular gland, facial artery and vein, nodes), submental, carotid and muscular triangles. Landmarks: hyoid C3, thyroid cartilage C4–C5, cricoid C6 (start of trachea and esophagus). The common carotid splits at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage.

External carotid branches (SALFOPSM): superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, and the two terminal branches, superficial temporal and maxillary. The internal carotid has no branches in the neck. The carotid sinus (dilation of the proximal ICA) holds baroreceptors; the carotid body (at the bifurcation) holds chemoreceptors; both report through the carotid sinus branch of IX, so pressure on the sinus can slow the heart. The carotid sheath holds the common/internal carotid (medial), IJV (lateral) and vagus (posterior, between them), with the deep cervical nodes along the IJV; the sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath, in the prevertebral fascia. The IJV begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus. Key nodes: jugulodigastric (tonsil, back of the tongue) and jugulo-omohyoid (tongue).

Root of the neck and cervical viscera

The superior thoracic aperture (T1, first ribs, manubrium) passes the trachea, esophagus, great vessels, vagus and phrenic nerves, thoracic duct and the lung's cupula (a stab wound here can cause a pneumothorax). The brachial plexus and subclavian vessels go over the first rib to the axilla instead.

  • Phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5): down the front of the anterior scalene, between the subclavian artery and vein, sole motor supply of the diaphragm.
  • Vagus: the right crosses in front of the right subclavian artery, and the right recurrent laryngeal hooks under it; the left recurrent laryngeal hooks under the aortic arch. Both climb in the tracheoesophageal groove.
  • Brachiocephalic veins form behind each sternoclavicular joint from the IJV and subclavian vein (the venous angle) and join to form the SVC; the left is longer.
  • Thoracic duct: from the cisterna chyli to the left venous angle; drains everything except the right upper quadrant, which the right lymphatic duct drains. Injury leaks chyle (chylothorax).
  • Thyroid: isthmus over tracheal rings 2–4, inside the pretracheal fascia (so it moves with swallowing). Superior thyroid artery (ECA) runs with the external laryngeal nerve (injury: can't raise pitch, weak monotone voice); inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk) is close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (injury: hoarseness). A thyroid ima artery is present in about 10%. Superior and middle thyroid veins go to the IJV, the inferior to the brachiocephalic veins. The four parathyroids sit on the back of the lobes; removing them causes hypocalcemia and tetany.
  • Esophagus: begins at C6 behind the trachea, leans left; narrow points at the cricopharyngeus, where the aortic arch and left main bronchus cross, and at the diaphragm (T10), where swallowed objects lodge.
  • Airway access: cricothyrotomy through the median cricothyroid ligament in an emergency; tracheostomy below the cricoid, more risky in infants (tiny trachea, esophagus behind).

Fascia and spaces

The investing layer wraps the SCM, trapezius and the parotid and submandibular glands. The pretracheal (visceral) layer wraps the thyroid, trachea and esophagus, and continues behind the pharynx as the buccopharyngeal fascia. The prevertebral layer wraps the vertebral muscles; its front part is the alar fascia. The retropharyngeal space (buccopharyngeal fascia in front, alar fascia behind) runs from the skull base to the upper mediastinum; the danger space (alar in front, prevertebral behind) runs to the diaphragm. Infection from the teeth, tonsils or pharynx can track through them into the mediastinum.
full.hn-skull:
What's tested
  • Bones of the neurocranium and viscerocranium; sutures, bregma, lambda and the pterion over the middle meningeal artery
  • Fontanelles and skull fractures (basilar fractures leak CSF)
  • Contents of the three cranial fossae and the foramina with what passes through each
  • Meninges, dural folds, dural venous sinuses and the cavernous sinus (contents and thrombosis)
  • Epidural, subdural and subarachnoid bleeds; the circle of Willis and stroke
  • Each cranial nerve: functional components, where it leaves the skull, its ganglia and its classic lesion

Skull bones and landmarks

Neurocranium (8): frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, occipital (unpaired) and parietal, temporal (paired). Viscerocranium: maxilla, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine, inferior concha (paired), and mandible and vomer (unpaired). Bregma = coronal + sagittal sutures; lambda = sagittal + lambdoid. The pterion, where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid meet, is the thinnest part of the lateral skull and lies over the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.

  • Fontanelles: anterior (at bregma) closes around 18 months; posterior (at lambda) by 2–3 months. A bulging fontanelle suggests raised intracranial pressure; a sunken one, dehydration.
  • Fractures: linear (most common), depressed (fragments push on the brain), comminuted, and basilar (CSF from the nose or ear; anosmia with a cribriform plate fracture).
  • Fossae: anterior (frontal and ethmoid; frontal lobes, olfactory bulbs), middle (sphenoid and temporal; temporal lobes, pituitary in the sella turcica), posterior (mostly occipital; cerebellum, pons, medulla).

Meninges and dural sinuses

Dura (periosteal + meningeal layers), arachnoid, pia. The meningeal layer folds in as the falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli and diaphragma sellae. Dural sinuses lie between the two dural layers. Arachnoid granulations return CSF to the superior sagittal sinus. Dura above the tentorium is supplied by V; in the posterior fossa by C1–C3 and X. The middle meningeal artery (maxillary artery, through the foramen spinosum) supplies the dura and skull.

  • Flow: superior sagittal → confluence of sinuses → transverse → sigmoid → IJV at the jugular foramen. Inferior sagittal + great cerebral vein → straight sinus → confluence.
  • The cavernous sinus, beside the sella, drains backward through the superior petrosal (to the transverse/sigmoid) and inferior petrosal (to the IJV) sinuses. It receives the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins and connects to the pterygoid plexus by emissary veins through the foramen ovale.
  • Through the cavernous sinus: ICA and CN VI. In its lateral wall: III, IV, V1, V2.
  • Cavernous sinus thrombosis: infection from the danger triangle of the face (angular → ophthalmic veins) or from the teeth (pterygoid plexus). The first nerve sign is usually CN VI palsy (the eye can't abduct and drifts in), then ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, eyelid swelling and V1/V2 numbness.

The circle of Willis joins the internal carotid system (ACA, MCA, anterior and posterior communicating arteries) and the vertebrobasilar system (PICA, AICA, superior cerebellar, PCA). The MCA is the most common stroke artery: contralateral face and arm weakness and sensory loss, and aphasia if the dominant side. Ischemic strokes are about 87% of strokes; hemorrhagic about 13%.

Cranial nerves

Sensory only: I, II, VIII. Motor only: III, IV, VI, XI, XII. Both: V, VII, IX, X. Parasympathetic: III, VII, IX, X. Brainstem: III–IV midbrain, V–VIII pons, IX–XII medulla.

full.hn-face:
What's tested
  • Bones and openings of the orbit; the orbital floor (blow-out) fracture
  • Layers of the eye, accommodation, the pupillary and corneal reflexes, aqueous humor and glaucoma
  • Extraocular muscle actions and nerves (LR6 SO4, the rest III); the course of III, IV, V1 and VI in the orbit
  • Muscles of facial expression, the five branches of VII, Bell palsy; sensory supply of the face by V1, V2, V3
  • Facial arteries and veins, the danger triangle; scalp layers; lacrimal secretion and drainage
  • Parotid relations, what runs through it, the duct, its IX–otic–auriculotemporal pathway and Frey syndrome

The orbit

Seven bones: frontal (roof), zygomatic and greater wing of the sphenoid (lateral wall), maxilla, zygomatic and palatine (floor), and ethmoid, lacrimal, maxilla and lesser wing of the sphenoid (medial wall and apex). The nasal bone is not part of it. Openings: optic canal (II, ophthalmic artery), superior orbital fissure (III, IV, V1, VI, superior ophthalmic vein), inferior orbital fissure (infraorbital nerve and vessels, zygomatic nerve), supraorbital notch, infraorbital foramen, nasolacrimal canal.

Blow-out fracture: a blow to the eye raises orbital pressure and breaks the thinnest walls, most often the floor (into the maxillary sinus), then the medial wall (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid). Signs: the inferior rectus is trapped (can't look up, double vision), numbness of the cheek, side of the nose and upper lip (infraorbital nerve), sunken eye.

The superior tarsal muscle (smooth muscle in the lid) is sympathetic: its loss gives the partial ptosis of Horner syndrome. V1 splits into frontal (supraorbital, supratrochlear), lacrimal and nasociliary (ethmoidal nerves, infratrochlear, long ciliary nerves and the external nasal branch to the tip of the nose, which is why shingles on the nose tip warns of eye involvement). The ophthalmic artery is the first branch of the ICA; its central retinal branch is an end artery. Orbital veins drain to the cavernous sinus.

The eyeball and its reflexes

  • Layers: fibrous (sclera; cornea, avascular and very sensitive), vascular (choroid, ciliary body, iris), and the retina.
  • Ciliary ganglion: presynaptic parasympathetic fibers of III (Edinger-Westphal) synapse here; short ciliary nerves go to the sphincter pupillae (constriction) and ciliary muscle. Sympathetic fibers to the dilator pupillae pass through without synapsing.
  • Accommodation (near vision): ciliary muscle contracts, zonular fibers relax, the lens rounds up, and the pupils constrict and converge. Far vision: ciliary muscle relaxed, zonules taut, lens flat.
  • Aqueous humor: made by the ciliary processes → posterior chamber → through the pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork at the iridocorneal angle → canal of Schlemm → veins. Blocked drainage raises intraocular pressure and damages the optic nerve (glaucoma).
  • Pupillary light reflex: II in, III out (both pupils). Corneal reflex: V1 in, VII out (both eyes blink).

The face

The supraorbital, infraorbital and mental foramina line up vertically and carry the cutaneous ends of V1, V2 and V3. The mental foramen sits below the mandibular second premolar; in an edentulous ridge that has resorbed, it ends up on the crest and a denture can press on the mental nerve. The zygomatic arch is a common fracture site; mandible fractures are often paired.

  • Muscles of facial expression: arch 2, all VII, insert into skin. The buccinator (from the pterygomandibular raphe and the alveolar processes) keeps food on the teeth and is pierced by the parotid duct; it is not a muscle of mastication.
  • VII leaves the stylomastoid foramen, gives branches to the posterior digastric, stylohyoid and posterior auricular muscles, then splits inside the parotid into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches.
  • Bell palsy (lower motor neuron): the whole half of the face, forehead included; the eye won't close (dry eye, corneal risk), the mouth droops and drools. An inferior alveolar injection placed too far back, into the parotid, can numb VII for a few hours with the same picture.
  • Sensation: V1 forehead, upper lid, bridge and tip of the nose; V2 lower lid, cheek, side of the nose, upper lip; V3 lower lip, chin, temple and the front of the ear. The angle of the mandible is the great auricular nerve (C2–C3).
  • Arteries: facial artery (crosses the mandible at the front edge of the masseter, labial branches, ends as the angular artery), superficial temporal, transverse facial. Veins: supraorbital + supratrochlear → angular → facial → (with the retromandibular) common facial → IJV. The angular vein connects to the ophthalmic veins, and the deep facial vein to the pterygoid plexus; with few or no working valves, infection from the danger triangle (corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose) can reach the cavernous sinus.

Scalp

S-C-A-L-P: skin; dense connective tissue with vessels held open when cut (scalp wounds bleed freely); epicranial aponeurosis (frontalis and occipitalis); loose connective tissue, the "danger zone" where blood and pus spread and emissary veins lead into the skull; pericranium. Fluid in the loose layer can't spread back or to the sides but can run forward into the eyelids (black eyes). Supply: in front of the ears V, behind them C2–C3 (greater and lesser occipital); arteries from the ECA (superficial temporal, occipital, posterior auricular) and ICA (supraorbital, supratrochlear).

Lacrimal apparatus

Gland in the superolateral orbit → tears swept medially → puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus. Secretion: superior salivatory nucleus → VII → greater petrosal nerve → nerve of the pterygoid canal → synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion → zygomatic nerve (V2) → lacrimal nerve (V1) → gland.

Parotid gland

The largest salivary gland, serous, wrapped in the tough parotid sheath from the investing fascia (so mumps is painful). It wraps the back of the ramus, in front of the ear, mastoid and SCM, over the masseter and medial pterygoid. Running through it, superficial to deep: facial nerve (forms its plexus, supplies nothing in the gland), retromandibular vein (formed in the gland by the superficial temporal and maxillary veins), external carotid artery (ends in the gland as the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries). The parotid (Stensen) duct crosses the masseter a finger's breadth below the zygomatic arch, pierces the buccinator and opens at the parotid papilla opposite the maxillary second molar.

Secretomotor path: inferior salivatory nucleus → IX → tympanic nerve and plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → synapse in the otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve (V3) → gland. VII passes through but gives it no secretory fibers. Frey syndrome: after parotid surgery, cut parasympathetic fibers regrow into the sweat glands of the overlying skin (great auricular and auriculotemporal territory), so eating causes sweating and flushing of the cheek. A parotid tumor with facial weakness suggests malignancy.
full.hn-itf:
What's tested
  • Boundaries, openings and contents of the temporal and infratemporal fossae
  • Muscles of mastication: attachments, actions, the lateral pterygoid as the opener, jaw deviation in a V3 lesion
  • V3 and its branches (anterior vs posterior division), the chorda tympani joining the lingual nerve, the otic ganglion
  • The three parts of the maxillary artery and their branches; the pterygoid plexus and its links to the cavernous sinus
  • Anatomy behind the inferior alveolar, buccal, mental and posterior superior alveolar blocks and their complications
  • TMJ: articular surfaces, disc and compartments, ligaments, movements, dislocation and nerve supply

Temporal and infratemporal fossae

The temporal fossa lies between the superior temporal line and the zygomatic arch; its floor is the frontal, parietal, temporal and greater wing of the sphenoid (the pterion), its roof the temporal fascia, and it holds the temporalis. The infratemporal crest of the greater wing separates it from the infratemporal fossa below.

  • Infratemporal fossa boundaries: lateral, the ramus of the mandible; medial, the lateral pterygoid plate; anterior, the back of the maxilla; posterior, the styloid process and carotid sheath; roof, the greater wing of the sphenoid with the foramen ovale (V3) and foramen spinosum (middle meningeal artery); no bony floor.
  • Contents: lateral and medial pterygoids, the lower temporalis, the maxillary artery (first and second parts), the pterygoid venous plexus, V3 and its branches, the chorda tympani and the otic ganglion.
  • Openings: the pterygomaxillary fissure leads medially into the pterygopalatine fossa (the maxillary artery goes through it); the mandibular notch carries the masseteric nerve and vessels.

The digastric, geniohyoid and mylohyoid help open the jaw. A V3 motor lesion wastes the masseter and temporalis on that side, and on opening the jaw deviates toward the lesion, pushed by the working lateral pterygoid of the other side.

The mandibular nerve (V3)

V3 leaves through the foramen ovale, the only trigeminal division with motor fibers. The otic ganglion sits just below the foramen, medial to V3. Main trunk: meningeal branch and the nerve to the medial pterygoid (which also supplies the tensor veli palatini and tensor tympani).

  • Anterior division (mostly motor): masseteric, deep temporal, nerve to the lateral pterygoid and the buccal nerve, its only sensory branch (cheek skin and mucosa, buccal gingiva of the mandibular molars).
  • Posterior division (mostly sensory): auriculotemporal (splits around the middle meningeal artery; skin of the temple, auricle, external acoustic meatus and the TMJ; carries parotid secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion), lingual (general sensation of the front two-thirds of the tongue, floor of the mouth and lingual gingiva; joined by the chorda tympani, which leaves the skull through the petrotympanic fissure carrying taste and submandibular secretomotor fibers), and inferior alveolar (gives the motor nerve to the mylohyoid just before the mandibular foramen, then runs in the mandibular canal to all mandibular teeth and ends as the mental and incisive nerves).

Anatomy of the mandibular and posterior maxillary blocks

  • Inferior alveolar block: the needle passes through the buccinator, lateral to the pterygomandibular raphe, into the pterygomandibular space (ramus laterally, medial pterygoid medially) toward the mandibular foramen, guarded by the lingula and the sphenomandibular ligament. It numbs the mandibular teeth, the lower lip and chin, and usually the lingual nerve (tongue). It misses the buccal nerve, which needs its own injection for the buccal gingiva of the molars. Too far back: the parotid and a temporary facial palsy. Injury or bleeding in the medial pterygoid: trismus.
  • Mental/incisive block: at the mental foramen, below or between the premolars.
  • Posterior superior alveolar block: up and back behind the maxillary tuberosity, next to the pterygoid plexus; too deep a needle can cause a fast-growing hematoma of the cheek. The mesiobuccal root of the maxillary first molar is often supplied by the middle superior alveolar nerve instead, so it may stay sensitive.

The pterygoid plexus mirrors the maxillary artery's branches, drains the teeth (alveolar veins) and empties into the maxillary vein, which joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein. It connects to the cavernous sinus by emissary veins through the foramen ovale, to the inferior ophthalmic vein, and to the facial vein through the deep facial vein, so dental infection can reach the cranial cavity.

Temporomandibular joint

  • Synovial joint between the condyle and the mandibular fossa and articular eminence of the temporal bone. Its articular surfaces are covered by fibrocartilage (dense fibrous tissue), not hyaline cartilage, and so is the avascular articular disc.
  • The disc splits the joint into a superior compartment (gliding: disc and condyle slide forward onto the eminence) and an inferior compartment (hinge: condyle rotates under the disc). Small opening is rotation; wide opening adds translation, pulled by the lateral pterygoid. Behind the disc is the vascular, innervated retrodiscal tissue.
  • Ligaments: lateral (temporomandibular) ligament, the main one, limits backward and downward movement of the condyle; with the postglenoid tubercle it makes posterior dislocation rare. Sphenomandibular ligament, from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula (a Meckel's cartilage remnant). Stylomandibular ligament, from the styloid process to the angle, limits protrusion.
  • Dislocation is almost always anterior and often bilateral: in a wide yawn the condyle slides in front of the articular eminence and the elevators spasm, locking the mouth open. Reduce by pressing down on the molars, then back.
  • Thin bone of the mandibular fossa separates the condyle from the middle cranial fossa; a hard blow under the chin can drive the condyle upward.
  • Nerves: auriculotemporal (main) and masseteric. Because the auriculotemporal also supplies the external acoustic meatus, TMJ pain is often felt in the ear.

  • How primary teeth differ from permanent teeth, and the primary teeth that look like no other tooth

Terms

Humans are heterodont (several tooth forms) and diphyodont (two dentitions). Succedaneous teeth replace primary teeth: the permanent incisors, canines and premolars (20 teeth). The permanent molars erupt behind the primary teeth and replace nothing, so they are not succedaneous. Premolars replace the primary molars. The anatomic crown is covered by enamel and the anatomic root by cementum; the clinical crown is whatever shows in the mouth. Dental formulas (one side): primary I 2/2, C 1/1, M 2/2 = 10 × 2 = 20; permanent I 2/2, C 1/1, P 2/2, M 3/3 = 16 × 2 = 32. The mixed dentition runs from about 6 to 12 years.

Numbering systems

  • Universal (used in the US): permanent 1–32, starting at the maxillary right third molar (#1), across to the maxillary left third molar (#16), down to the mandibular left third molar (#17) and back to the mandibular right third molar (#32). Primary teeth are letters A–T in the same path: A is the maxillary right second molar, J the maxillary left second molar, K the mandibular left second molar, T the mandibular right second molar.
  • Palmer: a right-angle bracket shows the quadrant, and teeth are counted from the midline, 1–8 permanent and A–E primary.
  • FDI (two digits): first digit = quadrant, 1 maxillary right, 2 maxillary left, 3 mandibular left, 4 mandibular right; primary quadrants 5–8 in the same order. Second digit = tooth counted from the midline (1–8 permanent, 1–5 primary).

Calcification and root formation

  • Primary teeth begin to calcify in utero, at about 4–6 months (14–16 weeks). The permanent first molar is the only permanent tooth that starts calcifying at birth; permanent incisors start at 3–4 months after birth (the maxillary lateral nearer 1 year).
  • Cusp tips and incisal edges calcify first, and crowns mineralize before roots.
  • A permanent crown is finished about 3–4 years before eruption; its root is finished about 2–3 years after eruption. A primary root is finished about 1–1½ years after eruption, so all primary roots are complete by about age 3.
  • The permanent tooth erupts at about the time its primary predecessor exfoliates.

Primary eruption

Order: central incisor → lateral incisor → first molar → canine → second molar (the first molar comes before the canine). Mandibular teeth lead their maxillary partners. The class's chart: mandibular centrals 6 months, mandibular laterals 7, maxillary centrals 7½, maxillary laterals 9, first molars 12 (mandibular) and 14 (maxillary), canines 16 and 18, second molars 20 and 24 months. All 20 are in by about 2–2½ years.

  • The first permanent tooth is the mandibular first molar (the "6-year molar"); the first succedaneous tooth is the mandibular central incisor.
  • Mandibular teeth usually erupt first; the premolars are the exception (maxillary premolars can come in first).
  • The maxillary canine erupts after the maxillary premolars, so it is the last anterior tooth in and the one most often blocked out or impacted.

Primary compared with permanent

  • Smaller and whiter; enamel and dentin thinner and less mineralized, so they wear faster.
  • Crowns short incisocervically and wide mesiodistally for their height, with a marked constriction at the CEJ and prominent cervical ridges (facial and lingual on anteriors, buccal on molars, biggest at the mesiobuccal of the first molars).
  • Large pulps and high pulp horns (the mesiobuccal horn of the molars especially), so a shallow preparation can expose the pulp; the molar pulp chamber sits mostly in the crown.
  • Roots long and slender for the crown; anterior roots bend facially in the apical third; molar roots have almost no trunk and flare widely to make room for the premolar buds.
  • No mamelons, fewer anomalies, and spaces between teeth are normal (contacts are often missing).

What's tested

Surfaces, angles and lobes

A line angle is where two surfaces meet (mesiolabial); a point angle is where three meet (mesiolabioincisal). Teeth grow from lobes: anterior teeth from 4 (three labial lobes plus the cingulum). The labial lobes leave mamelons (three bumps on a new incisal edge that wear away) and two faint labial depressions. Perikymata are the fine wavy enamel ridges on newly erupted teeth. The cingulum is the lingual bulge in the cervical third of every anterior tooth.

Heights of contour

The height of contour is the crest of curvature of a surface. It deflects food over the gingiva. Overcontoured (too bulky): food skips the gingiva and plaque collects at the margin, so the gingiva becomes inflamed; this is the more common restorative error. Undercontoured (too flat): food is driven into the sulcus and the gingiva is injured.

Contacts, embrasures and the CEJ

  • Contacts move cervically as you go back from the midline, and each tooth's distal contact is more cervical (and slightly more lingual) than its mesial. Exceptions: the mandibular central incisor (both contacts at the same level, incisal third), the mandibular first premolar (mesial more cervical) and the primary maxillary canine (mesial more cervical).
  • From the incisal view, anterior contacts are centered faciolingually; from the occlusal view, posterior contacts sit slightly buccal of center.
  • Each contact has four embrasures (facial, lingual, incisal or occlusal, gingival). Lingual embrasures are larger than facial ones, and incisal embrasures open up going distally. Contacts stabilize the arch, stop food impaction and protect the papilla.
  • The CEJ curves toward the apex on the facial and lingual and toward the incisal or occlusal on the proximal surfaces. The curve is deepest on the mesial of the central incisors, shallows going back, is similar on adjacent surfaces, and is greater on the mesial than the distal.

Maxillary incisors

  • Central: the largest incisor crown and the widest anterior tooth mesiodistally; trapezoidal labially, triangular proximally. The mesioincisal angle is sharp (almost square) and the distoincisal rounded; the mesial contact is in the incisal third, the distal at the incisal-middle junction. Cingulum slightly distal. One conical root with a blunt apex, a rounded-triangle cross-section, about 1–1½ times the crown.
  • Lateral: a smaller, rounder central with a deeper lingual fossa and stronger marginal ridges; the cingulum is centered and a lingual pit is common. Both incisal angles are more rounded (the distal most). A palatogingival groove (about 3%) runs from the cingulum onto the root and can hold a deep localized periodontal pocket. The root often bends distally and has more accessory canals. It is the second most variable tooth after the third molars (peg laterals, congenital absence).

Mandibular incisors

  • Central: the smallest permanent tooth and the most symmetric (hard to call right or left); the first succedaneous tooth; the tooth least prone to caries. Its contacts are at the same height. It occludes with only one opposing tooth (the maxillary central), as does the maxillary third molar.
  • Lateral: slightly larger, with a longer root; the cingulum is distal to center and the incisal edge has a distolingual twist that follows the arch, so from the mesial you see more lingual surface.
  • Both: incisal edge lingual to the root axis; little lingual anatomy; a ribbon-like root, narrow mesiodistally and broad faciolingually, with proximal depressions (deeper on the distal).

The maxillary canine is the "cornerstone": its long root in dense bone supports the corner of the mouth (the canine eminence) and makes it the best tooth to guide lateral movements. It erupts last among the anterior teeth (11–12 years), so it is often blocked out or impacted. Wear: maxillary canines wear on the mesial cusp ridge and lingual surface, mandibular canines on the distal cusp ridge and labial surface. A prominent cingulum is not a second cusp, and a flat mesial cusp ridge does not make a mandibular canine an incisor.

Premolars

Premolars develop from 4 lobes (3 buccal, 1 lingual); the three-cusp mandibular second premolar has 5 (two lingual lobes). Crowns taper to the lingual, and the buccal cusp is the larger. Maxillary premolar cusps sit over the root; mandibular premolar crowns tilt lingually.

  • The maxillary first premolar's mesial concavity runs from the crown onto the root: hard to match with a matrix and to clean.
  • Most commonly rotated tooth: the maxillary second premolar. A mandibular second premolar is often congenitally missing.

Molars: class traits

Wider mesiodistally than tall, the shortest crowns occlusocervically, clinical crowns shrinking from first to third. Crowns taper buccal to lingual, except the maxillary first molar, which is wider on the lingual (its large distolingual cusp and the Carabelli cusp). Centric cusps: maxillary lingual, mandibular buccal; non-centric cusps protect the cheek (maxillary buccal) and tongue (mandibular lingual). Distal marginal ridges and contacts are more cervical than mesial. Root trunks lengthen and roots converge from first to third molar.

Maxillary molars

  • First molar: largest maxillary tooth; rhomboid outline (MB and DL angles acute, ML and DB obtuse). Cusps largest to smallest ML, MB, DB, DL, plus the Carabelli cusp on the lingual of the ML cusp. The ML cusp is the longest. The oblique ridge joins the DB and ML cusps (only maxillary molars have one) and is crossed by the transverse groove of the oblique ridge. Four fossae: central (largest), distal oblique, mesial triangular, distal triangular. The lingual groove and pit are caries-prone.
  • Second molar: DL cusp small or absent (a 3-cusp, heart-shaped form), Carabelli rare, less prominent oblique ridge, roots closer and more distally inclined with a longer trunk.
  • Third molar: most variable tooth and the most often missing; bulbous, wrinkled crown; roots short and often fused.
  • Roots: three (MB, DB, palatal). By length and bulk palatal > MB > DB. The broad MB root often holds two canals (the MB2), so the tooth usually has four canals. (One class guide gives the second molar four canals and the first three; the standard teaching is an MB2 in most first molars.) The first molar's roots flare most and its trunk is shortest.
  • Furcations: mesial about 3–4 mm from the CEJ (most coronal, entered from the palatal side), buccal about 4 mm, distal about 5 mm (most apical).

Mandibular molars

  • First molar: 5 cusps in 80–85% (MB, DB, D buccally; ML, DL lingually), pentagon outline, two buccal grooves and one lingual groove. MB is the widest cusp, ML the tallest and sharpest, D the smallest. The crown tilts lingually.
  • Second molar: 4 cusps, a "+" groove pattern (one buccal, one lingual groove), rectangular outline; a buccal cervical ridge on the MB cusp; roots closer and straighter.
  • Roots: two, mesial and distal. The mesial root is broader, more curved and has two canals (MB, ML), with a deeper distal-side depression; the distal root is straighter, usually one canal. A third, distolingual root occurs occasionally. The furcation is about 3 mm from the CEJ buccally and 4 mm lingually.

Quick ways to orient a posterior tooth

  • Maxillary or mandibular? Premolars: cusps centered over the root (maxillary) or crown tilted lingually (mandibular). Molars: three roots (maxillary) or two (mandibular).
  • Mesial or distal? Maxillary first premolar: the mesial concavity and marginal groove. Maxillary second premolar: the lingual cusp tip leans mesially. Mandibular first premolar: the mesiolingual groove and the larger distal fossa. Mandibular second premolar: the ML cusp is larger than the DL. Maxillary molars: the small DL cusp is distal, the Carabelli cusp mesial. Mandibular molars: the small distal cusp is distal, the crown tapers distally and the roots tilt distally.
  • Buccal or lingual? Two buccal roots on a maxillary molar; the crown tilts away from the buccal on a mandibular tooth.
full.da-anomalies:
What's tested
  • Naming an anomaly from a description or a radiograph: number, position, size, shape, root and structure
  • Fusion versus gemination versus concrescence, and how the tooth count tells them apart
  • The hereditary defects (amelogenesis and dentinogenesis imperfecta) against the acquired ones (fluorosis, tetracycline, Turner tooth)
  • Attrition, abrasion, erosion and abfraction
  • Identifying a permanent tooth step by step, right or left included

Anomalies are more common in the permanent dentition and in the maxilla.

Number and position

  • Anodontia: true (complete) anodontia is rare and goes with ectodermal dysplasia (hair, skin, sweat glands); partial anodontia (hypodontia) is one or more teeth missing; agenesis means the tooth never formed. Most often missing: third molars (maxillary more than mandibular), then the maxillary lateral incisors and mandibular second premolars (the class ranks the laterals ahead; other sources put the premolars first).
  • Supernumerary teeth are often malformed. The mesiodens, between the maxillary centrals, is the most common; it can hold the centrals apart (a diastema) or block their eruption. A distomolar/paramolar sits in the third molar area; the mandibular premolar area is the other common site.
  • Malposition: impaction is most common in third molars, then maxillary canines (last anterior to erupt). Transposition: two teeth swap places (canine and first premolar). Rotation: most often the maxillary second premolar.

Size and shape

  • Microdontia (the peg lateral, a maxillary lateral formed from one lobe) and macrodontia.
  • Gemination: one tooth bud tries to split; a notched or bifid crown on one root and one canal; the count is normal when the double tooth is counted as one.
  • Fusion: two buds join through dentin; the count is one short; most common in the primary dentition and the mandibular incisor area.
  • Concrescence: two formed teeth joined by cementum only, usually maxillary molars.
  • Congenital syphilis: Hutchinson incisors (notched, screwdriver-shaped) and mulberry molars (constricted crowns with many small cusps).
  • Talon cusp: a claw-like extra cusp off the cingulum of an anterior tooth, often with a pulp horn; it can interfere with occlusion. Shovel-shaped incisors have heavy marginal ridges (more common in Asian, Arctic and Native American dentitions). Tuberculum intermedium: an extra lingual cusp between the ML and DL cusps of a mandibular molar. Tubercles are more common on mesial than distal marginal ridges.
  • Dens in dente (dens invaginatus): enamel folded into the tooth through a deep pit at the cingulum, most often a maxillary lateral; it decays early and the pulp can die.

A defect on every tooth in both dentitions points to a hereditary cause; a band on the teeth forming at one age points to an event; a single tooth points to a local cause.

Changes after eruption

  • Attrition: tooth against tooth (bruxism, porcelain against enamel); flat, shiny, matching facets.
  • Abrasion: a foreign object: hard brushing and abrasive paste (cervical, worse on the side opposite the dominant hand), a pipe, pins or nails held in the teeth; rounded in cross section.
  • Erosion: acid without bacteria (citrus, soda, reflux, bulimia); smooth, dished-out, yellow dentin showing. Vomiting erodes the lingual of the maxillary anterior teeth.
  • Abfraction: enamel rods breaking at the CEJ as the tooth flexes under heavy lateral loads; V-shaped, in the cervical third.

Identifying a permanent tooth

  1. Class: no cusp = incisor; 1 cusp = canine (a big cingulum is not a second cusp); 2–3 = premolar; 4–5 = molar.
  2. Arch: maxillary incisors are wider with conical roots, mandibular ones narrow with ribbon roots; maxillary canines have stronger anatomy; mandibular premolars tilt lingually; maxillary molars have 3 roots, mandibular 2.
  3. Type: central or lateral, first or second (the traits in the earlier pages).
  4. Mesial and facial: find the landmark, such as the rounder distoincisal angle, the distal bulge of a canine, the maxillary first premolar's mesial concavity, the small distal cusp of a mandibular first molar, or the two buccal roots of a maxillary molar.
  5. Right or left: hold the facial toward you with the mesial at an imaginary midline; the side it lands on is the patient's side (the patient's right is on your left).

What's tested
  • Bond types and their strength, water's properties, pH, buffers and the bicarbonate system
  • Amino acid classes, the side-chain pKa values (histidine near 6), chirality and the four levels of protein structure
  • Collagen: Gly-X-Y, the triple helix, vitamin C–dependent hydroxylation, the synthesis steps inside and outside the cell, and the collagen diseases
  • Hemoglobin: T and R states, cooperativity, the Bohr effect, CO2 and 2,3-BPG, fetal hemoglobin, and myoglobin for contrast
  • Carbohydrates: aldoses and ketoses, epimers and anomers, the disaccharides (sucrose and caries), glycogen, glycoproteins and GAGs
  • Lipids: fatty acids, triglycerides, membrane lipids, cholesterol, lipoproteins, β-oxidation and lipogenesis
  • Nucleic acids: purines and pyrimidines, nucleoside versus nucleotide, base pairing, antiparallel strands, chromatin packing

Chemistry that the rest depends on

Covalent bonds (shared electrons) are the strongest; C–C and C–H are nonpolar, O–H is polar. The noncovalent forces, strongest to weakest, are ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds (a hydrogen on N, O or F attracted to another N, O or F) and van der Waals forces. Everything above a protein's primary structure is held by noncovalent forces, plus covalent disulfide bonds.

Water is polar, so it is a good solvent for polar and charged molecules and a poor one for nonpolar ones. It has a high specific heat (1 cal/g/°C), high surface tension from hydrogen bonding, ice is less dense than liquid water, and it is amphoteric. Blood pH is 7.35–7.45. A buffer resists pH change best when the pH equals its pKa; the bicarbonate system is the main blood buffer.

Amino acids and protein structure

An amino acid has an α carbon carrying an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a side chain (R). At physiological pH it is a zwitterion (NH3+ and COO−). All except glycine are chiral, and proteins use L amino acids (L and D name the configuration, not the direction a molecule turns polarized light). Peptide bonds are planar with partial double-bond character.

Histidine's pKa near 6 lets it gain or lose a proton near physiological pH, so it buffers and works in active sites (and in hemoglobin's Bohr effect). Only the aromatic amino acids (Phe, Tyr, Trp) absorb UV at 280 nm. Modified amino acids: hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine (collagen), γ-carboxyglutamate (vitamin K–dependent clotting factors), selenocysteine (selenoenzymes).

  • Primary: the amino acid sequence, joined by peptide bonds.
  • Secondary: backbone hydrogen bonds. The α-helix has 3.6 residues per turn (proline breaks helices); β-sheets are parallel or antiparallel (antiparallel is more stable); β-turns reverse the chain and are rich in proline and glycine.
  • Tertiary: the folded 3D shape, with hydrophobic residues buried inside and polar ones outside. Fibrous proteins (keratin, collagen) are strong and insoluble; globular proteins are soluble with a hydrophobic core.
  • Quaternary: several chains together (hemoglobin is a tetramer), which allows cooperativity and regulation. A single-chain protein has none.

Collagen

The most abundant protein in the body (about a third of it); type I is over 90% (bone, dentin, PDL, skin, tendon). Type II is cartilage, type III is reticular fibers, blood vessels and granulation tissue, type IV is basement membrane. The sequence repeats Gly-X-Y, X and Y often proline and hydroxyproline. Each chain is a left-handed helix; three wind into a right-handed triple helix (tropocollagen, about 300 nm). Glycine is every third residue because only glycine fits in the center of the triple helix.

Hemoglobin

Hemoglobin (α2β2) carries O2 on Fe2+ in heme: four porphyrin nitrogens, a histidine as the fifth ligand, O2 as the sixth. Without O2 the iron sits out of the heme plane; binding pulls it into the plane, breaks salt bridges and shifts the tetramer from the T (tense, deoxy) to the R (relaxed, oxy) state. That makes binding cooperative and the curve sigmoidal, so hemoglobin loads O2 in the lungs and unloads it in tissues. Myoglobin is a monomer (storage) with a hyperbolic curve and higher affinity.

Most heme is in red blood cells. Sickle cell disease comes from glutamate → valine at position 6 of β-globin (HbS); thalassemias make too little of one chain.

Carbohydrates

Monosaccharides are aldoses (aldehyde) or ketoses (ketone). Epimers differ at one carbon: glucose and galactose at C-4, glucose and mannose at C-2. Ring closure makes a hemiacetal (six-membered pyranose, five-membered furanose) and a new chiral C-1, giving the α and β anomers, which interconvert. Enantiomers are mirror images. Sugars with a free anomeric carbon are reducing sugars. A sugar's carbonyl can join a protein's amino group as a Schiff base (nonenzymatic glycation, the basis of HbA1c).

  • Sucrose (glucose + fructose): the substrate Streptococcus mutans turns into sticky extracellular glucans (dextran) for plaque.
  • Lactose (galactose + glucose), split by lactase; maltose (glucose + glucose), from starch digestion.
  • Glycogen: glucose in α-1,4 chains with α-1,6 branches (storage). Cellulose: β-1,4 (plants).
  • N-linked glycans go on asparagine in the ER (dolichol carrier); O-linked on serine or threonine in the Golgi. Mannose-6-phosphate sends enzymes to lysosomes.
  • Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs): unbranched repeating disaccharides with an amino sugar; hyaluronic acid, heparin (anticoagulant), chondroitin and keratan sulfate. On a core protein they form proteoglycans, which hold water as the ECM's gel.

Lipids

Mostly hydrocarbon, so they dissolve in nonpolar solvents. Fatty acids: saturated (no double bonds, pack tightly) or unsaturated (cis double bonds kink the chain and lower the melting point). Triglycerides are glycerol with three fatty acids joined by ester bonds: the main energy store, in adipose tissue. Phospholipids are amphipathic and form the bilayer; glycolipids sit on the outer leaflet; cholesterol steadies fluidity; steroids have four fused rings. Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from enterocytes through the lymph; LDL carries cholesterol to tissues; HDL brings it back to the liver.

Lipolysis splits triglycerides (lipases). Fatty acids enter the mitochondrion on the carnitine shuttle and undergo β-oxidation in the matrix to acetyl-CoA. Lipogenesis runs in the cytosol of the liver when carbohydrate is plentiful; acetyl-CoA leaves the mitochondrion as citrate.

Nucleic acids

A nucleotide is a pentose, a phosphate and a base; a nucleoside lacks the phosphate. Purines (adenine, guanine) have two rings and break down to uric acid; pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have one. Phosphodiester bonds link the 5′ phosphate of one nucleotide to the 3′ OH of the next. The two DNA strands are antiparallel and complementary: A–T with two hydrogen bonds, G–C with three (so GC-rich DNA is harder to separate). DNA wraps around an octamer of histones as the nucleosome, then the 10 nm "beads on a string", the 30 nm fiber and the mitotic chromosome. Bacterial DNA is one circular, supercoiled chromosome in the nucleoid, plus plasmids.
full.f1-cells:
What's tested
  • Prokaryotic versus eukaryotic cells; each organelle's job and its "address tag" (signal peptide, mannose-6-phosphate, ubiquitin, nuclear localization signal)
  • The cytoskeleton, the cell cycle and apoptosis (caspases)
  • Membrane structure, diffusion, osmosis, tonicity and the reflection coefficient
  • Passive, primary active and secondary active transport (cotransport and countertransport)
  • Equilibrium potentials (Nernst), the resting potential and the Na+/K+ pump
  • The phases of the action potential, refractory periods, myelin, and the effect of potassium, tetrodotoxin and local anesthetics
  • Electrical and chemical synapses, the main neurotransmitters, EPSPs and IPSPs, the neuromuscular junction, and the toxins and diseases that act there

Cells and organelles

Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles: a nucleoid, a peptidoglycan wall, often flagella and pili. Eukaryotes (human cells, fungi, parasites) compartmentalize work in membrane-bound organelles. Every cell has a plasma membrane.

Endocytosis takes material in: phagocytosis (pseudopods engulf large particles into phagosomes), pinocytosis (small pits take in fluid) and receptor-mediated endocytosis (ligand-bound receptors in coated pits, as for LDL). Exocytosis sends material out.

The cytoskeleton is held together by noncovalent bonds so it can rebuild quickly. Microtubules (tubulin) are the most rigid: motor-protein highways, the mitotic spindle and the core of cilia and flagella. Actin filaments (microfilaments) support microvilli, the cell surface and cell movement. Intermediate filaments (keratin-related, varying by cell type) are rope-like, take tension and link the nucleus to the membrane. The extracellular matrix (collagen, elastin, proteoglycans, hyaluronic acid, adhesive proteins) attaches through integrins.

The cell cycle: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (checks and repair), M (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis). Apoptosis is programmed, non-inflammatory death carried out by caspases; the plasma membrane goes last. Too much cell death or too little (cancer) causes disease.

Membranes and transport

The fluid mosaic membrane: a phospholipid bilayer with integral (transmembrane) and peripheral proteins, cholesterol (cuts permeability to small molecules), carbohydrates on the outer face only, and lipid rafts rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids. The two leaflets differ in composition.

Diffusion is passive and downhill; for an uncharged solute its rate rises with surface area and gradient and falls with membrane thickness (Fick). Osmosis is water moving toward the side with more osmotically active particles. Osmotic pressure depends on the number of particles (NaCl gives two, glucose one) and on how well they cross, the reflection coefficient σ: 0 means the solute crosses freely and draws no water; 1 means it is impermeant and exerts its full pressure.

  • Hypotonic solution: water enters, the cell swells (and can lyse). Hypertonic: water leaves, the cell shrinks. Isotonic: no change.

Epithelial cells sit on a basal lamina, are joined by tight junctions and move solutes in one direction (vectorial transport), through the cells or between them (paracellular).

Membrane potentials

Bulk solutions are electrically neutral; only a thin layer of charge at the membrane is separated (the membrane acts as a capacitor, ion channels as resistors). The equilibrium potential of an ion is the voltage that balances its concentration gradient: E = (61.5/z) log([out]/[in]) at body temperature, so a tenfold gradient gives about 60 mV (the class used ±60 mV). E(K+) is about −90 mV and E(Na+) about +60 mV. At rest the membrane is most permeable to K+ through leak channels, so the resting potential (about −70 mV) sits close to E(K+). The Na+/K+ pump keeps the gradients; its own electrogenic current adds only a few millivolts.

The action potential

  • Threshold (about −55 mV): a stimulus opens enough voltage-gated Na+ channels that Na+ entry depolarizes the membrane further and opens more (positive feedback).
  • Upstroke and overshoot toward E(Na+): about 100 mV above rest. All-or-none: a bigger stimulus doesn't make a bigger action potential.
  • Repolarization: Na+ channels inactivate and slower voltage-gated K+ channels open, so K+ leaves.
  • Afterhyperpolarization: K+ channels are slow to close, so the potential dips below rest.

During the absolute refractory period Na+ channels are inactivated and no stimulus can fire another action potential. In the relative refractory period some Na+ channels are still inactivated and K+ channels are still open, so only a larger-than-normal stimulus works. Myelin speeds conduction: the action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next (saltatory conduction); larger diameter also speeds it.

Hyperkalemia depolarizes the resting membrane, which inactivates Na+ channels and lowers excitability (dangerous for the heart). Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels from outside, so threshold is never reached. Local anesthetics cross the axon membrane in their uncharged form, then the charged form blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels from the cytoplasmic side. In inflamed, acidic tissue more of the drug is charged outside the nerve and less gets in, so the block is weaker.

Synapses and neurotransmitters

A neuron has dendrites (input), a cell body (integration), an axon (conduction) and terminals (output). Electrical synapses pass current through gap junctions: very fast, two-way, mostly excitatory (cardiac and some smooth muscle). Chemical synapses are more common and can excite or inhibit: the action potential opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the terminal, Ca2+ triggers vesicle fusion, transmitter crosses the cleft and binds receptors. Ionotropic receptors are ion channels; metabotropic receptors are G protein–coupled. Small-molecule transmitters are made and packaged in the terminal; neuropeptides are made in the cell body.

EPSPs depolarize (Na+ entry, usually glutamate); IPSPs hyperpolarize (Cl− entry, usually GABA or glycine). Both are graded and local and add up (summation) at the axon hillock.

GlutamateMain excitatory transmitter of brain and spinal cord (three ionotropic receptors); recycled as glutamine
GABAMain inhibitory transmitter of the brain (ionotropic Cl− channel; metabotropic receptor acting on K+)Benzodiazepines enhance the Cl− channel

What's tested
  • Replication: semiconservative, leading and lagging strands, the enzymes and their jobs, prokaryotes versus eukaryotes, telomeres and telomerase
  • RNA: how it differs from DNA, the RNA types and their share of cell RNA, ribosome sizes, nucleases
  • Prokaryotic transcription: RNA polymerase subunits (σ), promoters, termination, the lac operon
  • Eukaryotic transcription: the three RNA polymerases, TFIID and the TATA box, enhancers, acetylation and methylation
  • RNA processing: cap, splicing, poly(A) tail, editing, export and decay
  • Translation: tRNA charging, the ribosome's A, P and E sites, factors, wobble, bacterial versus eukaryotic
  • Mendel's laws, modes of inheritance and pedigree risk; types of mutation and the classic mutation diseases
  • Oncogenes, tumor suppressors (two hits), DNA repair genes, benign versus malignant

DNA replication

Replication is semiconservative (each daughter has one old and one new strand) and happens in S phase. It starts at origins (one in bacteria, many in eukaryotes) and runs both ways from each. Polymerases add only to a free 3′-OH, so new DNA grows 5′ → 3′. The leading strand is made continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand is made away from it in short Okazaki fragments, each also built 5′ → 3′.

ProteinJob
Helicase (DnaB)Breaks the hydrogen bonds and opens the fork
Single-strand binding proteinKeeps the separated strands from re-annealing
Topoisomerase (gyrase in bacteria)Relieves the overwinding ahead of the fork (fluoroquinolones block gyrase)
Primase (DnaG)Lays down the RNA primer polymerases need
DNA polymerase III (bacteria)Main replicating enzyme; 3′ → 5′ exonuclease proofreading
DNA polymerase I (bacteria)Removes RNA primers (5′ → 3′ exonuclease) and fills the gaps
DNA ligaseSeals the nicks between Okazaki fragments (phosphodiester bond)

Eukaryotes: many origins, slower (50–100 nucleotides a second versus about 1,000 in bacteria), polymerase α (with primase) starts each fragment, δ and ε do most of the copying and proofread, PCNA is the sliding clamp, RNase H (with a flap nuclease) removes primers. Linear chromosomes lose a little at each end every round, so they end in telomeres (TTAGGG repeats in humans). Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase carrying its own RNA template, extends them; it is active in germ and stem cells and in most cancers.

The nature of RNA

RNA has ribose with a 2′-OH (so dilute base hydrolyzes it, while DNA resists), uses uracil instead of thymine and is usually single-stranded.

RNAShare of cell RNAJob
rRNAAbout 80%Scaffold and catalyst of the ribosome (ribosomes are about two-thirds rRNA)
tRNAAbout 15%Carries one amino acid on its 3′ CCA end; cloverleaf in 2D, L-shaped in 3D
mRNAAbout 2–5%Carries the code; bacterial mRNA lasts minutes
snRNASmallSplicing (in snRNPs)
Small non-coding RNAs (miRNA, siRNA)SmallPost-transcriptional silencing

Ribosomes: bacterial 70S = 30S (16S rRNA) + 50S (23S + 5S); eukaryotic 80S = 40S (18S) + 60S (28S, 5.8S, 5S). Bacterial mRNA is polycistronic (several proteins per message) with no introns; eukaryotic mRNA codes one protein and is spliced.

Prokaryotic transcription

One RNA polymerase makes all RNA. The holoenzyme (α2ββ′σ) starts transcription; σ recognizes the promoter's −35 (TTGACA) and −10 Pribnow box (TATAAT) sequences. β and β′ form the catalytic site; rifampin binds β. RNA polymerase needs no primer, builds 5′ → 3′, opens about 14 bp (closed → open complex), and after 7–12 nucleotides σ leaves and the core enzyme elongates. Termination is rho-dependent (rho, an ATP-dependent helicase) or intrinsic (a GC-rich hairpin followed by a run of U's, which pulls the RNA off).

The lac operon: lacZ, lacY, lacA share one promoter and operator. Negative control: the lacI repressor binds the operator; allolactose (from lactose) pulls it off. Positive control: when glucose is low, cAMP rises and the CAP–cAMP complex binds upstream, bends the DNA and recruits polymerase. Transcription is highest with lactose present and glucose absent; glucose and lactose together give only low expression (catabolite repression).

Eukaryotic transcription

DNA wraps histone octamers (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4; H1 links nucleosomes into the 30 nm fiber). Histones are rich in positive lysine and arginine.

  • RNA polymerase I: the large rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S) in the nucleolus. II: mRNA (and most snRNA), blocked by α-amanitin. III: tRNA and 5S rRNA.
  • General transcription factors build the pre-initiation complex; TFIID carries the TATA-binding protein, which binds the TATA box about 25 bp upstream.
  • Enhancers bind activators and work at a distance, upstream, downstream or in introns, in either orientation.
  • Histone acetylation loosens chromatin and turns genes on; DNA methylation (at CpG) recruits deacetylases and silences genes.

RNA processing (in the nucleus)

  • 5′ cap: 7-methylguanosine joined by a 5′–5′ triphosphate bond. Needed for export, translation and stability. RNA polymerase I and III products are uncapped.
  • Splicing starts while transcription continues. The spliceosome (snRNPs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) removes introns, which begin with GU and end with AG; the branch-point A attacks the 5′ splice site to form a lariat; the snRNAs catalyze the transesterifications. Alternative splicing gives several proteins from one gene.
  • Poly(A) tail: after the AAUAAA signal the transcript is cut 10–30 nucleotides downstream and poly(A) polymerase adds A's with no template. Poly(A)-binding protein protects the message and helps translation.
  • Editing changes single bases: A → I (ADAR) and C → U (apoB-48 in the gut).

Translation

Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach each amino acid to its tRNA's 3′ end using ATP, and an editing site removes a wrong, smaller amino acid: this charging is the main fidelity step. The genetic code has 64 codons: AUG starts (methionine; formyl-Met in bacteria) and UAA, UAG, UGA stop. The code is degenerate, and wobble at the codon's third base lets one tRNA read several codons. The reading frame is kept by starting at AUG and moving exactly three nucleotides each step.

The ribosome has three sites: A (incoming aminoacyl-tRNA), P (the tRNA holding the growing chain) and E (exit). The peptidyl transferase is the large subunit's rRNA, so the ribosome is a ribozyme.

BacteriaEukaryotes
Finding the startShine-Dalgarno sequence pairs with 16S rRNA, about 7 bases before AUGSmall subunit binds the 5′ cap (with the tail's help) and scans to the first AUG
Initiation factorsIF-1, IF-2 (a G protein carrying fMet-tRNA), IF-3Many eIFs
ElongationEF-Tu delivers tRNA, EF-Ts recharges it with GTP, EF-G translocateseEF1A, eEF1B, eEF2 (diphtheria toxin inactivates eEF2)

Classical genetics

Alleles are versions of a gene; the genotype is the allele combination (homozygous or heterozygous), the phenotype is the trait. Segregation: the two alleles separate into different gametes. Independent assortment: alleles of different (unlinked) genes sort independently. Multiply probabilities for "and", add them for "or". A monohybrid cross of heterozygotes gives 3:1; a dihybrid cross gives 9:3:3:1.

ModePedigree clueExamples
Autosomal dominantEvery generation; males and females alike; an affected child has an affected parent; 50% risk per childHuntington disease, familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor)
Autosomal recessiveSkips generations; unaffected carrier parents; 25% risk when both carrySickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis
X-linked recessiveMostly males; through carrier mothers; never father to sonHemophilia A (factor VIII)
X-linked dominantAn affected father passes it to all daughters and no sons
Y-linkedFather to every son
MitochondrialMother to all her children; never through the fatherEnergy-failure diseases of muscle and nerve

An unaffected sibling of someone with a recessive disease (both parents carriers) has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier.

Mutations

  • Point mutations: a transition swaps purine for purine or pyrimidine for pyrimidine; a transversion swaps a purine for a pyrimidine. By effect: silent (same amino acid), missense (another amino acid; sickle cell, Glu → Val), nonsense (premature stop, truncated protein), splice-site.
  • Insertions or deletions: not a multiple of three shifts the frame (frameshift); a multiple of three adds or removes whole amino acids (the common cystic fibrosis mutation removes one phenylalanine).
  • Expanding triplet repeats: more repeats mean earlier, more severe disease in later generations (anticipation): Huntington disease (CAG).
  • Spontaneous mutations come from replication errors; induced ones from chemicals (alkylating and intercalating agents) and radiation (ionizing radiation, including X-rays, breaks the backbone). Somatic mutations affect only the person's own cell line; germline mutations can pass to children.

Genetics of cancer

Cancer is uncontrolled growth from accumulated somatic mutations in cell-cycle genes. Benign tumors are encapsulated, well differentiated, slow and don't metastasize; malignant ones invade, are poorly differentiated, divide often and metastasize. Stages: hyperplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive cancer.

  • Oncogenes: a mutated proto-oncogene (normally pro-growth) becomes overactive ("stepping on the gas"); one mutated copy is enough. Activated by amplification (HER2/ErbB2 in breast cancer), a point mutation that leaves the protein always on (RAS), translocation making a fusion protein (BCR-ABL, chronic myeloid leukemia), or insertion next to a strong promoter.
  • Tumor suppressors ("removing the brakes"): both copies must be lost, Knudson's two-hit hypothesis. RB (retinoblastoma), p53 (stops the cycle or triggers apoptosis after DNA damage; abnormal in over half of cancers), APC (colon).
  • DNA repair genes: BRCA1/2 (double-strand break repair; inherited as a dominant risk, though each cell still needs a second hit).
  • An inherited first hit is in every cell, so cancer comes earlier and more often. High-risk HPV (types 16 and 18) causes oropharyngeal and cervical cancer: its E6 protein degrades p53 and E7 inactivates RB.
  • Cancer cells lose contact inhibition, turn on telomerase, induce angiogenesis (VEGF from oxygen-starved cells) and spread by blood, lymph and nerves.
full.f2-genpath:
What's tested
  • Reversible versus irreversible cell injury, and the nuclear changes of cell death
  • The six necrosis patterns and the organ or disease each one belongs to (coagulative heart and kidney, liquefactive brain and abscess, caseous TB, fat necrosis pancreas)
  • Apoptosis versus necrosis, and the intrinsic (cytochrome c) and extrinsic (Fas) pathways, which both end in caspases
  • How cells are injured: ATP loss in hypoxia, free radicals and the enzymes that clear them, reperfusion injury
  • The four adaptations with an example of each, intracellular accumulations, and dystrophic versus metastatic calcification
  • Acute inflammation (vascular changes, exudate versus transudate, leukocyte recruitment) and chronic inflammation (M1 and M2 macrophages, granulomas, repair and scar problems, acute-phase proteins)
  • Neoplasia: naming, benign versus malignant, grade versus stage

Cell injury: reversible or not

Reversible injury goes back to normal if the cause is removed. The first sign is cell swelling (the ATP-driven sodium pump fails and water follows sodium in). Others: plasma membrane blebs, dilated ER with ribosomes falling off, swollen mitochondria, fatty change, myelin figures and clumped chromatin. The organ is heavier and firmer.

Irreversible injury ("the point of no return") comes from four failures: mitochondria can't make ATP again, membranes lose integrity, lysosomal enzymes leak and digest the cell, and DNA and chromatin break down. The nucleus shows it: pyknosis (shrinks and darkens), karyorrhexis (fragments) and karyolysis (fades). The changes are seen in order: biochemical (enzymes such as troponin leak into blood), then electron microscopy, then light microscopy, then the gross organ.

Mitochondria are the first organelle hit by hypoxia: less oxidative phosphorylation means less ATP, so the cell switches to anaerobic glycolysis, lactic acid builds up and the pH falls (that is what clumps the chromatin).

MechanismKey points
Hypoxia and ischemiaIschemia = blocked blood flow; hypoxia = too little oxygen. ATP falls, protein synthesis stops
Oxidative stressFree radicals (superoxide, hydroxyl radical, peroxynitrite) made faster than removed. Cleared by superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase
Ischemia-reperfusionRestoring blood flow to viable tissue adds injury (radicals, neutrophils), e.g., after a transplant
ToxinsDirect-acting bind a vital molecule; latent ones are converted (often by P450) to reactive metabolites that make radicals
ER stressMisfolded proteins pile up; the unfolded protein response adds chaperones, and if that fails the cell dies by apoptosis
DNA damageRadiation, chemotherapy, radicals. p53 arrests the cycle to repair or triggers apoptosis

Necrosis patterns

PatternWhat it looks likeClassic setting

LiquefactiveTissue digested to fluid by neutrophil enzymes; pusBacterial or fungal abscess (e.g., dental abscess); brain infarct

Apoptosis

ApoptosisNecrosis
CellShrinks, breaks into apoptotic bodiesSwells, membrane ruptures, contents leak
InflammationNoneYes
WhenPhysiologic (tissue turnover, end of an immune response) or pathologicAlways pathologic
  • Intrinsic (mitochondrial): loss of survival signals, DNA damage or radiation → sensors block BCL2 → mitochondrial channels open → cytochrome c leaks out → caspases.
  • Extrinsic (death receptor): Fas ligand on a cytotoxic T cell binds Fas on the target cell → death domain adaptors → caspases.
  • Both end in caspase activation. Related forms: autophagy (the cell eats its own organelles in starvation), necroptosis (features of both), pyroptosis (inflammatory, releases IL-1).

Adaptations, accumulations, calcification

AdaptationMeaningPhysiologicPathologic
HypertrophyBigger cells (cells that can't divide)Uterus in pregnancy, weightlifter's muscleHeart muscle in hypertension
HyperplasiaMore cells; stops when the stimulus stopsBreast at puberty, liver after partial removalEndometrium with unopposed estrogen, prostate, HPV warts
AtrophySmaller cells (less workload, nerve, blood, nutrition or hormone; aging)MenopauseBrain in dementia
MetaplasiaOne adult cell type replaced by another, through reprogrammed stem cells—Columnar to squamous in a smoker's bronchus; can lead to cancer
  • Accumulations: lipid (liver steatosis from alcohol, diabetes, obesity), protein, glycogen (storage diseases such as Pompe disease, acid alpha-glucosidase missing), pigments. Endogenous pigments: lipofuscin (wear and tear), melanin, hemosiderin. Exogenous: carbon (anthracosis), tattoo ink.
  • Dystrophic calcification: normal serum calcium, deposits in damaged tissue (atheroma, old heart valves, necrosis).
  • Metastatic calcification: high serum calcium (hyperparathyroidism, bone destruction, vitamin D excess, kidney failure), deposits in normal tissue (vessels, kidneys, lungs, stomach).

Acute inflammation

Causes: infection, necrosis, foreign bodies, immune reactions. Sentinel cells recognize microbes (toll-like receptors), damaged cells (DAMPs) and complement. Vessels: brief vasoconstriction, then histamine vasodilation (heat, redness), then leaky endothelium (fast, short-lived), then stasis. Exudate = high protein and cells (inflammation; pus if full of neutrophils). Transudate = low protein, few cells (high hydrostatic or low oncotic pressure, e.g., heart failure).

  1. Rolling: selectins.
  2. Firm adhesion: integrins (on the leukocyte) binding ICAM-1 and VCAM-1.
  3. Transmigration: PECAM-1 (CD31).
  4. Chemotaxis: chemokines, C5a, leukotriene B4, bacterial products.

Neutrophils dominate early, then macrophages. They kill by phagocytosis (phagosome fuses with lysosome) with reactive oxygen species (NADPH oxidase), nitrogen species and lysosomal enzymes. Outcomes: resolution, scarring, or chronic inflammation. Patterns: serous (blister), fibrinous (body-cavity linings; can leave adhesions), purulent, abscess (pus walled off), ulcer (sloughed surface, common in mucosa).

Chronic inflammation and repair

  • Causes: persistent infection, autoimmune or allergic disease, long toxic exposure. Histology: lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells, tissue destruction and fibrosis (acute = neutrophils, tissue preserved).
  • M1 (classical) macrophages: switched on by microbial products and IFN-γ from CD4 T cells; make ROS, NO, IL-1, TNF, IL-6, IL-12; kill microbes. M2 (alternative): switched on by IL-4 and IL-13; secrete IL-10 and TGF-β; repair, new vessels, collagen. Eosinophils fight parasites; mast cells act in both acute and chronic inflammation.
  • Granulomas: epithelioid macrophages and giant cells with a lymphocyte rim. Immune granulomas need T cells (caseating in TB; noncaseating in Crohn disease); foreign-body granulomas form around sutures or splinters.
  • Repair: platelet plug → inflammation and proliferation with granulation tissue (new small vessels, fibroblasts, macrophages, little collagen) → remodeling (collagen gives tensile strength). Labile tissues (epithelium, marrow) always divide; stable (liver, kidney, pancreas) wait in G0; permanent (neurons, heart muscle) heal only by scar. First intention = clean apposed edges, little scar; second intention = large gap, more granulation and contraction.
  • Slow healing: infection, protein or vitamin C deficiency, steroids, pressure, poor blood flow (diabetes), foreign bodies. Scar problems: hypertrophic scar (raised, inside the wound, can regress), keloid (grows past the wound edges, doesn't regress), exuberant granulation, contracture.
  • Acute-phase response: fever (pyrogens → IL-1 and TNF → prostaglandins reset the hypothalamus), leukocytosis, and liver proteins: CRP (opsonin; heart-attack risk marker), fibrinogen (raises the sedimentation rate), serum amyloid A (secondary amyloidosis), hepcidin (holds iron: anemia of chronic disease).

Neoplasia

A neoplasm is monoclonal growth that ignores normal controls. Dysplasia is disordered, premalignant growth, usually in epithelium; it may not progress.

TissueBenignMalignant
MesenchymalFibroma, chondroma, lipomaSarcoma: fibrosarcoma, chondrosarcoma
EpithelialAdenoma (gland), papilloma (finger-like)Carcinoma: adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma
Rule breakersMalignant despite "-oma": lymphoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, seminoma, hepatoma. Mixed tumors: pleomorphic adenoma, teratoma
FeatureBenignMalignant
DifferentiationWell differentiatedVariable; anaplasia (bizarre nuclei, atypical mitoses, lost polarity)
GrowthSlowUsually faster; may outgrow its blood supply and necrose
InvasionFibrous capsule, pushesInfiltrates
MetastasisNeverThe hallmark: lymphatic, blood, seeding of body cavities
  • Clinical: cachexia; paraneoplastic syndromes (about 10-15% of patients: endocrine, nerve, muscle, blood).
  • Diagnosis: biopsy, exfoliative cytology (Pap smear, brush), fine-needle aspiration. Tumor markers screen or follow a tumor; they don't diagnose it.
  • Grade = differentiation under the microscope (1 = well differentiated). Stage = extent: TNM (tumor size and invasion, nodes, distant metastasis), AJCC I-IV. Stage predicts prognosis better than grade.
full.f2-virology:
What's tested
  • What makes a virus a virus; enveloped versus naked viruses (stability, release by budding or lysis)
  • The Baltimore classes, which viruses bring their own RNA polymerase or reverse transcriptase, and the six steps of the life cycle
  • The human herpesviruses HHV-1 to HHV-8: their diseases and where each stays latent
  • HPV, adenovirus, parvovirus B19 and the poxviruses; the RNA viruses (picornaviruses, coronavirus, measles, RSV, rabies, influenza drift and shift)
  • HIV: structure, entry, life cycle, stages and CD4 counts, tests, drug targets and oral signs
  • Hepatitis A to E (spread, chronicity, prevention) and hepatitis B serology
  • The oncogenic viruses and how they drive cancer (E6 and p53, E7 and Rb)

Virus basics

Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites: a DNA or RNA genome (never both) in a protein capsid, sometimes wrapped in a lipid envelope taken from the host membrane. They have no ribosomes and make no energy; they are assembled from parts, not divided, and pass through bacterial filters. Capsids are helical or icosahedral (20 faces). Viral attachment proteins bind host receptors, and the receptors set tropism (HIV gp120 needs CD4).

Life cycle: attachment → entry (naked viruses by endocytosis, enveloped ones by fusion) → uncoating → transcription, replication and translation (every virus uses host ribosomes) → assembly → release. DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus, except the poxviruses, which bring their own enzymes and replicate in the cytoplasm. Most RNA viruses stay in the cytoplasm. Viral growth follows a one-step curve, not exponential growth. Disease comes largely from the immune response (fever, rash, liver damage) plus direct killing of cells.

DNA viruses

  • Herpesviruses: large enveloped dsDNA. Immediate-early, early (DNA polymerase), then late (structural) genes; capsids assemble in the nucleus and bud through the nuclear envelope. The hallmark is latency: the genome sits as a circular episome until it reactivates. Drugs such as acyclovir (a nucleoside analog activated by the viral kinase) stop replication but can't touch latent virus.
  • HPV (papillomavirus): naked, circular dsDNA; warts and cancers; vaccine made from capsid protein. Polyomaviruses: large T antigen binds p53; serious only in the immunocompromised.
  • Adenovirus: naked, linear dsDNA; respiratory illness (military recruits), conjunctivitis ("shipyard eye"), gastroenteritis; tough in pools and on fomites; no antiviral.
  • Poxviruses: large, brick-shaped, cytoplasmic; smallpox (eradicated) and mpox, live vaccinia vaccine. Chickenpox is not a poxvirus.
  • Parvovirus B19: tiny naked ssDNA; grows in erythroid precursors in the marrow; fifth disease (slapped cheeks, rash from the immune response) in children, polyarthritis in adults; no vaccine.

RNA viruses

  • (+)ssRNA: the genome is mRNA, so it is infectious; RdRp is made first, then a (−) antigenome as template; replication in cytoplasmic "factories." Picornaviruses (naked, one polyprotein cut by viral proteases, VPg primer; shut off the host's cap-dependent translation): polio, rhinovirus, coxsackie A (herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease) and HAV. Coronaviruses: largest RNA viruses, enveloped; SARS-CoV-2 spike binds ACE2, cut by TMPRSS2; severe disease from immunothrombosis in the alveoli.
  • (−)ssRNA: all enveloped and helical; bring RdRp in the virion; genes near the start are read most. Measles (paramyxovirus; H and F; syncytia): very contagious, infectious before symptoms; cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, then rash; Koplik spots (blue-white specks on red buccal mucosa) come first; MMR live vaccine. RSV (G and F): bronchiolitis, the top cause of pneumonia in infants; maternal vaccine. Rabies (bullet-shaped rhabdovirus): bite, muscle, then retrograde axonal transport to the brain; Negri bodies; long incubation lets vaccine work after exposure.
  • Influenza (orthomyxovirus, 8 segments): hemagglutinin binds sialic acid (α2,6 in humans, α2,3 in birds); neuraminidase cuts it to release new virus (oseltamivir blocks it). Drift = small mutations, all viruses, yearly epidemics. Shift = segments swapped (reassortment), influenza A only, pandemics. Hemagglutination inhibition tests immunity.

Retroviruses and HIV

Enveloped, two copies of (+)ssRNA. Genes: gag (matrix, capsid p24, nucleocapsid), pol (protease, reverse transcriptase, integrase), env (gp120 binds, gp41 fuses), plus Tat, Rev and accessory proteins. Cycle: gp120 binds CD4 then a coreceptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) → fusion → reverse transcription to DNA (the provirus) → integrase inserts it → host RNA polymerase II transcribes → budding → protease cuts Gag so the particle matures and becomes infectious. Lentiviruses (HIV) have long incubations; the other retrovirus groups can cause cancer.

  • Spread: sex (more with genital lesions), mother to child (mostly at delivery; antiretrovirals prevent most), blood, shared needles. Needlestick risk is about 0.3%, versus about 1.8% for HCV and up to 30% for HBV.
  • Stages: acute (flu-like, rash, sore throat; CD4 drops and partly recovers) → clinical latency (years, CD4 falls, symptoms start below 500) → AIDS at CD4 below 200/µL (or an AIDS-defining illness); 5-10 years untreated.
  • Tests: antibody or antigen-antibody (p24) screening; plasma HIV RNA is the most sensitive and tracks treatment; CD4 count stages the disease.
  • Drugs target entry (CCR5), reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease (maturation) and capsid. Even treated patients carry more heart, liver, kidney and cancer risk; the gut lymphoid tissue never fully recovers.
  • Oral signs: candidiasis, oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV), Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), linear gingival erythema, necrotizing periodontal disease, HPV warts. No vaccine: fast mutation, sugar-shielded gp120, latency.
