What's tested
  • Gram-positive versus gram-negative envelopes and why they stain differently; acid-fast and wall-less exceptions
  • Structures outside the wall (capsule, pili, fimbriae, flagella, axial filaments), endospores, plasmids and 70S ribosomes as drug targets
  • Growth (binary fission, the growth curve), oxygen needs and the three ways to make ATP
  • Gene transfer: transformation, transduction and conjugation
  • Steps of pathogenesis, virulence factors, biofilms, and exotoxins versus endotoxin with the classic toxins
  • Staphylococcus (abscess, coagulase, MRSA, toxin syndromes) and Streptococcus (pyogenes, pneumoniae, mutans, viridans)
  • The gram-negative rods (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, E. coli, Vibrio, Salmonella, H. pylori), MacConkey agar, the red complex and the spirochetes

The envelope and the gram stain

Gram stain: crystal violet → iodine → alcohol (decolorizer) → safranin. The alcohol step decides it: a thick peptidoglycan wall holds the violet (gram-positive, purple); a thin wall under an outer membrane lets it wash out, and the counterstain makes it pink (gram-negative). Shape and arrangement (cocci in clusters or chains, rods, spirals) complete the first identification.

FeatureGram-positiveGram-negative
Peptidoglycan (NAG-NAM chains cross-linked by peptides)Thick, outside the one membraneThin, in the periplasm between two membranes

Outer membraneNoneYes: blocks many drugs; efflux pumps add resistance
EndotoxinNoYes (lipid A)

  • Exceptions: mycobacteria have waxy mycolic acids (acid-fast stain; resist drying, drugs and host defenses); Mycoplasma has no wall (sterols in its membrane); Chlamydia and Rickettsia are obligate intracellular and stain poorly. Archaea differ from bacteria by branched, ether-linked membrane lipids and no peptidoglycan.
  • Drug targets: wall building has three phases, all blockable. β-lactams block the transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins) that cross-link the wall; vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala ends. Resistance: β-lactamase, or PBP2a from the mecA gene (MRSA). 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S) are targets too; DNA itself isn't, but replication enzymes are.
  • The bacterial plasma membrane carries the respiratory chain (ATP is made there) and is negatively charged, so cationic antimicrobial peptides target it. The chromosome is one circular, supercoiled DNA; plasmids carry toxin and resistance genes.

Structures outside the wall

  • Capsule (glycocalyx; tight capsule or loose slime layer): antiphagocytic, aids adherence. S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, Klebsiella.
  • Fimbriae and pili (pilin): stick to host cells; the sex (conjugation) pilus links bacteria to pass DNA.
  • Flagella: filament (seen by TLR5), hook, basal body; mono-, amphi-, lopho- or peritrichous. Axial filaments in spirochetes run between the membranes and make the cell corkscrew into tissue.
  • Endospores (Bacillus, Clostridium): dormant, resist heat, drying, disinfectants and antibiotics; germinate when conditions improve. Inclusion bodies store glycogen and other materials.

Growth, metabolism, genetics

Bacteria divide by binary fission (wall remodeling, so β-lactams act here); DNA replication starts at one origin and runs both ways. Growth curve: lag → log (exponential; drugs work best) → stationary → death. Most pathogens like neutral pH (H. pylori survives the stomach) and body temperature (T. pallidum prefers cooler parts of the body).

  • Aerobic respiration: glycolysis, TCA cycle, electron transport; final electron acceptor O2; most ATP (about 38).
  • Anaerobic respiration: same pathways; final acceptor an inorganic or other molecule (nitrate, sulfate, carbonate, fumarate); less ATP.
  • Fermentation: glycolysis only; pyruvate is reduced (lactic acid, ethanol) to regenerate NAD+; 2 ATP.
  • No nucleus, so transcription and translation are coupled, and many ribosomes read one mRNA.

Pathogenesis

Commensals (the microbiome, largest in the gut) protect by crowding out pathogens, priming immunity and making vitamins. Opportunists (e.g., Candida) cause disease when defenses drop: children, the elderly, the immunocompromised, after antibiotics. Infections are exogenous (food, water, air, fomites, sex), endogenous (normal flora, reactivation) or nosocomial (a catheter-linked UTI). Routes: contact, droplets, fomites, airborne, fecal-oral, vectors. Endemic = steady low level; epidemic = sudden rise; pandemic = across continents.

  1. Adherence: adhesins, pili and fimbriae, flagella, capsule and biofilm sugars; keeps bacteria from being washed away.
  2. Invasion and damage: toxins and enzymes; secretion systems (mostly gram-negative) inject toxins.
  3. Colonization and spread: biofilms (matrix mostly water; on teeth, lenses, devices; resist drugs and immunity; disperse when nutrients run out) and iron scavenging (siderophores, hemolysins).

Extracellular bacteria must avoid opsonization by antibody and complement; intracellular ones must survive the phagolysosome. Polymicrobial synergy: S. mutans with C. albicans makes more acid and more caries. Antagonism: bacteriocins, hydrogen peroxide, nutrient hoarding, surface blanketing. Antibiotics act only on growing cells, not dormant persisters; alternatives include phage therapy and vaccines.

Gram-positive cocci

  • Staphylococci: clusters, catalase-positive, tough on fomites. S. aureus is coagulase-positive; carried by most people at some point; invades through broken skin or mucosa. Virulence: coagulase (fibrin wall), protein A (binds the Fc of antibody, blocking opsonization), leukocidin (kills neutrophils), hemolysins. When neutrophils can't clear it, the body walls it off: an abscess (liquefactive necrosis in a fibrous capsule) that must be drained, since drugs can't get in. About 90% of strains make β-lactamase; methicillin resists that, but mecA (PBP2a) gives MRSA, treated with vancomycin.
  • S. aureus toxin syndromes: food poisoning (preformed, heat-stable enterotoxin; vomiting within hours), scalded skin syndrome (exfoliative toxins split desmosomes; infants), toxic shock syndrome (TSST-1 superantigen, cytokine storm; hypotension kills).
  • S. epidermidis: coagulase-negative skin flora; biofilm on catheters, prosthetic joints and valves; sepsis, endocarditis.
  • Streptococci: chains, catalase-negative. S. pyogenes (group A): M protein (antiphagocytic), pharyngitis, scarlet fever (pyrogenic exotoxin), necrotizing fasciitis, strep toxic shock, then rheumatic fever (cross-reactive antibodies hit the heart) or glomerulonephritis. S. pneumoniae: lancet-shaped diplococci with a thick capsule; the leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia, often after a viral infection; lobar consolidation, high fever, productive (rusty) sputum; vaccines cover its capsule types. Viridans streptococci (S. mutans, S. sanguinis, S. mitis): caries and infective endocarditis after bleeding in the mouth. S. mutans is acidogenic and aciduric (works down to about pH 4.4) and its glucosyltransferases build sticky glucans from sucrose.

Gram-negative rods and spirochetes

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa: aerobic non-fermenter, everywhere in the environment, multidrug-resistant; a top nosocomial pathogen (devices, ventilators); cystic fibrosis lungs, burns, contact-lens keratitis; aminoglycosides.
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae: non-motile, thick capsule, mucoid lactose fermenter; necrotizing pneumonia with abscesses, sepsis, UTI. Acinetobacter: drug-resistant wound infections (war wounds). These are ESKAPE pathogens.
  • Gut: secretory diarrhea comes from toxins that cut sodium absorption and raise chloride secretion; treat with fluids. EHEC O157:H7: Shiga toxin (stops protein synthesis) → bloody diarrhea, hemolytic uremic syndrome (kidney failure). Vibrio cholerae: comma-shaped, salt water and shellfish; cholera toxin raises cAMP → massive watery diarrhea; rehydrate. Salmonella: typhoid (enteric) fever, enterocolitis, bacteremia. H. pylori: helical, flagellated, microaerophilic; ulcers and gastric cancer.
  • Identification: analytical profile strips (biochemical tests, fast species ID) and selective and differential media. MacConkey agar grows only gram-negatives; lactose fermenters are pink (E. coli, Klebsiella), non-fermenters pale (Pseudomonas, Salmonella).
  • Periodontitis: gram-negative subgingival anaerobes; the red complex = Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola. T. denticola (spirochete) damages tissue with proteases and hydrogen sulfide.
  • Borrelia burgdorferi: Lyme disease from ticks; rash, fever, facial palsy, meningitis, recurrent arthritis; early 2-week antibiotic course. Eye infections to know: gonococcal conjunctivitis, trachoma (Chlamydia), Pseudomonas keratitis.
full.ns-anat:
What's tested
  • Glial cells and what each does; neuron shapes and axonal transport
  • Meninges, the dural reflections, herniation, and the three intracranial bleeds (source, space, shape on imaging)
  • The cavernous sinus and what runs in it; CSF flow through the ventricles
  • Lobes, sulci and the key cortical areas (motor, sensory, Broca, Wernicke, visual, auditory)
  • Development: germ layers, neural tube and crest, brain vesicles, neural tube defects and folate
  • Spinal cord levels, horns and funiculi, blood supply and the cord syndromes; spinal reflexes
  • Brainstem parts, the "rule of 4", medial and lateral medullary syndromes
  • Each cranial nerve's job, its parasympathetic ganglion and the lesion sign; thalamic and hypothalamic nuclei

Cells of the nervous system

  • Neurons: most CNS neurons are multipolar; bipolar neurons sit in the retina and olfactory epithelium; pseudounipolar neurons are the sensory neurons of the dorsal root and cranial ganglia. Nissl bodies are the neuron's rough ER. Anterograde transport (kinesin) carries cargo from the soma to the terminal; retrograde transport (dynein) carries it back to the soma, the route rabies, herpes and tetanus toxin use.
  • Astrocytes: the most numerous glia; take up K⁺ and glutamate, help form the blood-brain barrier, regulate blood flow and synapse formation, form the glial scar.
  • Oligodendrocytes myelinate many CNS axons (lost in MS); Schwann cells myelinate one PNS axon segment each (lost in Guillain-Barré) and help peripheral nerves regenerate.
  • Microglia: CNS macrophages (from mesoderm, not neural tube). Ependymal cells line the ventricles; the choroid plexus makes CSF. Satellite cells surround cell bodies in PNS ganglia.
  • Nerve wrappings: epineurium (whole nerve), perineurium (each fascicle), endoneurium (each fiber).

Meninges, bleeds and the cavernous sinus

The dura has a periosteal layer (on the skull, sensory supply from CN V, blood from the middle meningeal artery) and a meningeal layer that folds into the falx cerebri, falx cerebelli, tentorium cerebelli and diaphragma sellae, and splits to form the venous sinuses. The tentorium divides the skull into supratentorial (cerebrum) and infratentorial (cerebellum, brainstem) spaces; the brainstem passes through the tentorial notch. Herniation is brain pushed past a dural fold by raised pressure (bleed, tumor, trauma). The arachnoid is avascular; its villi and granulations return CSF to the venous sinuses. The pia follows every gyrus.

The cavernous sinus sits beside the sella turcica. The internal carotid artery and CN VI run through the sinus itself; CN III, IV, V1 and V2 run in its lateral wall. A spreading infection from the face's "danger triangle" can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis, and CN VI is often the first nerve hit (the eye cannot abduct).

Ventricles and cortex

CSF flows: lateral ventricles → interventricular foramen → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → median and lateral apertures to the subarachnoid space (and the central canal). The central sulcus separates frontal from parietal lobe, the lateral (Sylvian) fissure separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes, and the parieto-occipital sulcus separates parietal from occipital. White matter: association fibers (front to back, same hemisphere), commissural fibers (side to side, corpus callosum) and projection fibers (up and down, internal capsule).

Development

  • Gastrulation makes three germ layers; the notochord (mesoderm) induces the overlying ectoderm to become the neural plate by blocking BMP.
  • Neurulation: the plate folds into the neural tube (brain and spinal cord); neural crest cells leave its edges and form the PNS: dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, and in the head much of the face and teeth (odontoblasts, dental pulp).
  • Failure of the anterior neuropore to close gives anencephaly; failure of the posterior neuropore gives spina bifida. Folic acid before and in early pregnancy lowers the risk.
  • Vesicles: prosencephalon → telencephalon (cerebrum, lateral ventricles) and diencephalon (third ventricle); mesencephalon → midbrain (aqueduct); rhombencephalon → metencephalon (pons, cerebellum) and myelencephalon (medulla), both on the fourth ventricle.
  • Later steps: neurogenesis and migration (failure: lissencephaly, smooth brain; periventricular heterotopia), synaptogenesis, then apoptosis and pruning, then myelination, which continues into adulthood. Synapse-refinement errors are linked to autism and schizophrenia.

Spinal cord and reflexes

31 segments (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal). The cord ends at about L1–L2 (conus medullaris); below it the cauda equina floats in the lumbar cistern, which is why a lumbar puncture goes in at L3–L5. Enlargements: cervical C5–T1 (arms), lumbosacral L1–S3 (legs). The dorsal horn is sensory, the ventral horn holds lower motor neurons, and the lateral horn (T1–L2) holds sympathetic preganglionic neurons. White matter shrinks toward the sacral cord. Blood: one anterior spinal artery (anterior two thirds: corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts) and two posterior spinal arteries (dorsal columns); the artery of Adamkiewicz (around T9–T12) feeds the lower cord.

  • Anterior cord syndrome (anterior spinal artery): bilateral weakness and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion; vibration and position sense spared.
  • Brown-Séquard (hemisection): ipsilateral weakness and loss of fine touch, vibration and proprioception; contralateral loss of pain and temperature starting a level or two below.
  • Stretch reflex: monosynaptic; muscle spindle → Ia afferent → alpha motor neuron, with reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist. Golgi tendon organ: Ib afferents sense tension and relax the muscle. Withdrawal reflex: polysynaptic, flexes the stimulated limb and extends the opposite one. Gamma motor neurons set spindle sensitivity. Motor units are recruited smallest (slow) to largest (fast): the size principle.

Brainstem and the rule of 4

Midbrain (from the mesencephalon) has the colliculi (superior: visual reflexes; inferior: auditory), substantia nigra, red nucleus and cerebral peduncles; the pons has the locus coeruleus (norepinephrine) and crossing pontine fibers; the medulla has the pyramids (corticospinal decussation), olives and the area postrema (vomiting center, weak blood-brain barrier). The reticular formation keeps us awake; raphe nuclei make serotonin.

Rule of 4: four nerves above the pons (I–IV), four in the pons (V–VIII), four in the medulla (IX–XII). Four medial "M" structures: motor (corticospinal) tract, medial lemniscus, medial longitudinal fasciculus, motor nuclei III, IV, VI, XII. Four lateral "S" structures: spinocerebellar tract, spinothalamic tract, sensory nucleus of V, sympathetic pathway.

  • Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal or vertebral branches): contralateral weakness and loss of vibration/position sense, tongue deviates toward the lesion (XII).
  • Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome (PICA or vertebral): ipsilateral face pain/temperature loss with contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), ipsilateral ataxia, vertigo, and hoarseness and trouble swallowing (nucleus ambiguus, IX and X).

Diencephalon

Thalamus: the relay for every sense except smell. VPL (body) and VPM (face, and taste) → somatosensory cortex; LGN → visual cortex; MGN → auditory cortex; VA/VL carry basal ganglia and cerebellar output to motor cortex; the anterior nucleus is part of the limbic (Papez) circuit. A thalamic stroke (PCA branches) causes contralateral loss of all sensation and can leave thalamic pain. Damage to the dorsomedial thalamus and mammillary bodies with thiamine deficiency gives Wernicke-Korsakoff (confusion, eye-movement palsy, ataxia, then amnesia). Hypothalamus: lateral nucleus hunger, ventromedial satiety, anterior heat loss, posterior heat conservation, suprachiasmatic clock, supraoptic and paraventricular make ADH and oxytocin. Epithalamus: the pineal gland makes melatonin.

What's tested
  • The dorsal column–medial lemniscus and spinothalamic pathways: neurons, where each crosses, what a lesion takes away
  • The trigeminal sensory system: its three nuclei, VPM, the jaw-jerk and corneal reflexes
  • Upper versus lower motor neuron signs; corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts; Guillain-Barré, myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton
  • Cerebellar divisions, peduncles, circuitry and signs (always on the same side)
  • Basal ganglia direct and indirect pathways; Parkinson and Huntington disease

The two sensory highways

Somatosensory pathways are three-neuron chains: first-order neuron in a dorsal root or cranial ganglion, second-order neuron in the cord or brainstem (its axon crosses), third-order neuron in the thalamus projecting to the postcentral gyrus through the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

Receptors: phasic (fast-adapting) ones signal change and vibration; tonic (slow-adapting) ones signal steady pressure. Small receptive fields (fingertips, lips) localize precisely. Pain reaches more than one place: VPL/VPM → S1 and S2 for where and how strong, medial thalamus → insula for the autonomic part, intralaminar nuclei → anterior cingulate for the emotional part.

The trigeminal system (the dental pathway)

  • First-order cell bodies sit in the trigeminal (semilunar) ganglion, with one exception: proprioceptive neurons from the muscles of mastication and the periodontal ligament have their cell bodies in the mesencephalic nucleus, the only primary sensory neurons inside the CNS.
  • Principal (main) sensory nucleus (pons): discriminative touch from the face and teeth, the face's version of the dorsal columns.
  • Spinal trigeminal nucleus (pons down to upper cervical cord): pain and temperature, the face's spinothalamic system. Its descending tract explains why a lateral medullary stroke takes away pain on the same side of the face.
  • Second-order axons cross and ascend as the trigeminothalamic tract to the VPM, then to the face area of the postcentral gyrus (lateral, low on the homunculus).
  • Reflexes: jaw jerk (monosynaptic, mesencephalic nucleus → motor nucleus of V; brisk with an upper motor neuron lesion above the pons); corneal reflex (afferent V1, efferent VII, both eyes blink).

Motor pathways: UMN and LMN

The motor system is a two-neuron chain. The upper motor neuron starts in the primary motor cortex (and premotor areas), runs through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, basilar pons and medullary pyramid. About 90% of corticospinal fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract (limbs); the rest form the anterior tract (trunk, both sides). The lower motor neuron sits in the ventral horn or a cranial nerve motor nucleus and goes to muscle. Corticobulbar fibers reach the cranial nerve motor nuclei, mostly from both hemispheres; the exceptions are the lower face (VII) and, in many people, the tongue (XII), which get mainly crossed input. So a cortical stroke weakens the contralateral lower face but spares the forehead.

SignUpper motor neuronLower motor neuron

A lesion above the decussation (cortex, internal capsule, brainstem) weakens the opposite side; a lesion in the cord weakens the same side. ALS has both UMN and LMN signs. Premotor lesions cause apraxia: strength is normal, but learned movements cannot be planned.

  • Guillain-Barré syndrome: autoimmune attack on peripheral myelin, often after a Campylobacter or viral infection; ascending flaccid weakness and tingling with lost reflexes; can involve the face and breathing. Treated with IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange.
  • Myasthenia gravis: antibodies against postsynaptic ACh receptors; fatigable weakness that worsens through the day, often ptosis, diplopia, and weak chewing and swallowing. Treated with cholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine). Dental: book short morning visits.
  • Lambert-Eaton syndrome: antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, often with small cell lung cancer; proximal weakness that improves with use.

Cerebellum

  • Vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe): balance and eye movements; damage gives nystagmus and a wide-based, unsteady stance.
  • Spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate zone): posture and tone; damage gives truncal ataxia and gait problems.
  • Cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres): planning skilled limb movement; damage gives limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria (past-pointing) and dysdiadochokinesia (cannot alternate fast movements), and slurred speech.

Peduncles: superior (midbrain, mainly output), middle (pons, input from cortex through the pontine nuclei), inferior (medulla, input from the spinocerebellar tracts and the inferior olive). Cortex layers: molecular, Purkinje, granular. Purkinje cells are the only output of the cerebellar cortex and are inhibitory (GABA), as are basket and stellate cells; mossy fibers, climbing fibers (from the inferior olive) and granule cells are excitatory (glutamate). Deep nuclei: dentate, emboliform and globose (interposed), fastigial. Because the pathway crosses twice (into the cerebellum through the pons, out through the superior peduncle, then back in the pyramids), cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion. Arteries: SCA, AICA, PICA.

Basal ganglia, Parkinson and Huntington

Loop: cortex → striatum (caudate and putamen) → globus pallidus internus/substantia nigra pars reticulata → VA/VL thalamus → cortex. The output (GPi) is inhibitory on the thalamus. The direct pathway inhibits GPi, freeing the thalamus: it promotes movement. The indirect pathway (through GPe and the subthalamic nucleus) strengthens GPi: it inhibits movement. Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta excites the direct pathway through D1 and inhibits the indirect pathway through D2, so both actions promote movement.

  • Parkinson disease (hypokinetic): loss of nigral dopamine neurons with Lewy bodies (α-synuclein). Signs appear after most striatal dopamine is gone: resting tremor ("pill-rolling"), rigidity (cogwheel), bradykinesia, postural instability. Early non-motor signs: lost smell, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder (strongest predictor), depression, orthostatic hypotension. The drugs are in the disease section.
  • Huntington disease (hyperkinetic): autosomal dominant CAG repeat in the HTT gene (chromosome 4); 40 or more repeats always cause disease; repeats lengthen in sperm, so onset comes earlier in the next generation (anticipation, mostly through the father). Loss of GABA neurons in the caudate (indirect pathway) → chorea, with psychiatric change (often first), dementia, dysarthria and dysphagia; death is often from aspiration pneumonia. Chorea is treated with VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine) or antipsychotics. A subthalamic nucleus lesion causes hemiballismus on the opposite side.

Cerebral circulation and stroke

Anterior circulation: internal carotid → ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, then ACA and MCA. Posterior circulation: vertebrals (PICA) → basilar (AICA, SCA, pontine branches) → PCA. The circle of Willis joins them through the anterior and posterior communicating arteries; berry aneurysms favor the anterior communicating artery. About 80% of strokes are ischemic and 20% hemorrhagic. Recognize with FAST (face, arm, speech, time).

Treatment: for ischemic stroke, IV thrombolysis (tPA) within about 4.5 hours once bleeding is ruled out by CT, and clot retrieval for large-vessel blockage; afterward aspirin or other antiplatelet drugs, anticoagulants for atrial fibrillation, statins and risk-factor control (hypertension is the biggest modifiable one). Dental points: the patient is often on antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs (control bleeding locally instead of stopping them), elective care traditionally waits until the patient is stable, often about 6 months; keep visits short and watch blood pressure.
full.ns-phys:
What's tested
  • Why the resting membrane potential sits near the K⁺ equilibrium potential; the Nernst equation; what changing [K⁺] does
  • The ion channels before, during and after an action potential; refractory periods; myelin and saltatory conduction
  • Electrical versus chemical synapses; Ca²⁺ and vesicle release; ionotropic versus metabotropic receptors; NMDA; EPSPs and IPSPs
  • Local anesthetics: structure and class, mechanism, pKa and onset, lipid solubility and potency, protein binding and duration, metabolism, allergy, toxicity (LAST)
  • General anesthesia: its components, how the drugs act (GABA-A, NMDA), MAC, the levels of sedation

Resting membrane potential

At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to anything else, so the resting potential (about −65 to −70 mV in a neuron) sits close to EK (about −90 mV). A small Na⁺ leak pulls it a little more positive. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) keeps the gradients; it does not itself create most of the voltage. The Nernst equation gives one ion's equilibrium potential (no net movement): E = (61/z) log([out]/[in]) at body temperature, so a tenfold gradient gives about 60 mV. Raising extracellular K⁺ (hyperkalemia) makes EK less negative and depolarizes the cell. Equal concentrations on both sides give E = 0. The Goldman equation combines all ions by their relative permeability. Typical values: ENa ≈ +60 mV, EK ≈ −90 mV, ECa ≈ +130 mV, ECl ≈ −70 mV.

The action potential

  • Threshold: a stimulus depolarizes the membrane enough to open voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.
  • Upstroke: Na⁺ rushes in; the membrane heads toward ENa and overshoots 0 mV.
  • Repolarization: Na⁺ channels inactivate and the slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ leaves.
  • Afterhyperpolarization: K⁺ channels close slowly, so the membrane dips below rest.
  • Absolute refractory period: Na⁺ channels are inactivated; no stimulus can fire the cell. Relative refractory period: a stronger stimulus can.

Passive properties: the membrane is a capacitor (time constant τ = RmCm); the length constant says how far a signal spreads before fading. Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so current runs farther and faster; the action potential regenerates only at the nodes of Ranvier, where Na⁺ channels cluster (saltatory conduction). Bigger diameter and more myelin mean faster conduction: Aα (proprioception) > Aβ (touch) > Aδ (sharp pain, cold) > C (unmyelinated, dull pain, warmth). Demyelination (MS in the CNS, Guillain-Barré in the PNS) slows or blocks conduction.

Synapses

Electrical synapses are gap junctions: very fast, two-way, used where cells must fire together. Chemical synapses (the usual kind, a 20–50 nm cleft) work in steps: the action potential opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the terminal, Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion through the SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25), transmitter crosses the cleft and binds receptors, and it is removed by diffusion, reuptake or enzymes (acetylcholinesterase for ACh). Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks ACh release (flaccid paralysis; used cosmetically and for bruxism and spasticity); tetanus toxin blocks release of the inhibitory transmitters glycine and GABA (spastic paralysis, lockjaw). The neuromuscular junction is "fail-safe": one motor neuron action potential always fires the muscle fiber.

  • Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated channels: fast (nicotinic ACh, AMPA, NMDA, GABA-A, glycine). Metabotropic receptors are G-protein-coupled: slower, longer-lasting (muscarinic ACh, adrenergic, dopamine, most peptide receptors, GABA-B). The receptor, not the transmitter, decides the effect: ACh excites skeletal muscle (nicotinic) but slows the heart (muscarinic).
  • NMDA receptor: a coincidence detector. It needs glutamate (and glycine) plus depolarization to push out its Mg²⁺ block; it lets in Ca²⁺, the trigger for long-term potentiation. Ketamine blocks it.
  • EPSP: depolarization toward threshold (Na⁺ in through mixed cation channels). IPSP: hyperpolarization or clamping toward ECl or EK (GABA-A and glycine open Cl⁻ channels). EPSPs and IPSPs add up in time and space at the axon hillock.
  • Small transmitters (glutamate, GABA, amines, ACh) release with single action potentials; neuropeptides need bursts.
  • Gray type I synapses are asymmetric and excitatory; type II are symmetric and inhibitory.

Local anesthetics

Every local anesthetic has a lipophilic aromatic ring, an intermediate chain (ester or amide link) and a hydrophilic amine. Naming trick: amides have an "i" before "-caine" (lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, articaine, bupivacaine); esters do not (procaine, benzocaine, tetracaine, chloroprocaine, cocaine).

Mechanism: the drug is injected as a salt and exists as uncharged base and charged cation. The uncharged base crosses the nerve sheath and membrane; inside, the cation binds the voltage-gated Na⁺ channel from the inner side. The rate of depolarization falls until threshold is never reached, so no action potential is conducted. Resting potential and threshold are unchanged. Binding is use-dependent: open and inactivated channels bind more, so fast-firing nerves block first. Small and myelinated fibers block first (sharp pain, temperature, then touch and pressure, then motor). Block spreads from the outer (mantle) bundles inward to the core, so proximal teeth go numb before distal ones.

PropertyControlsRule
pKaOnsetThe closer the pKa to tissue pH (7.4), the more uncharged base and the faster the onset. Inflamed tissue is acidic, so more drug is trapped as cation and the block can fail.
Lipid solubilityPotencyMore lipid-soluble = more potent (and more toxic): bupivacaine, tetracaine
Protein bindingDurationMore bound = longer: short procaine and chloroprocaine; intermediate lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, articaine; long bupivacaine, ropivacaine, tetracaine
VasoactivityDuration and toxicityMost dilate vessels (cocaine constricts); epinephrine slows uptake, lengthens the block and lowers blood levels
StereochemistryCardiac toxicityR isomers bind cardiac Na⁺ channels more: racemic bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic; ropivacaine is the pure S isomer
  • Esters: hydrolyzed in plasma by pseudocholinesterase; the metabolite PABA causes most true local anesthetic allergies. Patients with atypical pseudocholinesterase have long-lasting effects (and prolonged succinylcholine paralysis).
  • Amides: metabolized in the liver (CYP450); metabolites leave by the kidney. Caution in severe liver disease. True amide allergy is very rare; reactions are usually to the preservative methylparaben or to sodium bisulfite, the antioxidant in cartridges with a vasoconstrictor. No cross-allergy between the classes.
  • Articaine: an amide with a thiophene ring and an ester side chain, so most of it is broken down in plasma (short half-life).
  • Prilocaine (and benzocaine) can cause methemoglobinemia (prilocaine's metabolite is o-toluidine): cyanosis that oxygen does not fix; treated with methylene blue.
  • Dental arithmetic: 2% lidocaine = 20 mg/mL, so a 1.8 mL cartridge holds 36 mg; 1:100,000 epinephrine = 0.01 mg/mL, 0.018 mg per cartridge.

LAST (local anesthetic systemic toxicity), usually from intravascular injection or overdose: the CNS goes first: circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness, twitching, then seizures, then CNS depression; at higher levels the heart: hypotension, arrhythmia, arrest. Potency tracks toxicity; acidosis makes it worse. Treatment: stop injecting, airway, oxygen, a benzodiazepine for seizures, and 20% lipid emulsion (the "lipid sink").

General anesthesia

General anesthesia combines unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia and immobility (akinesia), plus control of autonomic reflexes. There is no single "off switch" in the brain; the drugs slow communication between neurons by enhancing inhibition (most act at GABA-A receptors, raising Cl⁻ current: propofol, etomidate, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, volatile agents) or blocking excitation (ketamine and nitrous oxide block NMDA receptors). Arousal (ascending reticular activating system) and awareness (corticothalamic networks) are separate: ketamine disrupts awareness while arousal is preserved ("dissociative"), keeps airway reflexes and breathing, raises blood pressure and can cause emergence hallucinations. Phases: induction, maintenance, emergence.

  • MAC (minimum alveolar concentration): the inhaled concentration at which 50% of patients do not move to a surgical incision. Lower MAC = more potent; potency rises with lipid solubility. Nitrous oxide's MAC is over 100%, so it cannot give general anesthesia alone; it is used for dental sedation and needs 100% oxygen at the end to prevent diffusion hypoxia.
  • Low blood solubility means fast induction and recovery (nitrous oxide, desflurane, sevoflurane).
  • Levels of sedation: minimal (normal response to voice), moderate (purposeful response to voice or light touch; airway kept), deep (purposeful response only to repeated or painful stimuli; airway may need help), general anesthesia (not arousable even by pain).
  • Reversal agents: flumazenil for benzodiazepines, naloxone for opioids.
full.ns-sens:
What's tested
  • Hearing: cochlear fluids, hair-cell transduction, the central pathway (ECOLIMA), tonotopy, sound localization, cochlear implants
  • Taste and smell: nerves for each part of the tongue, the taste pathway, why smell skips the thalamus
  • Vestibular organs and reflexes; the eye-movement systems, extraocular muscles and nerve palsies
  • Visual pathway targets and the visual field defect from each lesion site
  • Sympathetic versus parasympathetic layout and transmitters; the enteric plexuses; the hypothalamus in brief
  • Pain fibers, the spinothalamic route, gate control, descending modulation, peripheral and central sensitization; nociceptive versus neuropathic pain and their drugs
  • Headache and facial pain: upper-half versus lower-half causes, trigeminal neuralgia, migraine, cluster, giant cell arteritis
  • Facial trauma: wound care, graft types, bone-graft healing, superior orbital fissure and orbital apex syndromes

Hearing

The outer ear funnels sound; the middle ear's ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) amplify it by focusing force from the large tympanic membrane onto the small oval window. The stapedius (VII) damps loud sound, so Bell palsy can cause hyperacusis. The cochlea has three chambers: scala vestibuli and scala tympani hold Na⁺-rich perilymph; the scala media holds K⁺-rich endolymph, giving the endocochlear potential. Sound moves the basilar membrane; stereocilia of the inner hair cells bend toward the tallest one (the kinocilium), tip links open mechanically gated channels, K⁺ flows in and depolarizes the cell, Ca²⁺ channels open and glutamate excites spiral ganglion neurons of CN VIII. Tonotopy: the cochlear base codes high pitch, the apex low pitch, and the map is kept up to the cortex. Pathway (ECOLIMA): Eighth nerve → Cochlear nuclei → superior Olive → Lateral lemniscus → Inferior colliculus → Medial geniculate nucleus → Auditory cortex (Heschl gyrus). Localization: interaural time differences (low pitch, medial superior olive) and intensity differences (high pitch, lateral superior olive). A cochlear implant sits in the scala tympani and stimulates spiral ganglion cells directly, bypassing hair cells.

Taste and smell

RegionTasteGeneral sensation
Anterior 2/3CN VII (chorda tympani, riding the lingual nerve)V3 (lingual nerve)
Posterior 1/3 (incl. circumvallate papillae)CN IXCN IX
Epiglottis, pharynxCN XCN X

Taste fibers go to the nucleus of the solitary tract → VPM → gustatory cortex (anterior insula and frontal operculum), all on the same side. Flavor combines smell (I), taste (VII, IX, X) and texture and temperature (V). Smell is the one sense with no thalamic relay: receptor neurons → olfactory bulb (mitral and tufted cells) → piriform cortex, amygdala and entorhinal cortex, which is why smells call up emotion and memory. Loss of smell (anosmia) follows head trauma that shears the fibers at the cribriform plate, infections and aging, and is an early sign of Parkinson and Alzheimer disease.

Vestibular system and eye movements

Semicircular canals sense rotation (angular acceleration); the otolith organs sense linear acceleration and head tilt: the utricle horizontal, the saccule vertical. Bending toward the kinocilium excites, away inhibits; the two sides work push-pull (turning the head left excites the left horizontal canal). The vestibulo-ocular reflex moves the eyes opposite to the head at the same speed so the image stays still.

  • Eye movement systems: saccades (fast, yoked; frontal eye fields → superior colliculus → PPRF), smooth pursuit, vergence (eyes in opposite directions for near; with accommodation and miosis, the near triad), optokinetic and vestibular (VOR).
  • Muscles: LR6 SO4, the rest CN III. CN III palsy: eye down and out, ptosis, and a dilated pupil when the outer parasympathetic fibers are compressed (aneurysm). CN IV palsy: vertical diplopia, head tilted away. CN VI palsy: eye cannot abduct.
  • MLF lesion (internuclear ophthalmoplegia): on looking to the side, the eye on the lesion side fails to adduct and the other eye shows nystagmus; convergence is spared. Bilateral INO in a young adult suggests MS.

Vision

Photoreceptors (rods for dim light, cones for color) → bipolar cells → ganglion cells, the retina's only output and only cells that fire action potentials. About 90% of ganglion cells go to the LGN → V1 (striate cortex, Brodmann 17) for conscious vision; others go to the superior colliculus (saccades, orienting), pretectum (pupillary light reflex; efferent through Edinger-Westphal and CN III, so light in one eye constricts both pupils), and the suprachiasmatic nucleus (circadian clock).

Autonomic and enteric nervous systems

  • Sympathetic: thoracolumbar (T1–L2 lateral horn), short preganglionic fibers to the chain (paravertebral) or prevertebral ganglia, long postganglionic fibers. Preganglionic ACh on nicotinic receptors; postganglionic norepinephrine on α and β receptors, except sweat glands (ACh, muscarinic). Splanchnic nerves pass the chain without synapsing; the adrenal medulla gets preganglionic fibers directly and releases mostly epinephrine into the blood.
  • Parasympathetic: craniosacral (III, VII, IX, X; S2–S4), long preganglionic fibers to ganglia near or in the organ, short postganglionic fibers, ACh on muscarinic receptors.
  • Saliva: parasympathetic drive gives copious watery saliva; sympathetic gives scant, thick saliva. Anticholinergic drugs cause dry mouth.
  • Enteric nervous system (esophagus to internal anal sphincter, works on its own): myenteric (Auerbach) plexus between the muscle layers for motility; submucosal (Meissner) plexus for secretion and local blood flow.
  • Hypothalamus: supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei make ADH and oxytocin for the posterior pituitary; releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary by portal veins; arcuate dopamine holds prolactin down; lateral = hunger, ventromedial = satiety.

Pain

Nociceptors are free nerve endings (mechanical, thermal through TRP channels, chemical). Aδ fibers (thin, myelinated) carry fast, sharp, well-localized first pain; C fibers (unmyelinated) carry slow, dull, burning, poorly localized second pain. Transmitters in the dorsal horn: glutamate, substance P, CGRP. Second-order neurons (laminae I, II, V) cross in the anterior white commissure and ascend in the spinothalamic tract to VPL (face: VPM) for where and how strong, and to intralaminar and medial nuclei → anterior cingulate and insula for the unpleasant, emotional part.

  • Gate control: large Aβ touch fibers excite inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn that damp Aδ and C input; rubbing a bumped elbow helps.
  • Descending modulation: cortex and hypothalamus → periaqueductal gray → rostral ventromedial medulla (serotonin) and locus coeruleus (norepinephrine) → dorsal horn, with endogenous opioids. It can inhibit (placebo, exercise) or facilitate (stress).
  • Peripheral sensitization: the inflammatory "soup" (prostaglandins, bradykinin) lowers nociceptor threshold → primary hyperalgesia at the injury. Central sensitization: dorsal horn neurons become hyperexcitable through NMDA receptors, Ca²⁺ and kinases ("wind-up") → secondary hyperalgesia around the injury and allodynia (pain from touch).

Nociceptive pain comes from tissue damage (surgery, trauma, an abscess), proportional to injury, with inflammation and raised heart rate and cortisol; treated with NSAIDs (COX inhibitors), acetaminophen, corticosteroids and opioids (mu agonists; side effects include respiratory depression, constipation, miosis; naloxone reverses; codeine is a prodrug made active by CYP2D6; tramadol adds serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake block and lowers seizure threshold). Neuropathic pain comes from injury to the nervous system (diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, post-stroke pain): burning, shooting, out of proportion, with allodynia; responds poorly to opioids and well to adjuvants: tricyclics (amitriptyline), SNRIs (duloxetine), gabapentin and pregabalin (α2δ Ca²⁺ channel subunit), and carbamazepine (Na⁺ channel block, first line for trigeminal neuralgia).

Headache and facial pain

"Upper-half" pain (above the eyes) is mostly primary headache, glaucoma, giant cell arteritis or pseudotumor; "lower-half" pain is most often dental, then TMD and burning mouth; sinus disease (overdiagnosed), cardiac pain referred to the jaw, atypical facial pain and trigeminal neuralgia can be either. Red flags: thunderclap onset, new headache after 50, papilledema, fever, visual loss.

Facial trauma and reconstruction

  • Wound care: copious irrigation, exploration, remove debris (road grit tattoos the skin), check the facial nerve, parotid duct and nasolacrimal duct, early debridement, remove only free bone pieces under 1 cm without periosteum, drains for hematoma.
  • Grafts: autograft (same person, the gold standard), allograft (another person), xenograft (another species), alloplast (synthetic). Bone-graft healing: phase I (first 4 weeks) bone made by cells transplanted with the graft, disorganized; phase II (starts about 2 weeks, peaks about 6) bone made by host cells, with resorption and remodeling that continue indefinitely.
  • Orbit: seven bones; the optic nerve lies about 40–45 mm behind the infraorbital rim. Fracture complications: diplopia, enophthalmos, infection, ectropion, rarely blindness.
  • Superior orbital fissure syndrome: a fracture into the fissure injures III, IV, VI and V1 → ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, proptosis, a fixed dilated pupil, forehead numbness and lost corneal reflex. Orbital apex syndrome = the same plus blindness (optic nerve).
full.rn-filtration:
What's tested
  • The kidney's jobs, where it sits, and the paths of blood and urine through it
  • The nephron's parts, the glomerular filtration barrier and the juxtaglomerular apparatus
  • Bladder innervation and the micturition reflex
  • Renal blood flow, renal plasma flow, GFR and filtration fraction; Starling forces; what afferent and efferent resistance do; autoregulation
  • Clearance: the formula, inulin, creatinine and PAH, and what a clearance ratio says
  • Body fluid compartments, their ions, plasma osmolarity, fluid shifts and IV fluids

What the kidneys do

  • Excrete metabolic wastes (urea, creatinine, uric acid, hormone metabolites) and foreign substances such as drugs.
  • Regulate water and electrolytes, ECF volume, plasma osmolarity (with ADH), blood pressure (renin and angiotensin II) and acid-base balance (pH about 7.35–7.45).
  • Make hormones: erythropoietin from interstitial cells of the cortex when local O2 falls; calcitriol, the active vitamin D, by 1α-hydroxylation in the proximal tubule (regulated by PTH and FGF23); renin from juxtaglomerular cells.
  • Metabolism: gluconeogenesis in the cortex during fasting (most is still the liver's) and ammoniagenesis from glutamine in the proximal tubule, which buffers urinary H+ and makes new HCO3−.

Key relationship: filtered − reabsorbed + secreted = excreted.

Anatomy

  • Paired retroperitoneal organs at about T12–L3; the right kidney sits lower because of the liver. An adrenal gland caps each upper pole.
  • Relations: right kidney – liver, duodenum, IVC; left kidney – spleen, stomach, pancreas. Posteriorly the subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves cross the posterior abdominal wall, a concern in a posterior surgical approach.
  • Blood path: renal artery → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular (cortical radiate) → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries (and vasa recta for juxtamedullary nephrons) → renal vein.
  • Urine path: collecting duct → renal papilla (tip of a pyramid) → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter → bladder → urethra.
  • Nephron (the functional unit): renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman capsule) → proximal tubule → loop of Henle (thin descending, thin ascending, thick ascending) → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct. Most nephrons are cortical with short loops; juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops and vasa recta and build the concentrating gradient.

The filtration barrier and the JG apparatus

  • Three layers: fenestrated endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane (negatively charged) and podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms. Large (about 70 kDa and up) and negatively charged proteins such as albumin are held back; the small amount that leaks is taken up by endocytosis in the proximal tubule.
  • Mesangial cells sit inside the glomerulus, support the capillary loops and can contract.
  • Juxtaglomerular apparatus: the macula densa (tubule cells at the end of the thick ascending limb, where the tubule touches its own glomerulus) senses NaCl; JG (granular) cells in the afferent arteriole wall secrete renin; extraglomerular mesangial cells lie between them.

Bladder and micturition

  • Ureters and bladder are lined by urothelium (transitional epithelium), impermeable to water and NaCl, which flattens as the bladder fills. The trigone lies between the two ureteric openings and the urethral opening. The detrusor is the bladder's smooth muscle.
  • Sympathetic (hypogastric nerve): relaxes the detrusor and contracts the internal sphincter – storage.
  • Parasympathetic (pelvic nerves, S2–S4): contracts the detrusor through muscarinic receptors and relaxes the internal sphincter – voiding.
  • Somatic (pudendal nerve, S2–S4): keeps the external sphincter closed voluntarily; voiding starts when this drive is inhibited.
  • Reflex: at roughly 300 mL, stretch receptors signal the sacral cord; the pontine micturition center coordinates voiding when the cortex allows it.

Blood flow and filtration

  • The kidneys get 20–25% of cardiac output (about 1.2 L of blood a minute). Renal plasma flow is about 600–650 mL/min.
  • GFR is about 120–125 mL/min, or 180 L/day; about 178 L is reabsorbed and 1.5–2 L becomes urine.
  • Filtration fraction = GFR / RPF, normally about 20%.
  • Starling forces: glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out; Bowman space hydrostatic pressure and glomerular capillary oncotic pressure oppose it; Bowman space oncotic pressure is about zero. The class example: (45 − 10) − 19 = 16 mmHg net. Oncotic pressure rises along the capillary as protein-free fluid leaves.

  • Regulators: sympathetic nerves constrict both arterioles and lower RBF and GFR; angiotensin II constricts the efferent more and holds GFR up when perfusion falls; prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) dilate the arterioles and protect flow in hemorrhage or heart failure (NSAIDs remove this protection); low-dose dopamine dilates.
  • Autoregulation keeps RBF and GFR nearly constant from about 80 to 200 mmHg by two mechanisms: the myogenic response of the afferent arteriole and tubuloglomerular feedback – more NaCl at the macula densa → adenosine → afferent constriction → GFR back down. Sustained changes in NaCl delivery also change renin release.

Clearance

  • C = (U × V) / P: the volume of plasma cleared of a substance per minute (U, urine concentration; V, urine flow; P, plasma concentration).
  • Inulin: freely filtered, neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR (the gold standard).
  • Creatinine: made by muscle at a steady rate and freely filtered, with a little secretion, so it slightly overestimates GFR; it's the clinical marker (eGFR also uses cystatin C). Plasma creatinine varies inversely with GFR: if GFR halves, plasma creatinine doubles at steady state.
  • PAH: filtered and secreted almost completely in one pass, so its clearance estimates renal plasma flow.
  • Clearance ratio (Cx / Cinulin): = 1, filtered only; > 1, filtered and secreted (PAH, organic acids and bases); < 1, filtered and reabsorbed (Na+, Cl−, urea) or not filtered. Glucose and albumin normally have a clearance of 0.

Body fluid compartments

  • 60–40–20: total body water is 60% of body weight; ICF 40%; ECF 20%. The ECF is 3/4 interstitial fluid and 1/4 plasma. In a 70-kg man: TBW 42 L, ICF 28 L, ECF 14 L, plasma 3.5 L.
  • Plasma is 55% of blood volume (hematocrit about 45%); interstitial fluid is an ultrafiltrate of plasma without its proteins and cells.
  • ECF ions: Na+ (main cation), Cl− and HCO3−. ICF ions: K+ and Mg2+, with proteins and organic phosphates (ATP, ADP) as the anions.
  • Plasma osmolarity ≈ 2[Na+] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8; normal about 275–290 mOsm/kg. At steady state ICF and ECF osmolarity are equal; water moves until they match.

full.rn-tubule:
What's tested
  • Epithelial transport: apical and basolateral sides, transcellular and paracellular paths, cotransporters and exchangers
  • The proximal tubule: Na+-coupled reabsorption, HCO3− and Cl− handling, glucose and its transport maximum, water, glomerulotubular balance
  • The loop of Henle: what each limb does with water and NaCl, NKCC2, countercurrent multiplication, urea recycling and the vasa recta
  • The distal tubule and collecting duct: NCC, principal and intercalated cells, aldosterone and ADH
  • Which diuretic acts on which segment

Ground rules

  • The apical membrane faces the lumen; the basolateral membrane faces the interstitium and blood. Solutes cross transcellularly (through the cell) or paracellularly (between cells, through tight junctions).
  • A cotransporter (symporter) moves two solutes the same way (SGLT2, NKCC2, NCC); an exchanger (countertransporter) moves them opposite ways (Na+/H+ exchanger).
  • Everything is powered by the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase, which keeps cell Na+ low so Na+ flows in across the apical membrane and drags other solutes with it.

Thick ascending limbabout 25%Na+-K+-2Cl− (NKCC2)ImpermeableLoop diuretics

Proximal tubule

  • Reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered Na+, Cl−, K+ and water, about 80–85% of HCO3−, most phosphate, and nearly all glucose and amino acids. Reabsorption is iso-osmotic: water follows solute through aquaporin-1 and between the cells.
  • Early proximal tubule: the apical Na+/H+ exchanger secretes H+, which reclaims filtered HCO3− with the help of carbonic anhydrase; HCO3− leaves basolaterally on a Na+-HCO3− cotransporter. Glucose enters with Na+ on SGLT2 and leaves on GLUT transporters.
  • Late proximal tubule: by now Cl− is concentrated in the lumen, so it is reabsorbed through a Cl−/anion (formate) exchanger and paracellularly, with Na+.
  • Glucose transport maximum (Tm): the carriers saturate. Once the filtered load passes Tm (plasma glucose above about 180–200 mg/dL, the renal threshold), the excess is excreted – glycosuria with an osmotic diuresis. SGLT2 inhibitors (the "-flozins": empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) cause glycosuria on purpose to treat type 2 diabetes; watch for genital yeast infections, UTIs, volume loss and euglycemic ketoacidosis.
  • Glomerulotubular balance: when GFR rises, the proximal tubule reabsorbs more, keeping the fraction reabsorbed about constant (a higher filtration fraction raises peritubular oncotic pressure, which pulls more fluid back).
  • The proximal tubule also secretes organic anions and cations: PAH, penicillin, uric acid, many drugs (probenecid competes with them).
  • Proximal diuretics: acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: HCO3− lost in the urine, mild hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis; used for glaucoma and altitude sickness) and mannitol (an osmotic agent filtered but not reabsorbed, holding water in the lumen; lowers intracranial and intraocular pressure).

Loop of Henle

  • Thin descending limb: permeable to water, not to NaCl. Water leaves into the salty medulla, so the fluid becomes more concentrated going down.
  • Thin ascending limb: impermeable to water; NaCl leaves passively, so the fluid becomes more dilute going up.
  • Thick ascending limb (TAL): NKCC2 (Na+-K+-2Cl−) moves salt into the cell; K+ leaks back to the lumen through ROMK, making the lumen positive, which pushes Ca2+ and Mg2+ (and some Na+) between the cells. Impermeable to water, so it is the diluting segment: fluid leaving it is hypo-osmotic (about 100 mOsm/kg). Reabsorbs about 25% of filtered Na+.
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) block NKCC2: the medullary gradient collapses, so urine can be neither concentrated nor fully diluted; Ca2+ and Mg2+ are lost too.

Making concentrated urine

  • Countercurrent multiplication: the TAL pumps NaCl into the interstitium without water, and the opposite flows in the two limbs multiply this small step into a gradient from about 300 mOsm/kg in the cortex to about 1,200 at the papilla.
  • Urea recycling: ADH makes the cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts permeable to water but not urea, so urea concentrates in the duct; in the inner medullary collecting duct ADH also inserts urea transporters, urea diffuses into the interstitium and supplies much of the inner medulla's osmolarity. Some urea re-enters the thin limbs and is recycled.
  • Vasa recta: hairpin capillaries that act as countercurrent exchangers; their slow flow keeps the gradient from being washed away. Very high water intake or tubular flow causes medullary washout, lowering the maximum urine concentration for a while.

Distal tubule and collecting duct

  • Distal convoluted tubule: starts at the macula densa; water-impermeable; NCC (Na+-Cl− cotransporter) reabsorbs about 5% of filtered NaCl. Ca2+ enters through an apical channel (TRPV5) and leaves through a basolateral Ca2+-ATPase and Na+/Ca2+ exchanger; PTH increases it. Thiazides block NCC and increase Ca2+ reabsorption.
  • Principal cells (about 60%): Na+ in through ENaC, K+ out to the lumen through ROMK; respond to aldosterone and ADH.
  • Aldosterone enters the cell, binds an intracellular mineralocorticoid receptor and, over hours, raises the number of ENaC channels, Na+-K+-ATPase pumps and K+ channels: more Na+ reabsorbed, more K+ (and H+) secreted.
  • ADH binds V2 receptors → cAMP → aquaporin-2 inserted in the apical membrane. It also raises urea permeability in the inner medullary duct and NKCC2 activity in the TAL.
  • Intercalated cells (about 40%): α-intercalated cells secrete H+ (apical H+-ATPase and H+-K+-ATPase, which also reabsorbs K+) and return HCO3− to the blood through the basolateral Cl−/HCO3− exchanger AE1; β-intercalated cells secrete HCO3− through apical pendrin.
  • K+-sparing diuretics: amiloride and triamterene block ENaC; spironolactone and eplerenone block the aldosterone receptor. Less Na+ entry means a less negative lumen and less K+ secretion, so the risk is hyperkalemia.
full.rn-balance:
What's tested
  • Water balance: hypo- and hypernatremia, where ADH is made, osmotic and non-osmotic control, SIADH and central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
  • Sodium balance: the volume sensors, the sympathetic nerves, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ANP; responses to hypo- and hypervolemia
  • Potassium: shifts into and out of cells, renal handling, what raises and lowers K+ secretion
  • Magnesium, calcium and phosphate: where each is reabsorbed; PTH, vitamin D and FGF23; diuretic effects
  • Acid-base: Henderson-Hasselbalch, HCO3− reabsorption, titratable acid and ammonium, the four simple disorders and their compensation

Water balance and ADH

  • Hyponatremia is plasma Na+ below 135 mmol/L (too much water for the sodium); hypernatremia is above 145 (too little water). Plasma Na+ reflects water balance; total body Na+ sets ECF volume.
  • ADH (vasopressin) is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
  • Osmoreceptors sit in the OVLT and subfornical organ, which lack a blood-brain barrier. A 1–2% rise in osmolarity releases ADH; thirst needs about 2–3%, so ADH responds first. Below the threshold ADH is fully suppressed.
  • Non-osmotic control: a 5–10% fall in blood volume or pressure, sensed by the left atrium, carotid sinus and aortic arch, releases ADH. Volume wins: hypovolemia resets the osmostat so ADH is released even at a low osmolarity. Nausea, pain, hypoxia, hypoglycemia and some drugs also release ADH; alcohol suppresses it.
  • Water loss → osmolarity up → ADH and thirst → aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct → small volume of concentrated urine. Water load → the reverse: large volume of dilute urine.

Telling water deprivation from SIADH: both make concentrated urine, but plasma osmolarity is high with water deprivation and low with SIADH.

Sodium balance

  • Sensors: low-pressure receptors in the atria and pulmonary vessels; high-pressure baroreceptors in the carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X); in the kidney, the afferent arteriole (perfusion pressure) and the macula densa (NaCl delivery). A 5–10% change is needed to respond.
  • Renal sympathetic nerves: constrict both arterioles (GFR down), release renin, raise proximal Na+ reabsorption.
  • Renin is released by JG cells for low afferent pressure, sympathetic (β1) activity and low NaCl at the macula densa (signaled by prostaglandins). Renin: angiotensinogen → angiotensin I; ACE (on endothelium, mostly lung) → angiotensin II.
  • Angiotensin II: arteriolar constriction (efferent more than afferent), more proximal Na+ reabsorption (Na+/H+ exchanger), aldosterone release, ADH release, thirst and salt appetite.
  • ANP from atrial myocytes, released by atrial stretch (volume expansion): dilates the afferent and constricts the efferent arteriole (GFR up), inhibits renin, aldosterone and ADH, and reduces Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct → natriuresis. It opposes RAAS.
  • Hypovolemia: sympathetic tone up, RAAS up, ADH up, ANP down → Na+ and water kept (over hours to days). Hypervolemia: the reverse.
  • In heart failure, cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome the ECF is expanded but the effective circulating volume is low, so the kidney keeps retaining Na+ and edema worsens.
  • Liddle syndrome: overactive ENaC → hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with low renin and aldosterone; amiloride treats it.

Potassium

  • About 98% of K+ is inside cells. Plasma K+ is normally 3.5–5.0 mEq/L: hypokalemia below 3.5, hyperkalemia above 5.0. Both disturb nerve, muscle and heart rhythm.
  • Into cells (plasma K+ falls): insulin (after a meal), β2 agonists such as epinephrine and albuterol, alkalosis, aldosterone.
  • Out of cells (plasma K+ rises): insulin deficiency, β-blockers, acidosis, hyperosmolarity, cell lysis (crush injury, hemolysis, chemotherapy), strenuous exercise.
  • Renal handling: freely filtered; the proximal tubule reabsorbs about 67% and the TAL about 20%, whatever the diet. The collecting duct sets excretion: principal cells secrete K+; α-intercalated cells reabsorb it on a low-K+ diet (H+-K+-ATPase).
  • K+ secretion rises with a high-K+ diet, aldosterone, alkalosis and high tubular flow or Na+ delivery (loop and thiazide diuretics → hypokalemia). It falls with acute acidosis, low aldosterone, K+-sparing diuretics and low GFR. NSAIDs blunt renin release and, with CKD, ACE inhibitors or spironolactone, can cause hyperkalemia.

Calcium, phosphate and magnesium

IonProximal tubuleThick ascending limbDistal tubuleExcreted
Ca2+ (99% in bone)about 65%, paracellular with Na+ and waterabout 20–25%, paracellular (lumen-positive)about 5–10%, transcellular, raised by PTH and thiazidesabout 1–2%
Mg2+ (mostly bone and cells)about 30%about 60%, the main site, paracellularabout 5–10%, apical Mg2+ channelabout 5%
Phosphate (85% in bone)about 80–85%, Na+-phosphate cotransporter (saturable)–littleabout 15%; a urinary buffer
  • Loop diuretics raise Ca2+ and Mg2+ excretion; thiazides lower Ca2+ excretion. ECF volume expansion raises Ca2+ excretion.
  • PTH is released when plasma Ca2+ falls (and when phosphate rises). It frees Ca2+ and phosphate from bone, raises Ca2+ reabsorption in the DCT, lowers phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule (phosphaturia) and stimulates 1α-hydroxylase. Net: Ca2+ up, phosphate down.
  • Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), made in the proximal tubule: its most important action is Ca2+ absorption from the gut; it also raises phosphate absorption, inhibits PTH and stimulates FGF23. PTH stimulates its synthesis; FGF23 inhibits it.
  • FGF23, from osteocytes and osteoblasts, is released when phosphate and calcitriol are high. It lowers proximal phosphate reabsorption and lowers calcitriol synthesis.
  • A sudden fall in plasma Ca2+ is buffered mostly from bone.

Acid-base

  • pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3−] / (0.03 × PCO2). Normal: pH 7.35–7.45, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3− 24 mEq/L. The lungs set PCO2 (volatile acid); the kidneys set HCO3− and excrete the fixed acids (sulfuric and phosphoric acid from protein metabolism, about 1 mEq/kg a day).
  • Defense in three steps: buffers (immediate), lungs (minutes), kidneys (hours to days).
  • Reclaiming filtered HCO3− (proximal tubule, about 80%): secreted H+ meets filtered HCO3− in the lumen → H2CO3 → CO2 + H2O (carbonic anhydrase); CO2 enters the cell, is turned back into H+ and HCO3−, and the HCO3− goes to the blood. No net acid is excreted.
  • Making new HCO3−: each H+ excreted on a urinary buffer adds a new HCO3− to the blood. Titratable acid is H+ on filtered buffers, mainly phosphate. Ammonium: the proximal tubule turns glutamine into NH4+ (secreted) and α-ketoglutarate, which yields new HCO3−; in the collecting duct NH3 diffuses into the lumen and traps secreted H+ as NH4+. Ammonium is the part that grows in chronic acidosis.
  • Net acid excretion = NH4+ + titratable acid − excreted HCO3−; at steady state it equals fixed acid production.

  • Anion gap = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−), normally about 8–12; a high gap means an added acid (ketoacids, lactate, salicylate, toxic alcohols, uremia).
  • Acid-base and K+ move together: acidosis drives K+ out of cells (hyperkalemia); alkalosis drives it in (hypokalemia). Vomiting gives metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia, kept going by volume contraction (angiotensin II and aldosterone).

What's tested

  • End-stage renal disease, azotemia versus uremia, and how uremia arises
  • What CKD does to the body: anemia, hypertension, hyperkalemia, acidosis, bone and mineral disease, bleeding, and the mouth and eyes

Chronic kidney disease

  • CKD: abnormal kidney structure or function present for 3 months or more, with effects on health. The leading causes are diabetes mellitus, then hypertension; it is more common with age.
  • eGFR (from serum creatinine or cystatin C) is the chief measure of function and sets the stage. uACR (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) picks up damage even when eGFR is above 60; under 30 mg/g is normal.
  • Function is kept near normal until more than about 50% of nephrons are lost, because the survivors hypertrophy and hyperfilter. Lost nephrons are not replaced; end-stage kidneys are small, scarred and nodular.

Azotemia and uremia

  • Azotemia is a lab finding: non-protein nitrogen (urea, creatinine) builds up in the blood because filtration has fallen. BUN is normally about 7–20 mg/dL. It may cause no symptoms.
  • Uremia is the clinical illness of kidney failure, the stage azotemia leads to: fatigue, nausea, itching, confusion, pericarditis, bleeding and the oral signs below.
  • Uremia comes from three things: retained products the kidney should excrete (nitrogen wastes), normal products in excess (hormones such as PTH), and loss of products the kidney makes (erythropoietin, calcitriol). Failing excretion also retains Na+ and water and causes hyperkalemia.

Complications of CKD

  • Anemia: normocytic, from low erythropoietin; it rises steeply from stage 3 on. Treated with erythropoietin analogs (epoetin, darbepoetin) and iron.
  • Hypertension (Na+ and water retention, renin), and cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of death in CKD.
  • Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis as excretion falls.
  • CKD mineral and bone disorder: falling GFR retains phosphate → FGF23 rises and calcitriol falls → less Ca2+ absorbed → plasma Ca2+ falls → secondary hyperparathyroidism (seen from stages 3–5) → renal osteodystrophy: bone resorption, demineralized jaws and brown tumors.
  • Bleeding: uremic toxins impair platelet adhesion and aggregation; hemodialysis adds heparin.
  • Infection risk and poor healing; drug clearance falls.
  • Oral: uremic stomatitis, xerostomia, altered or metallic taste, ammonia-like breath, pale mucosa from anemia, petechiae and ecchymoses, periodontal disease, renal osteodystrophy. Eyes: retinopathy, glaucoma, cataracts.
  • Dialysis is started at eGFR under about 15 or with uremic symptoms.

Glomerular disease

  • Kidney disease can hit glomeruli, tubules, interstitium or vessels. Glomeruli are hurt mostly by immune mechanisms (circulating immune complexes, or antibodies against antigens in the glomerulus); tubules by toxins and infection. Primary glomerulopathy involves only the kidney; secondary comes from a systemic disease (diabetes, lupus, amyloidosis, drugs, infection, cancer).
Nephritic syndromeNephrotic syndrome
HallmarkHematuria (RBC casts), hypertension, oliguria, azotemia; mild proteinuriaProteinuria over 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia and lipiduria
MechanismInflammation of the glomerulusPodocyte injury or GBM damage that lets protein through
ExamplesPost-streptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy, rapidly progressive GNMinimal change disease, FSGS, membranous nephropathy, MPGN; diabetes and amyloid (secondary)
  • Post-streptococcal GN: children, 1–4 weeks after group A strep throat or skin infection; cola-colored urine, edema, hypertension, low C3; hypercellular glomeruli with subepithelial "humps". Most children recover; adults more often progress.
  • IgA nephropathy: the most common glomerular disease worldwide; recurrent hematuria within a day or two of a respiratory infection; mesangial IgA. Benign in children, slowly progressive in adults.
  • Rapidly progressive GN: crescents of epithelial cells in Bowman space and fast loss of function. Type I anti-GBM (linear IgG and C3), type II immune complex, type III pauci-immune.
  • Minimal change disease: the most common nephrotic syndrome in children; normal light microscopy, fused (effaced) podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy; responds to steroids.
  • FSGS: sclerosis of some segments of some glomeruli; idiopathic or secondary; poor steroid response, about half reach kidney failure in 10 years.
  • Membranous nephropathy: the classic most common nephrotic syndrome in adults (ages 30–50); subepithelial immune deposits; slowly progressive.
  • MPGN: subendothelial (type I) or dense intramembranous (type II) deposits; "tram-track" GBM; poor course.

Tubules, stones and obstruction

  • Acute pyelonephritis: bacterial infection of the kidney and pelvis, usually ascending, most often E. coli. Fever, chills, flank pain, dysuria and frequency; WBC casts place it in the kidney. Complications: pyonephrosis, papillary necrosis, sepsis.
  • Acute tubular necrosis: ischemia or toxins; muddy brown casts; the commonest cause of acute kidney injury, usually reversible. Drug-induced interstitial nephritis: fever, rash, eosinophils in the urine.
  • Urolithiasis: calcium oxalate/phosphate stones about 75%, magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite, with urease-making bacteria) about 15%, then uric acid and cystine. Colicky flank pain to the groin, hematuria, infection.
  • Hydronephrosis: dilated pelvis and calyces with atrophy from obstruction. Bilateral (obstruction below the ureters) leads to kidney failure if not relieved; unilateral can stay silent.

Cysts and tumors

  • ADPKD: adults, always bilateral, PKD1 (chromosome 16, about 85%) or PKD2 (chromosome 4); hypertension, liver cysts, berry aneurysms. ARPKD: infants, PKHD1, small sponge-like cysts, congenital hepatic fibrosis.
  • Renal cell carcinoma: about 2% of adult cancers; smoking is a risk. Hematuria, flank pain and a mass; a yellow-orange, vascular tumor. Clear cell (70–80%, loss of VHL on 3p, cells full of lipid and glycogen); papillary (10–15%); chromophobe (about 5%, best prognosis, perinuclear halos). RCC spreads by blood and can surface as a metastasis in the jaw or gingiva.
  • Wilms tumor: children (about 2–5 years), a large flank mass; triphasic (blastemal, stromal, epithelial); good prognosis.
  • Benign: papillary adenoma, oncocytoma, and angiomyolipoma (tuberous sclerosis).

  • Why loop and thiazide diuretics waste K+: more Na+ and fluid reach the collecting duct, ENaC reabsorbs more Na+, the lumen becomes more negative, and K+ is secreted. Volume loss also raises aldosterone. Adding a K+-sparing drug (spironolactone is the classic partner in heart failure) offsets it.
  • Calcium: loop diuretics raise Ca2+ excretion; thiazides lower it.
  • Interactions: NSAIDs blunt diuretic and antihypertensive effects (they block renal prostaglandins) and, with K+-sparing drugs or ACE inhibitors, raise K+; thiazides and loop diuretics raise lithium levels, and so do NSAIDs; loop diuretics plus aminoglycosides add ototoxicity; low K+ makes digoxin toxic. Thiazides and loops are sulfonamides (ethacrynic acid is not).
  • In the chair: patients on diuretics are prone to orthostatic hypotension (sit them up slowly) and xerostomia; thiazides can cause lichenoid reactions. A short NSAID course is usually acceptable, but long use weakens blood pressure control.

The CKD and dialysis patient

  • Consult the physician or nephrologist: stage, cause, recent labs (CBC with platelets, coagulation tests, electrolytes), blood pressure control, medications and the dialysis schedule.
  • Hemodialysis runs about 3 times a week through an arteriovenous fistula or graft, usually in the forearm, with heparin. Treat on the day after dialysis: heparin's effect (a few hours) is gone and fluid, electrolytes and wastes are at their best. Avoid treating on a dialysis day.
  • Never take blood pressure, start an IV or draw blood on the fistula arm.
  • Bleeding: uremic platelet dysfunction makes bleeding likely even with a normal platelet count. Plan local hemostasis (pressure, sutures, hemostatic agents, tranexamic acid); the physician may give desmopressin before surgery.
  • Infection: wound healing is slow and immunity weak; dialysis patients have higher rates of hepatitis B and C. Antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely recommended just for a fistula or graft; follow the nephrologist's advice when asked.
  • Peritoneal dialysis uses no systemic heparin; its main risk is peritonitis.
  • Hypertension, anemia (pallor, fatigue) and diabetes often come with CKD: check blood pressure each visit and keep appointments short and low-stress.

Drugs when the kidneys fail

  • A drug cleared by the kidney accumulates as GFR falls: lower the dose or lengthen the interval (usually once GFR is under about 50, and especially under 30 mL/min). Drugs removed by dialysis are given after the session.
  • Avoid: NSAIDs (they cut renal prostaglandins and GFR, raise K+ and blood pressure, add to bleeding), high-dose aspirin, tetracyclines other than doxycycline (they raise BUN), meperidine (its metabolite normeperidine accumulates and causes seizures), and nephrotoxic drugs.
  • Adjust: amoxicillin, penicillin VK and cephalexin (longer interval), acyclovir and valacyclovir, metronidazole, codeine, morphine and tramadol (active metabolites build up), gabapentin.
  • Usually no change: amide local anesthetics such as lidocaine (metabolized by the liver; articaine by plasma esterases) at normal doses, clindamycin, azithromycin and doxycycline (cleared by the liver or gut). Acetaminophen is the analgesic of choice, with a longer interval in severe disease.

Oral and radiographic signs

  • Uremic fetor (ammonia-like breath), uremic stomatitis (painful white plaques or ulcers), xerostomia (fluid limits, drugs), metallic or altered taste, pale mucosa, petechiae, ecchymoses and gingival bleeding, periodontal disease. Children with CKD can show enamel hypoplasia and delayed eruption. Caries tends to be low (salivary urea raises pH), while calculus builds up.
  • Renal osteodystrophy from secondary hyperparathyroidism: loss of the lamina dura, a ground-glass trabecular pattern, demineralized jaws and brown tumors (giant cell lesions); soft tissue calcifications. Demineralized jaws raise the risk of fracture during extractions.

The kidney transplant patient

  • Clear dental infection before transplant; defer elective care in the first months after, and coordinate with the transplant team.
  • Immunosuppressants (tacrolimus or cyclosporine, mycophenolate, prednisone): infection, candidiasis, slow healing; cyclosporine causes gingival overgrowth (worse with a calcium channel blocker such as nifedipine or amlodipine); long-term steroids can suppress the adrenals, so major surgery may need a stress dose set by the physician.
  • Interactions: erythromycin and clarithromycin and azole antifungals (fluconazole, ketoconazole) block the liver enzyme that clears cyclosporine and tacrolimus, raising their levels and their kidney toxicity; NSAIDs add nephrotoxicity.

Hormones and their receptors

Peptides (insulin, GH, ACTH, PTH, ADH) are stored in granules, dissolve in plasma and bind surface receptors. Amines are epinephrine and norepinephrine (surface receptors) and thyroid hormone, the exception that crosses the membrane and binds a nuclear receptor. Steroids (cortisol, aldosterone, sex steroids, calcitriol) come from cholesterol, are made on demand, not stored, ride on binding proteins and act on intracellular receptors by changing gene transcription, so their effects start slowly and last.

Hypothalamus and pituitary

  • Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis, from Rathke pouch): hypothalamic releasing hormones reach it through the hypophyseal portal veins. Acidophils make GH and prolactin; basophils make FSH, LH, ACTH and TSH ("B-FLAT"); chromophobes have few granules.
  • Posterior pituitary (pars nervosa) makes nothing: ADH and oxytocin are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, travel down axons, are stored in Herring bodies and released into blood (neuroendocrine secretion). Pituicytes are glia.
  • Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin, so a stalk lesion or a dopamine blocker raises prolactin. TRH releases TSH (and prolactin); somatostatin inhibits GH (and TSH).
  • Negative feedback is the rule (long loop from the target hormone, short loop from the pituitary hormone). Primary (target gland) disease: the target hormone and the pituitary hormone move in opposite directions. Secondary (pituitary) disease: they move the same way.

Growth hormone

  • Pulsatile from somatotrophs, the biggest pulse in deep sleep soon after falling asleep. Up: GHRH (Gs), ghrelin, sleep, stress, exercise, hypoglycemia, amino acids. Down: somatostatin (Gi), glucose, free fatty acids, and GH and IGF-1 themselves (they raise hypothalamic somatostatin).
  • Linear growth runs mostly through IGF-1 (somatomedin) from the liver, acting on growth-plate chondrocytes. Metabolic effects: diabetogenic (anti-insulin, gluconeogenesis), lipolytic, builds muscle protein.
  • Fetal growth depends on insulin, not GH (big babies of diabetic mothers). Estrogen closes the growth plates in both sexes: plan implants after growth stops.
  • Excess, usually a somatotroph adenoma: before the plates fuse, gigantism; after, acromegaly: coarse face, frontal bossing, big hands and feet, a growing mandible (Class I to Class III), new diastemas, macroglossia, glucose intolerance, hypertension. Screen with IGF-1; confirm when GH fails to fall after an oral glucose load.
  • Deficiency: short stature. Laron syndrome (GH receptor defect): GH high, IGF-1 low. Somatopause: GH falls from the 30s, mainly from less GHRH.

Pituitary disorders

  • Adenomas: micro under 10 mm, macro 10 mm or more. A macroadenoma presses on the optic chiasm: bitemporal hemianopsia and headache.
  • Prolactinoma, the most common functioning adenoma: amenorrhea and galactorrhea in women, low libido and infertility in men; treated with a dopamine agonist (bromocriptine, cabergoline). Corticotroph adenoma = Cushing disease; gonadotroph adenomas are usually silent.
  • Hypopituitarism needs about 75% loss: Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary infarction: the first sign is failure to lactate), empty sella, surgery, radiation.

The adrenal gland

The cortex (about 90%) makes steroids in three zones, outside in, salt, sugar, sex: the glomerulosa makes aldosterone (driven by angiotensin II and high potassium; keeps sodium, excretes potassium and acid), the fasciculata (lipid-filled spongiocytes) makes cortisol under ACTH, and the reticularis makes androgens (DHEA). The medulla's chromaffin cells, modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons, release about 80% epinephrine on acetylcholine from preganglionic fibers; cortisol-rich blood draining from the cortex induces PNMT, the enzyme that turns norepinephrine into epinephrine.

Cortisol peaks in the early morning. It raises glucose (gluconeogenesis), breaks down muscle protein, mobilizes fat, increases bone resorption, suppresses inflammation and immunity and keeps vessels responsive to catecholamines. ACTH is its main regulator.

Corticosteroid drugs

A corticosteroid crosses the membrane, displaces hsp90 from the cytoplasmic receptor, and the complex changes transcription in the nucleus. About 90% of cortisol rides on CBG; a high dose saturates it and the free fraction jumps. Names end in -sone or -solone.
