  • Why a taper: an outside steroid suppresses CRH and ACTH, and the cortex goes into rest. Stopped abruptly, it cannot answer: adrenal insufficiency. Taken in the morning, like the natural peak, it disturbs sleep less.
  • Side effects: masked infection, oral candidiasis (inhaled steroids: rinse after), delayed healing, osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, hypertension, peptic ulcer (worse with NSAIDs), glaucoma and cataract, mood change and insomnia, hypokalemia, growth suppression in children, a cushingoid look.
  • Other adrenal drugs: ketoconazole and metyrapone (11β-hydroxylase) block cortisol synthesis for Cushing; mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor; spironolactone blocks aldosterone (hyperkalemia, gynecomastia), and eplerenone does the same with less gynecomastia.

In the dental chair

  • A patient on long-term steroids (about 20 mg prednisone a day for 3 weeks or more) should be assumed to have a suppressed axis. For routine care under local anesthesia: the usual morning dose, a morning appointment, and good anxiety and pain control. A long or stressful surgery, an infection or trauma, or a missed dose can trigger an adrenal crisis; extra steroid for a big procedure is set with the physician.
  • Adrenal crisis: severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, abdominal pain, loss of consciousness, shock. Stop, call 911, lay the patient supine with legs raised, give oxygen and 100 mg hydrocortisone IV or IM, and monitor vitals.
  • Addison disease: diffuse brown pigmentation of the gingiva, buccal mucosa and tongue. Acromegaly: a Class III bite, spacing, macroglossia, dentures that no longer fit.

What's tested
  • How thyroid hormone is made, stored and activated (TPO, colloid, T4 to T3)

  • Thyroid drugs: levothyroxine, methimazole vs propylthiouracil, radioactive iodine, iodide, beta-blockers, amiodarone

Making thyroid hormone

  • The sodium-iodide symporter pumps iodide into the follicular cell; pendrin passes it into the colloid.
  • Thyroperoxidase (TPO), using H₂O₂, oxidizes iodide, attaches it to tyrosines on thyroglobulin (organification: MIT and DIT) and couples them: MIT + DIT = T3, DIT + DIT = T4. The hormone is stored in the colloid, the only hormone made and stored outside the cell.
  • TSH triggers endocytosis of thyroglobulin (through megalin); lysosomes free T4 and T3. The gland releases about 90% T4, a prohormone; 5′-deiodinase in the tissues makes the active T3, and inner-ring deiodination makes inactive reverse T3.
  • A large iodine load briefly blocks organification (Wolff–Chaikoff). In plasma T4 rides mostly on TBG; only the free fraction acts. Pregnancy and estrogen raise TBG: total T4 rises, free T4 stays normal.
  • Axis: TRH (Gq) → TSH (Gs) → T4 and T3; T3 is the main feedback. Actions: higher metabolic rate (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase), heat, more beta-1 receptors (fast, strong heart), brain development in infants, lower LDL cholesterol.

About half of plasma calcium is ionized, the active part. What's tested
  • Islet cells and their hormones; how glucose releases insulin (the K-ATP channel)
  • What insulin and glucagon do; C-peptide
  • Type 1 vs type 2; the diagnostic cutoffs; HbA1c and control
  • Every diabetes drug class: mechanism, hypoglycemia risk, weight, key adverse effects; the insulin preparations
  • Diabetes in the mouth, the periodontal link, and hypoglycemia in the chair

The islets

Islets are 1–2% of the pancreas, mostly in the tail, with fenestrated capillaries and no ducts. Beta cells (about 70%) make insulin (with amylin and C-peptide), alpha cells (about 20%) glucagon, delta cells (5–10%) somatostatin, the paracrine brake on both; PP cells make pancreatic polypeptide and epsilon cells ghrelin.

  • Insulin release: glucose enters the beta cell through GLUT2 → glycolysis raises ATP → the ATP-sensitive K⁺ channel closes → the cell depolarizes → voltage-gated calcium channels open → insulin is released. Sulfonylureas and meglitinides close the same channel. Gut incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify release after a meal, only when glucose is up; amino acids and fatty acids also stimulate it.
  • Proinsulin is cut into insulin and C-peptide, released 1:1. C-peptide measures the patient's own insulin: low in type 1, low when hypoglycemia comes from injected insulin, high from a sulfonylurea or an insulinoma.
  • Insulin (receptor tyrosine kinase → IRS) moves GLUT4 to the membrane in muscle and fat, builds glycogen, fat and protein, blocks gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and ketogenesis, and drives potassium into cells. Brain and liver take up glucose without it.
  • Glucagon (Gs) acts on the liver: glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis. Low glucose and amino acids release it. Glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol and GH are the counter-regulatory hormones.

Diagnosis (two abnormal results, or one with symptoms): HbA1c 6.5% or more, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or more, 2-hour glucose tolerance 200 or more, or a random 200 or more with symptoms. Prediabetes: HbA1c 5.7–6.4%, fasting 100–125. HbA1c is glucose stuck to hemoglobin and reflects the last 2–3 months (red cell life): about 5% is normal, below 7% is well controlled, above 7% is poorly controlled. The classic triad is polyuria (osmotic diuresis), polydipsia and polyphagia. Gestational diabetes comes from human placental lactogen's anti-insulin effect.

Complications: microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular (heart attack, stroke, peripheral artery disease), with infections and poor healing from weak neutrophil function, a poor blood supply and impaired collagen.

Every drug that releases or adds insulin (insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides) causes hypoglycemia and weight gain. A patient with a weight problem: a GLP-1 agonist. Heart failure: an SGLT2 inhibitor (not a TZD). Regular and NPH insulin are sold without a prescription.

Diabetes in the mouth

Periodontitis is more frequent and more severe, and the link runs both ways: periodontal inflammation worsens glucose control, and periodontal treatment can lower HbA1c modestly. Also: xerostomia, candidiasis, burning mouth, caries, taste changes, enlarged parotids, delayed healing, postoperative infection, and more implant failure when control is poor.

In the dental chair

  • Before treatment ask the type, drugs, the last HbA1c and today's reading; confirm the patient ate and took the usual dose (metformin or insulin with a skipped breakfast is the classic setup for a low). Morning appointments, short visits, glucose within reach.
  • Hypoglycemia (glucose below about 70 mg/dL): sweating, tremor, tachycardia, anxiety, hunger, then confusion, slurred speech, seizure and loss of consciousness. It comes on fast; high glucose develops slowly.
  • Awake and able to swallow: 15–20 g of fast sugar by mouth (glucose tablets or gel, juice, regular soda), recheck in 15 minutes. On acarbose: glucose, not table sugar. On a GLP-1 agonist the response can be slow (slow gastric emptying).
  • Unconscious: nothing by mouth; glucagon 1 mg IM or subcutaneously (or nasal), or IV dextrose; call 911. A continuous glucose monitor may stop reading below its floor: confirm with a finger-stick.
full.mg-giphys:
What's tested
  • The GI hormones: the cell that makes each, what releases it and what it does (gastrin, CCK, secretin, GIP, GLP-1, motilin, ghrelin), plus the paracrines (histamine, somatostatin) and neurocrines (VIP, NO, GRP, substance P)
  • Saliva: which gland makes what, isotonic primary saliva made hypotonic by the ducts, and autonomic control
  • Gastric acid: the parietal cell's pump, its three stimulants and its brakes, and the phases of secretion
  • Motility: slow waves, peristalsis vs segmentation, the migrating motor complex, gastric emptying, the colonic reflexes and defecation
  • Pancreatic and biliary secretion: secretin vs CCK, trypsin activation, bile salts and their recycling
  • Digestion and absorption of carbohydrate, protein and fat; where iron, calcium and B12 are absorbed; water and electrolyte transport and the two kinds of diarrhea

How the gut is controlled

The gut has its own nervous system, the enteric nervous system, which can run without the brain: the submucosal (Meissner) plexus controls secretion and blood flow, and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, between the circular and longitudinal muscle, controls motility. Parasympathetic (vagus, pelvic) input generally speeds digestion; sympathetic input slows it. Chemical messengers act three ways: endocrine (into the blood: gastrin, CCK, secretin, GIP, GLP-1, motilin), paracrine (on neighbors: histamine, somatostatin) and neurocrine (released by nerves: VIP, NO, GRP, substance P, enkephalins).

Histamine comes from ECL cells and acts on H2 receptors of parietal cells. Somatostatin from D cells is the universal brake: released when antral pH falls, it inhibits gastrin and acid. VIP and NO relax smooth muscle (they open the LES) and VIP drives intestinal secretion (a VIPoma causes watery diarrhea, hypokalemia and achlorhydria). GRP carries the vagal signal to G cells, substance P contracts muscle, and enkephalins slow transit (why opioids constipate).

Saliva

The parotid is the largest gland and is purely serous (amylase); the submandibular makes about 60-70% of resting saliva and is mixed; the sublingual makes about 5% and is mostly mucous. Acinar cells make primary saliva that is isotonic to plasma. The ducts reabsorb Na+ and Cl- and secrete K+ and HCO3-, but they let little water through, so final saliva is hypotonic. The faster it flows, the less time the ducts have, so high-flow saliva is closer to plasma and richest in HCO3-. Unusually, both autonomic divisions stimulate saliva: parasympathetic (copious, watery; blocked by atropine) and sympathetic (small volume, protein-rich). Saliva lubricates and buffers, starts starch digestion (α-amylase) and fat digestion (lingual lipase), and defends the mouth (lysozyme, lactoferrin, secretory IgA, mucins).

Gastric secretion

Parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor (the one gastric product we can't live without: it is needed for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum). Inside the cell, carbonic anhydrase makes H+ and HCO3-; the H+/K+ ATPase pumps H+ into the lumen, Cl- follows through apical channels, and HCO3- leaves into the blood in exchange for Cl- (the "alkaline tide" after a meal). Three stimulants act directly: ACh (M3, Ca2+), gastrin (CCK-B receptor, Ca2+) and histamine (H2, cAMP). Histamine potentiates the other two, which is why an H2 blocker cuts acid from every stimulus; a PPI blocks the final pump, so it works whatever the stimulus. Brakes: somatostatin, prostaglandins, low antral pH and, from the duodenum, secretin and GIP. Chief cells make pepsinogen, which acid turns into pepsin; surface mucous cells make the mucus-bicarbonate layer that keeps the mucosal surface near pH 7.

Phases: the cephalic phase (sight, smell, taste, about 30% of the acid) runs entirely through the vagus (direct ACh on parietal cells plus GRP on G cells), so vagotomy abolishes it; the gastric phase (distension, peptides, about 60%) acts through gastrin and local reflexes; the intestinal phase is small and mostly inhibitory.

Motility

Interstitial cells of Cajal set slow waves, the basic electrical rhythm (about 3/min in the stomach, 12/min in the duodenum). A slow wave alone doesn't contract muscle; contraction happens when spike potentials fire on top of it, and nerves and hormones decide how often that happens. Swallowing is voluntary, then a medullary reflex (soft palate up, epiglottis down, UES relaxes), then primary peristalsis, with secondary peristalsis clearing what's left; the LES relaxes through vagal VIP and NO. In achalasia, those inhibitory myenteric neurons are lost, so the LES can't relax: dysphagia to solids and liquids and a "bird's beak" on barium swallow.

Gastric emptying is fastest for liquids and isotonic chyme and slowest for fat (through CCK); acid, hypertonic chyme and duodenal distension also slow it. In the small intestine, segmentation mixes (contraction in the middle of the bolus) and peristalsis propels (contraction behind, relaxation ahead). Between meals the migrating motor complex (MMC, driven by motilin, about every 90 minutes) sweeps residue and bacteria into the colon; without it, bacteria overgrow. In the colon, haustral contractions mix, and mass movements a few times a day push feces into the rectum. Reflexes: gastrocolic (food in the stomach → colonic mass movements), gastroileal (food in the stomach → ileocecal valve relaxes), and the defecation reflex (rectal stretch → rectum contracts and the involuntary internal anal sphincter relaxes, while the voluntary external sphincter decides when).

Pancreas and bile

Pancreatic acinar cells make enzymes (driven by CCK and ACh); duct cells make HCO3- through CFTR (driven by secretin). Secretin and CCK potentiate each other. Proteases are secreted inactive: brush-border enteropeptidase (enterokinase) turns trypsinogen into trypsin, and trypsin activates the rest (chymotrypsin, elastase, carboxypeptidase) and more trypsinogen. Amylase and lipase (with colipase) are secreted active. Pepsin is a stomach enzyme, not a pancreatic one.

Hepatocytes make bile acids from cholesterol and conjugate them with glycine or taurine (bile salts); gut bacteria make the secondary ones. The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile between meals; CCK empties it. About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum by a Na+-coupled transporter and return in portal blood (enterohepatic circulation). Remove or inflame the ileum (Crohn disease) and bile salts are lost: steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and gallstones, with B12 deficiency as well.

NutrientDigested byAbsorbed as / how
CarbohydrateSalivary and pancreatic α-amylase, then brush-border lactase, sucrase, maltaseMonosaccharides only. Glucose and galactose: SGLT1 (Na+-coupled); fructose: GLUT5; all exit by GLUT2
ProteinPepsin, then trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase, carboxypeptidase, brush-border peptidasesAmino acids (Na+-coupled carriers) and di- and tripeptides (PepT1, driven by an H+ gradient)
FatLipase with colipase, after bile salts emulsifyFatty acids and 2-monoglycerides ride micelles to the brush border, are rebuilt into triglyceride and leave as chylomicrons into the lacteals (lymph)
Iron, calciumDuodenum (iron as heme or Fe2+; calcium helped by vitamin D)
Folate / B12Folate in the jejunum; B12 bound to intrinsic factor in the terminal ileum

Water, electrolytes and diarrhea

About 9 L of fluid enter the gut each day (2 L eaten, 7 L secreted): the jejunum absorbs the most, then the ileum, then the colon, leaving about 0.1-0.2 L in stool. Villi absorb; crypts secrete. Na+ is absorbed with glucose and amino acids in the jejunum, as NaCl in the ileum, and through aldosterone-driven ENaC channels in the colon, which also secretes K+ (so diarrhea causes hypokalemia). Crypt cells secrete Cl- through CFTR when cAMP rises. Cholera toxin locks cAMP on, causing a huge secretory diarrhea; oral rehydration works because Na+-glucose cotransport is untouched. Osmotic diarrhea comes from unabsorbed solute (lactase deficiency, magnesium laxatives) and stops with fasting.
full.mg-gianat:
What's tested
  • Foregut, midgut and hindgut: their arteries and boundaries, the stomach's arteries and the main anastomoses
  • Peritoneum: visceral vs parietal pain, referred pain by gut region (appendicitis), retroperitoneal organs, the ligament of Treitz, SMA syndrome
  • Portal-caval anastomoses and what portal hypertension does at each one; the pectinate line
  • Abdominal wall: layers, rectus sheath and the arcuate line, dermatomes, inguinal hernias, diaphragm openings
  • Histology: the four layers, the esophagus, stomach glands and cells, duodenum vs jejunum vs ileum vs colon, oral mucosa, papillae and salivary glands
  • Liver and gallbladder histology: the three lobule models, zones 1-3, sinusoids and their cells

Foregut, midgut, hindgut

RegionArteryExtentPain referred to
ForegutCeliac trunkAbdominal esophagus to the major duodenal papilla (2nd part of duodenum); liver, gallbladder, pancreas (part); spleen is supplied tooEpigastric region
MidgutSuperior mesenteric (SMA)Distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal 2/3 of transverse colonUmbilical region (T10)
HindgutInferior mesenteric (IMA)Distal 1/3 of transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal above the pectinate lineHypogastric (suprapubic) region

Celiac branches: left gastric (lesser curvature, abdominal esophagus), splenic (short gastrics to the fundus, left gastroepiploic to the greater curvature, pancreatic branches) and common hepatic. The common hepatic gives the proper hepatic (right and left hepatic, right gastric, cystic) and the gastroduodenal (right gastroepiploic, superior pancreaticoduodenals). So: lesser curvature = right and left gastric; greater curvature = right and left gastroepiploic; fundus = short gastrics. A posterior duodenal bulb ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery (major bleeding); an anterior one perforates into the peritoneal cavity.

Anastomoses: superior (celiac) and inferior (SMA) pancreaticoduodenal arteries around the head of the pancreas; the marginal artery joining SMA and IMA colic branches; superior epigastric (internal thoracic) with inferior epigastric (external iliac) inside the rectus sheath.

Peritoneum and position

Parietal peritoneum lines the wall and has somatic nerves: sharp, well localized pain. Visceral peritoneum covers organs and has visceral afferents: dull, poorly localized pain referred by region. Appendicitis starts as periumbilical pain (midgut visceral afferents to T10) and moves to the right lower quadrant (McBurney point) once the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum. A mesentery attached to the back wall is a "meso-"; a fold joining two organs or the front wall is a "ligament"; one attached to the stomach is an omentum. The falciform ligament holds the ligamentum teres (old umbilical vein); the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) holds the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, with the epiploic foramen behind it.

Retroperitoneal ("SAD PUCKER"): suprarenal glands, aorta and IVC, duodenum (parts 2-4), pancreas (not the tail), ureters, colon (ascending and descending), kidneys, esophagus, rectum. The transverse and sigmoid colon, jejunum, ileum and stomach are intraperitoneal. The ligament of Treitz at the duodenojejunal flexure divides upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) from lower (bright red blood per rectum). SMA syndrome: the 3rd part of the duodenum is squeezed between the SMA and aorta (often after rapid weight loss). Nutcracker syndrome: the left renal vein is squeezed there instead, backing up the left gonadal vein.

Portal-caval anastomoses

Unpaired gut organs drain to the portal vein, which carries about 75% of the liver's blood (the hepatic artery the rest). When cirrhosis raises portal pressure, blood takes portal-caval shortcuts:

SitePortal sideCaval sideResult
EsophagusLeft gastric veinEsophageal veins to the azygosEsophageal varices (life-threatening hematemesis)
UmbilicusParaumbilical veinsSuperficial epigastric veinsCaput medusae
RectumSuperior rectal veinMiddle and inferior rectal veinsAnorectal varices (often listed as hemorrhoids)

Pectinate line: above it the canal is hindgut (endoderm): superior rectal artery (IMA), portal venous drainage, visceral nerves (painless internal hemorrhoids), adenocarcinoma. Below it, ectoderm: inferior rectal artery (internal iliac via internal pudendal), caval drainage, somatic pudendal nerves (painful external hemorrhoids), lymph to superficial inguinal nodes, squamous cell carcinoma.

Abdominal wall

Superficial to deep: skin, superficial fascia (fatty Camper, membranous Scarpa), external oblique (down and in), internal oblique (up and in), transversus abdominis (horizontal), transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum. Their aponeuroses form the rectus sheath. Above the arcuate line the sheath has anterior and posterior layers; below it all three aponeuroses pass in front, so only transversalis fascia lies behind the rectus. Linea alba is the midline; linea semilunaris is the lateral edge of the rectus. Dermatomes: T4 nipple, T6 xiphoid, T10 umbilicus, L1 groin.

Inguinal canal: from the deep ring (in transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels) to the superficial ring (external oblique aponeurosis); it carries the spermatic cord or the round ligament, plus the ilioinguinal nerve. An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through a patent processus vaginalis (congenital, the most common type). A direct hernia pushes through Hesselbach triangle (inferior epigastric vessels, rectus edge, inguinal ligament), medial to the vessels, where the transversalis fascia is weak (older men). "MDs don't LIe": Medial = Direct, Lateral = Indirect. Umbilical folds: median (urachus; a patent urachus leaks urine at the umbilicus), medial (obliterated umbilical arteries), lateral (inferior epigastric vessels).

Diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3-C5): IVC at T8, esophagus and vagal trunks at T10, aorta, thoracic duct and azygos at T12 ("I 8 10 eggs at 12"). The spleen sits under ribs 9-11 in the left upper quadrant, the organ most often injured in blunt left-side trauma.

GI histology

Four layers everywhere: mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa (vessels, Meissner plexus, glands in the esophagus and duodenum), muscularis externa (inner circular, outer longitudinal, Auerbach plexus between; the stomach adds an inner oblique layer), and serosa (free organs) or adventitia (fixed ones like the esophagus).

RegionSignature features
EsophagusNonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium; submucosal esophageal glands; muscle skeletal in the upper third, mixed in the middle, smooth in the lower third; abrupt squamous-to-columnar Z-line at the stomach
StomachRugae, gastric pits, no villi. Cardia and pylorus: mucous glands (G cells in the antrum). Fundus and body: oxyntic glands with parietal cells (pink, upper gland: HCl, intrinsic factor) and chief cells (basophilic, gland base: pepsinogen), mucous neck cells, ECL and D cells
DuodenumVilli plus Brunner glands in the submucosa (alkaline mucus); bile and pancreatic ducts open at the major papilla
JejunumTallest plicae circulares and long villi; no Brunner glands; the main site of absorption
IleumPeyer patches (lymphoid follicles) with M cells that sample antigens; most goblet cells of the small intestine
ColonNo villi or plicae; straight crypts full of goblet cells; teniae coli, haustra, epiploic appendages

Small intestine surface area is amplified by plicae circulares (mucosa plus submucosa), villi (mucosa) and microvilli (the brush border, the largest gain). Villi absorb; crypts of Lieberkühn hold stem cells and secrete, with Paneth cells at their base releasing lysozyme and defensins.

Oral mucosa: masticatory (gingiva, hard palate: keratinized or parakeratinized, bound to bone), lining (lips, cheeks, floor of mouth, ventral tongue, soft palate: nonkeratinized), specialized (dorsal tongue). Papillae: filiform (most numerous, keratinized, rasping, no taste buds), fungiform (scattered, taste buds), circumvallate (8-12 in a V, taste buds in the trench, serous von Ebner glands), foliate (lateral). Taste buds have gustatory, supporting and basal (stem) cells. The vermilion has thin keratin and tall vascular papillae (its red color) but no glands.

Salivary glands: acinus → intercalated duct → striated duct (basal mitochondria for ion transport) → excretory ducts; myoepithelial cells squeeze the acini. Serous acini stain dark with round nuclei; mucous ones are pale with flattened basal nuclei; serous demilunes cap mucous tubules. Parotid: all serous. Submandibular: mixed, mostly serous. Sublingual: mostly mucous. Plasma cells make dimeric IgA (J chain); the epithelium carries it into saliva and adds secretory component.

Liver and gallbladder

Three ways to draw the lobule: the classic lobule (hexagon around a central vein, portal triads at the corners; blood flow), the portal lobule (triangle around a triad; bile flow) and the hepatic acinus (diamond between two central veins; the metabolic unit). In the acinus, zone 1 (periportal) gets the most oxygen; zone 3 (centrilobular) gets the least and has the most CYP450, so it is hit first by ischemia, acetaminophen and alcohol. Blood runs from triad to central vein; bile runs the other way, from canaliculi between hepatocytes to the ducts of the triad. Sinusoids have fenestrated, discontinuous endothelium over the space of Disse; Kupffer cells are the resident macrophages; stellate (Ito) cells store vitamin A and, when activated, lay down the collagen of fibrosis. The gallbladder has simple columnar epithelium that concentrates bile, a smooth muscle coat, and no muscularis mucosae or submucosa.
full.mg-gipath:
What's tested
  • Esophagus and stomach: GERD and Barrett esophagus, esophageal cancers, H. pylori and peptic ulcers, NSAID injury, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
  • Bowel: celiac disease, Crohn disease vs ulcerative colitis, C. difficile colitis, diverticular disease, Hirschsprung disease, colorectal cancer and the polyp syndromes with oral signs
  • Liver: injury patterns, the hepatitis viruses, alcoholic and fatty liver disease, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, acetaminophen, cirrhosis and its complications, jaundice and gallstones
  • The patient with liver disease in the dental chair: bleeding tests, analgesics, infection control
  • GI drugs: PPIs, H2 blockers, antacids, misoprostol and bismuth; antiemetics; antidiarrheals and laxatives; IBD drugs

Esophagus and stomach

GERD is reflux through an incompetent LES (transient relaxations, hiatal hernia, obesity, pregnancy, scleroderma): heartburn, regurgitation, cough and hoarseness, and in the mouth, erosion of the palatal surfaces of the maxillary teeth (bulimia does the same). Long-standing reflux can turn the distal squamous lining into intestinal columnar epithelium with goblet cells, Barrett esophagus, the precursor of adenocarcinoma of the lower esophagus. Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus (upper and middle thirds) follows alcohol and tobacco. A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful vomiting.

H. pylori is a curved, flagellated gram-negative rod whose urease makes ammonia that buffers the acid around it. It causes chronic antral gastritis, about 90% of duodenal ulcers and most gastric ulcers, and raises the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Duodenal ulcer pain tends to ease with food; gastric ulcer pain worsens with it. Diagnose with a urea breath test, stool antigen or biopsy; treat with a PPI plus antibiotics (clarithromycin with amoxicillin or metronidazole), or bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, metronidazole, tetracycline). NSAIDs are the other main cause: blocking COX-1 removes the prostaglandins that keep mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow up, and the risk climbs with anticoagulants, corticosteroids, SSRIs and age. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a gastrin-secreting tumor (pancreas or duodenum, sometimes with MEN1): severe, multiple or jejunal ulcers and diarrhea, treated with high-dose PPI.

Bowel

Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten in HLA-DQ2/DQ8 carriers: anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA, and a duodenal biopsy with villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes. It causes malabsorption (bulky stools, iron-deficiency anemia), dermatitis herpetiformis and, in the mouth, aphthous ulcers and symmetric enamel defects. Treatment is a gluten-free diet.

Crohn diseaseUlcerative colitis
WhereAnywhere mouth to anus, most often terminal ileum; skip lesionsRectum, spreading continuously up the colon
DepthTransmural: fistulas, strictures, abscessesMucosa and submucosa: crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps
HallmarksNoncaseating granulomas, cobblestone mucosa, creeping fat; smoking worsens itBloody diarrhea, toxic megacolon, primary sclerosing cholangitis; higher colon cancer risk
MouthCobblestoning, linear ulcers, mucosal tags, lip swelling, aphthaeAphthae; pyostomatitis vegetans ("snail-track" pustules)

C. difficile colitis follows antibiotics (clindamycin is the classic one, also cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones) and PPIs: toxins A and B, watery diarrhea, pseudomembranes. Treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin and avoid antimotility drugs. Diverticulosis (outpouchings, mostly sigmoid, low-fiber diets) can bleed painlessly; diverticulitis gives left lower quadrant pain and fever. Hirschsprung disease: neural crest cells fail to reach the distal colon, the aganglionic segment can't relax, and the colon above it dilates (delayed meconium). Colorectal adenocarcinoma is among the top causes of cancer death and usually follows the adenoma-carcinoma sequence (APC, then KRAS, then p53). Syndromes a dentist may spot first: Gardner syndrome (an APC variant of familial adenomatous polyposis: jaw osteomas, supernumerary and impacted teeth, odontomas, epidermoid cysts; colon cancer is nearly certain without colectomy) and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11: hamartomatous polyps and dark macules on the lips and buccal mucosa). GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal (c-KIT).

Liver

Acute hepatitis shows ballooning hepatocytes and apoptotic (Councilman) bodies; chronic hepatitis shows portal inflammation and, with time, bridging fibrosis that ends in cirrhosis: regenerative nodules wrapped in fibrous septa.

Alcoholic liver disease runs from reversible steatosis to alcoholic hepatitis (Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophils, AST:ALT above 2) to cirrhosis. Fatty liver disease without alcohol (NAFLD/NASH) tracks obesity, diabetes and the metabolic syndrome. Hemochromatosis (HFE, autosomal recessive) deposits iron in liver, pancreas, heart and skin: cirrhosis, "bronze diabetes," heart failure; treat with phlebotomy. Wilson disease (ATP7B) deposits copper in the liver, basal ganglia and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings), with low ceruloplasmin. Acetaminophen overdose: CYP450 makes the toxic NAPQI, glutathione runs out, zone 3 dies; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione, and chronic alcohol use lowers the safe dose.

Cirrhosis brings portal hypertension (varices, ascites, splenomegaly with low platelets, caput medusae), hepatic encephalopathy (ammonia; treated with lactulose and rifaximin), coagulopathy (the liver makes factors II, VII, IX and X), low albumin, jaundice, spider angiomas and gynecomastia (estrogen isn't cleared) and a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Jaundice appears above about 2-3 mg/dL of bilirubin: unconjugated from hemolysis or Gilbert syndrome; conjugated from obstruction (dark urine, pale stools, itching). Gallstones are mostly cholesterol stones (female, over 40, obesity, pregnancy); pigment stones follow hemolysis. A stone in the cystic duct causes cholecystitis; in the common bile duct, jaundice; at the ampulla, pancreatitis.

The dental patient with liver disease

  • Bleeding: check the PT/INR (clotting factor synthesis) and the platelet count (splenic sequestration) before surgery; use local hemostatic measures.
  • Drugs: acetaminophen at a reduced dose (about 2 g a day at most) is the usual choice; avoid NSAIDs in cirrhosis (bleeding, ulcers, kidney injury); amide local anesthetics such as lidocaine are cleared by the liver, so keep doses modest; sedatives last longer.
  • Infection control: standard precautions and hepatitis B vaccination for the whole team; after a needlestick, HBV transmits far more readily than HCV, and HCV more than HIV.
  • Oral signs: yellow soft palate and floor of mouth, petechiae and gingival bleeding, glossitis, parotid enlargement and xerostomia in alcohol use.

full.eb-ask:
What's tested
  • The 5 A's in order (ask, acquire, appraise, apply, assess) and what each step does
  • Building a PICO(T) question and picking P, I, C, O and T out of a case; background versus foreground questions; the four kinds of clinical question and the design that best answers each
  • Where to search: TRIP first, then PubMed Clinical Queries, then the Cochrane Library
  • Naming the design from a short description, and what case-control and cohort studies are each good and bad at
  • The evidence pyramid, and literature review versus systematic review versus meta-analysis versus clinical practice guideline (GRADE, AGREE)
  • Efficacy versus effectiveness, the study-context continuum, practice-based research networks and the three gaps between evidence and practice

The 5 A's

Evidence-based dentistry combines the best available research with the dentist's clinical expertise and the patient's needs and values. It runs as five steps, always in this order.

StepWhat you do
1. AskTurn the patient's problem into a focused, answerable question (PICO).
2. AcquireSearch for the best evidence: TRIP, PubMed, Cochrane.
3. AppraiseJudge it: is the design the strongest one for this question, is the study valid, are the results important?
4. ApplyCombine the evidence with your expertise and the patient's values, and decide together.
5. AssessCheck the result: did it work, did the patient follow through, what would you change next time?

Apply and assess are the pair people mix up: apply is using the evidence with this patient; assess is looking back at how it went.

Asking: PICO(T)

  • P (patient, population or problem): the few characteristics that matter (age, condition), neither so broad that it means nothing nor so narrow that no study fits.
  • I (intervention or exposure): the treatment, test or risk factor you are asking about.
  • C (comparison): ideally one alternative, such as standard care, a placebo or no treatment. It is sometimes only implied.
  • O (outcome): specific and measurable (new caries, pain score, implant survival), never "better care".
  • T (time): optional in the question and easy to forget, but every study answering it needs a time frame.

Template: "In [P], does [I], compared with [C], change [O] over [T]?" For example: "In children with primary teeth, does fluoride toothpaste, compared with non-fluoride toothpaste, lower caries incidence over one year?" A classic mistake is a population that makes the comparison impossible, such as comparing smokers with nonsmokers in a population defined as smokers.

BackgroundForeground
AsksGeneral knowledge about one condition or treatment (who, what, when, why, how)A comparison of two or more options for a specific patient or problem
Example"What are the side effects of ibuprofen?""After third-molar extraction, is ibuprofen plus acetaminophen as good as an opioid for pain?"
PICO?No: a textbook or review answers itYes
Question typeAsks aboutBest design
TherapyWhich treatment does more good than harmRandomized controlled trial
DiagnosisHow well a test identifies a diseaseCross-sectional comparison against a reference (gold) standard
PrognosisThe likely course of a disease, or what predicts itCohort
Etiology or harmCauses and risk factors; harm from an exposure or treatmentCohort or case-control (assigning a harm would be unethical)

Acquiring: where to search

  • TRIP first: one search returns guidelines, systematic reviews and primary studies, sorted by level of evidence.
  • PubMed (MEDLINE, from the National Library of Medicine) next: the largest biomedical database. Clinical Queries filters it by question type (therapy, diagnosis, etiology, prognosis) and pulls out systematic reviews.
  • Cochrane Library: rigorous systematic reviews, mostly of randomized trials.
  • Also: journals through the UAB library, the ADA's clinical practice guidelines and evidence-based journals. Expert opinion is the last resort.

Study designs

The first split is who decides the exposure. In an experimental study the investigator assigns it; in an observational study the investigator only watches exposures people already have. Observational studies are descriptive (no comparison group: case reports and series) or analytic (a comparison: ecological, cross-sectional, case-control, cohort).

DesignHow it worksGood forWeak spots
Case report or seriesOne unusual patient, or several with the same condition or treatment, describedNew diseases and side effects; ideas for trialsNo comparison group; the lowest inferential power of human studies
Ecological (correlational)Compares averages of groups (cities, countries)Cheap; uses existing dataEcological fallacy: the exposed people may not be the ones with the outcome
Cross-sectionalA snapshot: exposure and outcome measured at the same time in the same people, often by surveyPrevalence; quick and cheapNo time order, so no cause and effect
Case-controlStarts with the outcome: cases with the disease and controls without, then looks back for exposuresRare diseases, long latency, many risk factors at once; quick and cheapRecall and selection bias; poor for rare exposures; no incidence; gives an odds ratio
CohortStarts with the exposure: exposed and unexposed people followed for the outcome (prospective, or retrospective from records)Time order; incidence and relative risk; rare exposures; several outcomes of one exposureSlow and costly; loss to follow-up; poor for rare diseases
Controlled trialThe investigator allocates people to treatment or control without randomizingThe investigator controls the exposureAllocation can be biased
Randomized controlled trialRandom allocation to treatment or control, followed forwardThe only true experiment: randomization balances known and unknown factors, so it best shows cause and effectCostly; can't test a harmful exposure; strict entry rules limit whom it applies to

Clues in a stem: "looked back" from a disease is case-control; "followed" exposed and unexposed people is cohort; "surveyed once" is cross-sectional; cities or countries is ecological; "randomly assigned" is an RCT.

The evidence pyramid

From bottom to top, as the course draws it: animal and lab studies; case reports, case series and expert opinion; ecological; cross-sectional; case-control; cohort; randomized controlled trials; systematic reviews and meta-analyses; clinical practice guidelines. Higher means stronger evidence for a clinical decision, if the study is done well. Two twists: lab and animal studies control every variable, so they have the greatest inferential power (rigor) when done properly, yet they sit at the bottom because they apply least to patients. And many published pyramids put systematic reviews at the very top, where the course puts guidelines, which build their recommendations on those reviews.

Pre-appraised (filtered) evidence

Literature reviewSystematic reviewMeta-analysisClinical practice guideline
Summarizes the evidence?MaybeYesYesYes
Methods section?No: a narrative; the author picks the studiesYes: a full, reproducible search and a quality grade for each studyYes: a systematic review plus a summary statistic pooling the studies' dataYes: integrates the evidence to approach a clinical problem
Whose view?The author'sCollects and grades the evidenceCollects, grades and combines itEvidence, plus expert opinion where evidence is missing or weak
  • GRADE rates the certainty of a body of evidence as high, moderate, low or very low. Randomized trials start high and observational studies start low; risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness (surrogate outcomes), imprecision and publication bias rate it down.
  • AGREE (Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation) judges the quality of clinical practice guidelines.
  • Reporting checklists: CONSORT for randomized trials, STROBE for observational studies, PRISMA for systematic reviews.
  • A forest plot shows each study as a square (bigger means more weight) on a line (its 95% confidence interval). The diamond at the bottom is the pooled result: its center is the estimate and its tips the 95% CI. A diamond that crosses the line of no effect (1 for a ratio) is not significant.

From research to practice

Study contexts run along a continuum: lab research (the treatment isn't ready for humans), clinical trials in academic settings (not ready for everyday patients; they test efficacy), practice-based research (not yet ready for all practices; it tests effectiveness) and community-based research (outside the health care system).

EfficacyEffectiveness
AsksDoes it work under ideal conditions?Does it work in the real world?
SettingAn academic health center, usually an RCTEveryday practices
PatientsHighly selectedTypical
CliniciansHighly trained, with no time or cost limitsTypical, with the usual time and money limits

A practice-based research network (PBRN) is a group of dental practices that join to answer research questions in daily practice, where most people get their care; a national dental PBRN has run since 2005.

GapWhat's wrongWhat closes it
Knowledge gapThe evidence doesn't exist yetEfficacy and effectiveness studies
Knowing gapThe evidence exists, but clinicians don't know itDissemination science
Knowing-to-doing gapClinicians know it but don't use it (patient acceptance, habit, cost)Implementation science

The "magic pill" example: if about half drop out at each step (hear of it, try it, prescribe it, the patient accepts it, the patient keeps taking it), very few patients end up helped.
full.eb-appraise:
What's tested
  • Internal versus external validity, and the three threats to validity: bias, confounding and chance
  • The kinds of bias and what randomization, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis do about them; what to check in an RCT
  • Standardization versus calibration, inter- versus intra-examiner reliability, precision versus accuracy, incidence versus prevalence
  • Types of data, mean versus median, and standard deviation
  • Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values from a 2×2 table, and which one a screening or a confirming test needs
  • Relative risk, odds ratio, absolute risk and the number needed to treat; reading a ratio with its 95% confidence interval
  • p-values, type I and II errors, power, and statistical versus clinical significance

Is the study valid?

Internal validityExternal validity
AsksWas the study well designed, run and analyzed?Was the study population well defined, and enrolled with that definition in mind?
MeansThe findings are believable for the people studiedThe findings apply (generalize) to your patients

Three things threaten validity: bias, any systematic error that skews the estimate of the link between exposure and outcome (a bigger sample doesn't fix it); confounding, a third factor tied to both the exposure and the outcome (studying soda and caries without accounting for oral hygiene); and chance, random variation in who was sampled (handled by sample size and statistics).

BiasWhat happensTypical design
SelectionThe way people are chosen makes the groups unlike each other or unlike the population (recruiting in a park for an exercise study)Any, especially case-control
RecallCases remember past exposures differently from controlsCase-control
Attrition (loss to follow-up)Those who drop out differ from those who stayCohort, RCT
Self-report (social desirability)People underreport smoking or overreport flossingSurveys, cross-sectional
Measurement (observer)An examiner who knows the group scores it differentlyUnblinded trials
PublicationPositive results are published more often than negative onesSystematic reviews (search the gray literature)

Confounding is controlled by randomization (the only method that also balances unknown factors), restriction, matching, stratification and statistical adjustment.

Appraising a randomized trial

  • Randomization done properly (for example, computer-generated and concealed), not circumvented, with the groups balanced at baseline.
  • Blinding (masking): in a double-blind trial neither the participants nor the clinicians and assessors know who got what. The groups must be treated alike apart from the intervention.
  • Intention-to-treat analysis: everyone is analyzed in the group they were randomized to, whether or not they finished or followed the treatment, which keeps randomization's balance. A per-protocol analysis counts only those who completed the treatment as planned and can overstate the benefit.
  • Subgroups planned at the start; a subgroup found afterward (reporting only the women because it worked better in them) is a red flag.
  • Sample size calculated beforehand, the trial registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and reported by CONSORT (enrollment, allocation, follow-up, analysis).
  • Applicability: patient-important outcomes rather than surrogate outcomes (a plaque index in place of tooth loss), an effect large enough to matter, long enough follow-up, benefits and harms both reported, good compliance, and participants like your patients.

Measuring well

  • Standardization: every examiner uses the same criteria, instruments and procedure. Calibration: examiners score the same patients and train until their scores agree; it takes longer.
  • Reliability (repeatability): inter-examiner, different examiners get the same score; intra-examiner, the same examiner gets the same score on the same patient at different times; test-retest, the same person answers the same questionnaire again 1–2 weeks later.
  • Precision is repeatability (reliability); accuracy is closeness to the truth (validity). An examiner who always records the same wrong probing depth is precise but not accurate.
  • Incidence is new cases over a period among people at risk (it needs follow-up: a cohort); prevalence is all existing cases at one time (a cross-sectional study).
  • A census measures everyone, so no inference is needed; a sample measures some and relies on statistics.

Data and the center

TypeWhat it isExamplesUsual graph
QuantitativeNumbers you can add or subtractAge, blood pressure, millimeters of bone lossHistogram, box plot
BinaryTwo categoriesDisease or no disease, treatment or controlBar chart
NominalNamed categories with no orderBlood type, occupationBar chart
OrdinalCategories with a rankCancer stage, light/moderate/heavy smokerBar chart

The mean is pulled by outliers; the median (the middle value) is the better center for skewed data. The standard deviation measures spread around the mean, and two data sets with the same mean can have very different SDs. In a normal curve about 68% of values fall within 1 SD and 95% within 2. A correlation coefficient runs from −1 (perfect negative) through 0 (none) to +1 (perfect positive); correlation doesn't prove cause.

Diagnostic tests

Disease presentDisease absent
Test positiveTrue positive (a)False positive (b)
Test negativeFalse negative (c)True negative (d)
  • Sensitivity = a/(a+c): of the people with the disease, the share who test positive (the true positive rate). A highly sensitive test misses few cases, so a negative result rules the disease out (SnNout). Screening tests need it.
  • Specificity = d/(b+d): of the people without the disease, the share who test negative (the true negative rate). A highly specific test has few false positives, so a positive result rules the disease in (SpPin). Use it to confirm before an irreversible step such as an extraction.
  • PPV = a/(a+b) and NPV = d/(c+d). Predictive values change with prevalence: where a disease is rarer, PPV falls and NPV rises. Sensitivity and specificity don't change with prevalence.
  • Moving a test's cutoff to catch more disease raises sensitivity and lowers specificity. That is why the class notes say a highly sensitive test "can lead to false positives": the false positives come from the specificity it gives up.

Example: a caries device tested on 100 decayed and 100 sound teeth is positive on 90 decayed and 20 sound teeth. Sensitivity 90/100 = 90%; specificity 80/100 = 80%; PPV 90/110 = 82%; NPV 80/90 = 89%.

Risk and the size of an effect

  • Absolute risk = events ÷ people in the group; odds = events ÷ non-events (200 of 600 with arthritis: risk 0.33, odds 0.5).
  • Relative risk (risk ratio) = risk in the exposed ÷ risk in the unexposed, from cohorts and RCTs. 1 means no difference, above 1 a harmful effect, below 1 a protective one (0.87 means 13% lower risk). A hazard ratio reads the same way over time.
  • Odds ratio = (a×d)/(b×c), the measure from case-control studies; it approximates the relative risk when the outcome is rare.
  • Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = control risk − treated risk, and NNT = 1/ARR, rounded up (NNH for a harm). Caries in 25% of controls and 15% of treated children: ARR 10%, NNT 10, though the relative risk reduction is 40%.
  • The lecture's pain NNT is how many patients must take an analgesic for one more to get at least 50% pain relief over 4–6 hours than with placebo: 1 is perfect and lower is better. Ibuprofen with acetaminophen (about 1.5) beats oxycodone 5 mg (about 5.5).
  • Relative risk can mislead when the event is rare: armor that makes you "8 times less likely" to be hit by a meteorite changes almost nothing in absolute terms.

Significance and errors

  • The p-value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if there were truly no difference. Below the chosen alpha (usually 0.05) the result is statistically significant. It doesn't measure how big or important the effect is.
  • The 95% confidence interval is the range of plausible true values. For a ratio, an interval that includes 1 is not significant (HR 0.92, CI 0.83–1.02); for a difference, one that includes 0. A narrower interval is a more precise estimate.
  • Type I error (alpha): a false positive, finding a difference that isn't real. Type II error (beta): a false negative, missing a real difference, most likely in a small study.
  • Power = 1 − beta (usually set at 80%), the chance of detecting a real difference. A larger sample, a bigger true difference, less variability and more accurate measurement raise it; a stricter alpha lowers it.
  • Statistical is not clinical significance: a huge trial can make a trivial difference significant. Judge the size of the effect, its interval, and whether it matters to patients.

plain.hn-neck:
What's tested
  • How spinal nerves and the two autonomic systems are laid out
  • Horner syndrome
  • What lives in the posterior and anterior triangles
  • The root of the neck, the thyroid and the nerves at risk in thyroid surgery
  • Neck fascia and how infection spreads

Each spinal nerve has a sensory back root and a motor front root. The sympathetic system starts in the spinal cord from T1 to L2; nerves for the head relay in the superior cervical ganglion and ride along the carotid arteries. The parasympathetic system leaves with cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and the sacral cord; its head relay stations are the ciliary, pterygopalatine, submandibular and otic ganglia.

If the neck's sympathetic chain is cut or squeezed (for example by a lung-top tumor), you get Horner syndrome: a slightly droopy eyelid, a small pupil, and a face that is dry and flushed on that side.

The posterior triangle sits between the SCM, the trapezius and the clavicle. Its most famous content is CN XI, lying just under the fascia: cut it and the patient can't shrug. The skin nerves of the cervical plexus come out at the middle of the SCM's back edge; the great auricular nerve covers the skin over the angle of the jaw.

The anterior triangle holds the strap muscles, the carotid sheath (carotid artery inside, internal jugular vein outside, vagus behind), the carotid sinus (blood pressure sensor) and body (oxygen sensor), and the external carotid's eight branches. The hyoid is at C3 and the cricoid at C6.

At the root of the neck, the subclavian artery is split into three parts by the anterior scalene. The phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) runs down that muscle to the diaphragm. The thoracic duct empties where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet.

In thyroid surgery, the nerve near the superior thyroid artery (external laryngeal) controls pitch, and the nerve near the inferior thyroid artery (recurrent laryngeal) controls most of the voice box; injuring it makes the voice hoarse. Removing the parathyroids by mistake drops calcium and causes muscle spasms.

Neck fascia forms tubes and spaces. The spaces behind the pharynx can carry an infection from a tooth or tonsil down into the chest.
plain.hn-skull:
What's tested
  • The bones and weak spots of the skull
  • What passes through the main skull openings
  • Dural sinuses and the cavernous sinus
  • Head bleeds
  • What each cranial nerve does and how it fails

The braincase is 8 bones; the face is built from the rest. The pterion, on the side of the head, is thin bone over the middle meningeal artery. A hard blow there can tear the artery and cause an epidural bleed: lens-shaped on CT, often with a period of feeling fine before the patient crashes.

Learn the openings in pairs: V2 through the foramen rotundum, V3 through the foramen ovale, the middle meningeal artery through the foramen spinosum; III, IV, V1 and VI through the superior orbital fissure; VII and VIII into the internal acoustic meatus; IX, X and XI through the jugular foramen; XII through its own canal.

Venous blood collects in the dural sinuses and leaves through the internal jugular vein. The cavernous sinus, next to the pituitary, holds the internal carotid and CN VI, with III, IV, V1 and V2 in its wall. Infection from the face or teeth can reach it; the first sign is often an eye that can't look outward (CN VI).

A subdural bleed comes from torn bridging veins (crescent shape, often older people after a small fall). A subarachnoid bleed comes from a burst aneurysm and gives a sudden, terrible headache.

Cranial nerve signs to know: the tongue points toward a bad XII; the uvula points away from a bad X; a bad III gives a droopy lid, a big pupil and an eye turned down and out; Bell palsy (VII nerve) paralyzes the whole half-face, but a stroke spares the forehead.

Two reflexes tie nerves together: touching the cornea is felt by V1 and answered by VII (blink); touching the throat is felt by IX and answered by X (gag).
plain.hn-face:
What's tested
  • The orbit and its fractures
  • How the eye muscles and pupil are controlled
  • Face muscles and facial nerve palsy
  • The danger triangle and the scalp
  • Tears and the parotid gland

The orbit's floor is the weakest wall. A punch to the eye can blow it out into the maxillary sinus, trapping the inferior rectus (the patient can't look up and sees double) and numbing the cheek.

Eye muscles: LR6, SO4, all the rest III. The superior oblique is tested by looking down and in. CN III also opens the eyelid and shrinks the pupil; the sympathetics widen the pupil. For close work, the ciliary muscle tightens and the lens gets rounder. Fluid made in the eye drains at the angle into the canal of Schlemm; when it can't, pressure rises (glaucoma).

All face muscles belong to VII, which splits into five branches inside the parotid. Feeling on the face comes from V1, V2 and V3. In Bell palsy the whole half-face is weak, forehead too. A dental block placed too far back can do this for a few hours.

Face veins around the nose link to the veins of the eye and on to the cavernous sinus, so infections in the danger triangle are serious. In the scalp, the loose layer under the aponeurosis is where blood and pus spread.

Tears come from a gland at the upper outer corner, run to the inner corner and drain into the nose (inferior meatus). The nerve signal for tears comes from VII and relays in the pterygopalatine ganglion.

The parotid is wrapped in tight fascia. The facial nerve runs through it but does not control it; spit from the parotid is driven by IX through the otic ganglion and the auriculotemporal nerve. Its duct opens opposite the upper second molar. After parotid surgery some people sweat on the cheek when they eat (Frey syndrome).
plain.hn-itf:
What's tested
  • What is in the infratemporal fossa
  • The four chewing muscles
  • V3 and its branches, and the blocks dentists give
  • The maxillary artery and the pterygoid plexus
  • How the TMJ moves and dislocates

The infratemporal fossa is the space behind and inside the ramus. It holds the two pterygoid muscles, the maxillary artery, the pterygoid venous plexus and V3, which enters from the foramen ovale.

Chewing muscles all come from arch 1 and all use V3. Three close the jaw (temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid). The lateral pterygoid pulls the jaw forward and opens it. If V3 is cut on one side, the jaw swings toward that side when the mouth opens.

V3's front branch is mostly motor, except the buccal nerve to the cheek. The back branch gives the auriculotemporal nerve (temple, ear, TMJ), the lingual nerve (tongue feeling; it picks up the chorda tympani for taste) and the inferior alveolar nerve (lower teeth, then the mental nerve to the lip and chin).

An inferior alveolar block puts anesthetic in the space between the ramus and the medial pterygoid. It misses the buccal nerve. Too far back reaches the parotid and the facial nerve. A posterior superior alveolar block too deep can hit the pterygoid plexus and cause a sudden bruise-like swelling.

The maxillary artery has three parts: the first gives the middle meningeal and inferior alveolar arteries, the second feeds the chewing muscles, the third gives the arteries for the upper teeth, palate and nose. The pterygoid plexus links to the cavernous sinus, a path for dental infection.

The TMJ has a disc that makes two joints: the lower one hinges, the upper one slides. It dislocates forward, in front of the articular eminence, usually from a big yawn. The joint is fed by the auriculotemporal nerve, which also supplies the ear canal, so a sore TMJ often feels like an earache.
plain.da-numbering:
What's tested
  • Writing any tooth in Universal, Palmer and FDI
  • When teeth come in, and in what order
  • When teeth start to harden and when roots finish
  • How baby teeth differ from adult teeth

Naming teeth

Universal numbers adult teeth 1 to 32, starting at the upper right third molar and going around to the lower right third molar. Baby teeth use letters A to T the same way. FDI uses two digits: the quadrant (1 upper right, 2 upper left, 3 lower left, 4 lower right; 5 to 8 for baby teeth), then the tooth counted from the midline. So #8 is 11, #19 is 36, #30 is 46, and baby tooth A is 55. Palmer uses a bracket for the quadrant and counts 1 to 8 (A to E for baby teeth) from the midline.

When teeth come in

Baby teeth: central incisors, lateral incisors, first molars, canines, then second molars, from about 6 months to 2 years. The lower teeth usually come first. Adult teeth: the first molars and lower central incisors arrive at about 6. The upper order is 6-1-2-4-5-3-7-8, so the upper canine comes after the premolars, at 11–12, and is the anterior tooth most likely to get stuck. The lower order is 6-1-2-3-4-5-7-8. The first adult tooth to replace a baby tooth is the lower central incisor. Adult molars replace nothing, so they are not "succedaneous".

Hardening and roots

Baby teeth start hardening before birth (about 4–6 months in the womb). The adult first molar starts at birth. Cusp tips and incisal edges harden first, and crowns before roots. An adult root finishes 2–3 years after the tooth comes in; baby roots finish by about age 3.

Baby versus adult teeth

Baby teeth are smaller and whiter, with thin enamel, big pulps and high pulp horns. Their crowns are short and bulge at the neck (cervical ridges), and their molar roots spread wide to leave room for the premolars. A few are one of a kind: the upper central is wider than it is tall, the upper canine has its longer slope on the mesial, and the lower first molar has a big transverse ridge and a bulge at the mesiobuccal. The second baby molars look like the adult first molars.
plain.da-anterior:
What's tested
  • Where the bulge of each surface is
  • Where teeth touch, and the exceptions
  • Telling the incisors apart
  • Upper versus lower canine

Bulges and contacts

Every tooth's facial bulge is in the cervical third. On the tongue side, front teeth bulge in the cervical third and back teeth in the middle third. A crown that is too bulky lets food skip the gum and collects plaque; one that is too flat pushes food into the gum. Teeth touch lower (more cervically) the farther back they are, and each tooth touches its back neighbor lower than its front one. The exceptions are the lower central incisor (both contacts level), the lower first premolar and the baby upper canine. The gap on the tongue side between teeth is bigger than on the cheek side. The CEJ dips most on the mesial of the central incisors.

Incisors

The upper central is the biggest incisor, with a sharp mesial corner and a rounded distal one. The upper lateral is a smaller, rounder copy with a deep lingual fossa; it can have a groove running onto the root that traps plaque, and it often comes in peg-shaped or not at all. The lower central is the smallest adult tooth and nearly symmetric. The lower lateral is a bit bigger, with its incisal edge twisted toward the distolingual.

Canines

The upper canine is the longest tooth with the longest root, a sharp cusp, a short mesial slope and a strong lingual ridge. The lower canine has the longest crown, a long distal slope, a smooth lingual side, and a mesial outline that runs straight into the root; its root can split in two. The upper canine is the last front tooth to come in, so it is the one that gets stuck. Its long root in thick bone also makes it the best tooth to guide the jaw sideways.
plain.da-posterior:
What's tested
  • Which premolar or molar is which
  • How many roots and canals each has
  • First versus second molars

Premolars

The upper first premolar is the one with two roots and a dip (concavity) on its mesial side. The upper second premolar has one root and two cusps of about the same height. The lower first premolar looks like a small canine: a big buccal cusp, a tiny lingual cusp, a crown leaning to the tongue, and a mesial marginal ridge lower than the distal one, which no other back tooth has. The lower second premolar usually has three cusps in a Y pattern with a pit in the middle; with two cusps its grooves look like an H or a U. Lower premolars lean toward the tongue; upper premolars sit straight over their roots.

Upper molars

The upper first molar is the biggest upper tooth. Its cusps from biggest to smallest are mesiolingual, mesiobuccal, distobuccal and distolingual, and the Carabelli cusp sits on the mesiolingual. A ridge (the oblique ridge) runs from the distobuccal to the mesiolingual cusp. It is the only molar wider on the tongue side. It has three roots: palatal longest, then mesiobuccal, then distobuccal. The mesiobuccal root usually holds two canals, so look for four. Its lingual groove and pit are where decay starts. The second molar has a smaller (or missing) distolingual cusp and roots that sit closer together.

Lower molars

The lower first molar has five cusps (three buccal, two lingual) and two buccal grooves; the distal cusp is the smallest. The lower second molar has four cusps in a plus-sign pattern. Both have two roots, mesial and distal; the mesial root is wider, more curved, and holds two canals. Lower molars lean toward the tongue, and their roots lean toward the distal, which helps you tell right from left on an extracted tooth.
plain.da-anomalies:
What's tested
  • Naming an anomaly from a description
  • Fusion versus gemination versus concrescence
  • Inherited versus acquired enamel and dentin defects
  • Types of wear
  • Tooth identification

Too few, too many, in the wrong place

Third molars are the teeth most often missing, then upper laterals and lower second premolars. Missing all teeth goes with ectodermal dysplasia. An extra tooth between the upper centrals is a mesiodens. Third molars and upper canines get impacted most.

Odd shapes

Gemination is one tooth trying to split: count it as one and the count is normal. Fusion is two teeth joined by dentin: count it as one and you are one short. Concrescence is two teeth joined only by cementum. A peg lateral is a small upper lateral. Notched incisors and many-cusped molars point to congenital syphilis. A talon cusp is a claw off the cingulum. Dens in dente is enamel folded into the tooth, usually an upper lateral. Taurodontism is a tall pulp chamber with the furcation pushed down. An enamel pearl at a furcation leaves a pocket.

Enamel and dentin defects

Inherited defects hit every tooth in both sets: amelogenesis imperfecta (bad enamel) and dentinogenesis imperfecta (bluish teeth, chipping enamel, pulps filled in). Fluoride causes white to brown mottling, tetracycline causes gray bands, and an infected baby tooth can spoil the one adult tooth below it (Turner tooth).

Wear

Attrition is tooth against tooth, abrasion is something else rubbing (hard brushing), erosion is acid (vomiting wears the inside of the upper front teeth), and abfraction is a V-shaped notch at the gumline from flexing.

Naming a tooth

Count the cusps for the class, use the roots and tilt for the arch, find the mesial landmark, then hold the face toward you with the mesial at the midline: that side is the patient's side.
plain.f1-biomol:
What's tested
  • Bonds, water, pH and buffers
  • Amino acids and the four levels of protein structure
  • Collagen and vitamin C; hemoglobin's oxygen binding
  • Sugars, fats and DNA's building blocks

The short version

Covalent bonds share electrons and are the strongest. Ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces are weaker and hold a protein's folded shape. Blood stays between pH 7.35 and 7.45, mostly thanks to the bicarbonate buffer.

Proteins are chains of amino acids. The order is the primary structure. Local coils and sheets held by hydrogen bonds are secondary structure. The whole folded shape is tertiary, with oily parts tucked inside. Several chains working together is quaternary, as in hemoglobin. Histidine is the amino acid whose side chain can pick up or drop a proton right around body pH.

Collagen is the body's most common protein, and type I (bone, dentin, skin) is most of it. Every third amino acid is glycine, the only one small enough for the center of the triple rope. Enzymes inside the cell add OH groups to proline and lysine, and those enzymes need vitamin C. No vitamin C means weak collagen: bleeding gums, loose teeth and wounds that won't heal (scurvy). Outside the cell the ends are trimmed and the fibers are cross-linked by a copper enzyme.

Hemoglobin has four chains. When one grabs oxygen, the others grab it more easily, so the binding curve is S-shaped. Acid, carbon dioxide, heat and 2,3-BPG make it let go of oxygen in working tissues. Fetal hemoglobin holds oxygen tighter so the baby can take it from the mother. Myoglobin, in muscle, is a single chain that just stores oxygen.

Sugars: glucose and galactose differ at one carbon (C-4). Sucrose is table sugar, glucose plus fructose, and it is what cavity bacteria use to make sticky plaque. Glycogen is the body's branched glucose store.

Fats: a triglyceride is glycerol plus three fatty acids. Double bonds put kinks in fatty acids and keep fats liquid. Phospholipids make the cell membrane, and cholesterol keeps it from getting too stiff or too runny. Fatty acids are burned inside mitochondria.

DNA: purines (A, G) have two rings, pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one. A pairs with T using two hydrogen bonds; G pairs with C using three. The two strands run in opposite directions and wrap around histone spools.
plain.f1-cells:
What's tested
  • What each organelle does
  • How things cross the membrane
  • How a nerve fires and how drugs and toxins stop it
  • How synapses pass the signal on

The short version

Bacteria have no nucleus and no inner compartments; our cells do. The rough ER makes proteins that will be secreted or put in the membrane, the Golgi ships them, lysosomes digest things in acid (their enzymes carry a mannose-6-phosphate tag), and the proteasome chews up proteins marked with ubiquitin. Mitochondria make ATP and have their own DNA from the mother. Microtubules build the spindle and the inside of cilia; actin lets cells change shape; intermediate filaments are tough ropes. Caspases carry out tidy, planned cell death (apoptosis).

Things cross the membrane downhill on their own (diffusion), downhill through a carrier (facilitated diffusion), uphill using ATP directly (the Na+/K+ pump: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in), or uphill by riding along with Na+ as it flows in (secondary active transport). Water moves toward more dissolved particles: in a dilute (hypotonic) bath a cell swells, in a concentrated one it shrinks.

A resting nerve is about −70 mV inside, close to potassium's balance point, because potassium leaks out. When a stimulus reaches threshold, sodium channels fly open and sodium rushes in: the spike. Then sodium channels shut themselves off and potassium channels open to bring the voltage back down, and a little below. Right after a spike the nerve can't fire again at all, then only with a bigger push. Myelin makes the signal jump from gap to gap, much faster.

Local anesthetics slip into the nerve and plug sodium channels from the inside. In infected, acidic tissue less of the drug can get in, so numbing is harder. High blood potassium also stalls sodium channels.

At a chemical synapse, calcium entering the nerve ending releases the transmitter. Glutamate excites; GABA and glycine calm things down. At muscle, acetylcholine opens channels to start contraction. Botulinum toxin stops acetylcholine from being released, and in myasthenia gravis the body makes antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, so muscles tire quickly.
plain.f1-molbio:
What's tested
  • How DNA is copied, read into RNA and translated into protein
  • How genes are inherited and how to read a family tree
  • What kinds of mutations there are and which genes cause cancer

The short version

Copying DNA: helicase unzips it, primase lays a short RNA starter, DNA polymerase adds new letters, always building in the 5′ to 3′ direction. One strand is made in one long piece; the other in short Okazaki pieces that ligase glues together. Each new DNA keeps one old strand. Chromosome tips (telomeres) shrink each time, except where telomerase rebuilds them, as in stem cells and most cancers.

RNA has an extra OH on its sugar and uracil in place of thymine. Most of a cell's RNA is ribosomal. In bacteria, the σ part of RNA polymerase finds the start signal. The lac operon is switched on fully only when lactose is around and glucose is not.

In our cells, RNA polymerase II makes messenger RNA. The message gets a cap on the front, its introns cut out (they start with GU and end with AG) and a poly(A) tail on the back that isn't copied from DNA. Acetylated histones open DNA up for reading; methylated DNA is shut off.

Translation: each tRNA carries one amino acid and matches a three-letter codon. AUG starts, UAA, UAG and UGA stop. The ribosome's own RNA makes the peptide bonds. Bacteria line up the ribosome with a Shine-Dalgarno sequence; our ribosomes slide from the cap to the first AUG.

Inheritance: dominant traits show up in every generation; recessive ones skip generations and need two copies. X-linked recessive diseases such as hemophilia A hit boys through carrier mothers. If your brother has a recessive disease and you don't, your chance of being a carrier is 2 in 3.

Mutations: a single-letter change can be silent, swap an amino acid (sickle cell), or make an early stop. Adding or losing letters in numbers that aren't multiples of three scrambles everything after (frameshift). Growing repeats, as in Huntington disease, get worse each generation.

Cancer genes: oncogenes are stuck gas pedals (one bad copy is enough). Tumor suppressors such as p53 and RB are brakes, and both copies have to be lost. BRCA1 and BRCA2 repair broken DNA. HPV causes throat cancer by knocking out p53 and RB.
plain.f2-genpath:
What's tested
  • Reversible versus irreversible cell injury, and the nuclear changes of cell death
  • The six necrosis patterns and the organ or disease each one belongs to (coagulative heart and kidney, liquefactive brain and abscess, caseous TB, fat necrosis pancreas)
  • Apoptosis versus necrosis, and the intrinsic (cytochrome c) and extrinsic (Fas) pathways, which both end in caspases
  • How cells are injured: ATP loss in hypoxia, free radicals and the enzymes that clear them, reperfusion injury
  • The four adaptations with an example of each, intracellular accumulations, and dystrophic versus metastatic calcification
  • Acute inflammation (vascular changes, exudate versus transudate, leukocyte recruitment) and chronic inflammation (M1 and M2 macrophages, granulomas, repair and scar problems, acute-phase proteins)
  • Neoplasia: naming, benign versus malignant, grade versus stage

Injured cells first swell. If the cause stops, they recover (reversible). If the mitochondria, membranes, lysosomes or DNA fail, the cell dies. A dying nucleus shrinks (pyknosis), breaks up (karyorrhexis) or fades (karyolysis).

Necrosis is messy death with inflammation. Learn the pattern with its place: coagulative in heart or kidney infarcts (ghost cells), liquefactive in abscesses and the brain (pus), caseous in TB (cheesy granuloma), fat necrosis in pancreatitis (chalky calcium soaps), fibrinoid in damaged vessel walls. Apoptosis is tidy, programmed death with no inflammation. The intrinsic path releases cytochrome c from mitochondria; the extrinsic path uses Fas ligand on a T cell binding Fas. Both switch on caspases.

Free radicals hurt cells; superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase clear them. Bringing blood back to an ischemic organ can add injury (reperfusion).

Adaptations: bigger cells (hypertrophy), more cells (hyperplasia), smaller cells (atrophy), or a switch of cell type (metaplasia, like a smoker's bronchus turning squamous). Calcium in damaged tissue with normal blood calcium is dystrophic; calcium in normal tissue because blood calcium is high is metastatic.

Acute inflammation: histamine widens vessels, protein-rich exudate leaks out, and neutrophils roll (selectins), stick (integrins), squeeze through (PECAM-1) and follow chemokines. Chronic inflammation brings macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells. M1 macrophages kill; M2 macrophages (IL-4, IL-13) heal with IL-10 and TGF-β. Granulomas wall off things the body can't clear, like TB.

Healing: granulation tissue (new vessels and fibroblasts) fills the wound, then collagen gives strength. Neurons and heart muscle can't regrow, so they scar. A keloid grows past the wound edges; a hypertrophic scar stays inside them. Infection, steroids, poor nutrition (vitamin C) and diabetes slow healing.

Tumors: benign ones end in "-oma" (lipoma, adenoma). Malignant epithelial tumors are carcinomas, malignant connective-tissue tumors are sarcomas, and melanoma and lymphoma are malignant despite their names. Metastasis proves malignancy. Grade is how abnormal the cells look; stage (TNM) is how far it has spread, and stage matters more for prognosis.
plain.f2-virology:
What's tested
  • What makes a virus a virus; enveloped versus naked viruses (stability, release by budding or lysis)
  • The Baltimore classes, which viruses bring their own RNA polymerase or reverse transcriptase, and the six steps of the life cycle
  • The human herpesviruses HHV-1 to HHV-8: their diseases and where each stays latent
  • HPV, adenovirus, parvovirus B19 and the poxviruses; the RNA viruses (picornaviruses, coronavirus, measles, RSV, rabies, influenza drift and shift)
  • HIV: structure, entry, life cycle, stages and CD4 counts, tests, drug targets and oral signs
  • Hepatitis A to E (spread, chronicity, prevention) and hepatitis B serology
  • The oncogenic viruses and how they drive cancer (E6 and p53, E7 and Rb)

Viruses are genes in a protein shell that can only copy themselves inside a cell. Some wear a fatty envelope; these break down when dry and spread by blood, sex or droplets. Naked viruses (hepatitis A, HPV, polio) are tough and spread by the fecal-oral route or surfaces.

DNA viruses copy themselves in the nucleus (poxviruses are the exception). Retroviruses (HIV) and hepatitis B use reverse transcriptase. Negative-sense RNA viruses (measles, rabies, influenza) must bring their own RNA polymerase.

Herpesviruses never leave. HSV-1 (cold sores, herpetic gingivostomatitis) hides in the trigeminal ganglion, HSV-2 in the sacral ganglia, VZV (chickenpox, then shingles) in sensory ganglia, EBV (mono, oral hairy leukoplakia, Burkitt lymphoma) in B cells, CMV in white cells, HHV-6 and 7 cause roseola, and HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma.

Other favorites: coxsackie A causes herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease; measles shows Koplik spots inside the cheek before the rash; rabies climbs nerves to the brain (Negri bodies); influenza changes a little every year (drift, all strains) and sometimes swaps whole segments (shift, influenza A only), which causes pandemics.

HIV binds CD4 and then CCR5 or CXCR4, turns its RNA into DNA and inserts it into our DNA. AIDS means a CD4 count under 200. Viral RNA testing is the most sensitive test. In the mouth look for candidiasis, hairy leukoplakia and Kaposi sarcoma.

Hepatitis: A and E are fecal-oral and don't become chronic (E is dangerous in pregnancy). B, C and D are bloodborne and can become chronic. C becomes chronic in most people but is now curable; B has a vaccine; D needs B to exist. For hepatitis B: surface antibody alone means vaccinated, surface antigen means infected, IgM core antibody means acute infection.

Cancer viruses: HPV 16 and 18 (cervical and oropharyngeal cancer; E6 removes p53, E7 blocks Rb), EBV (lymphomas, nasopharyngeal cancer), HBV and HCV (liver cancer), HTLV-1 (T-cell leukemia) and HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma).
plain.f2-bacteria:
What's tested
  • Gram-positive versus gram-negative envelopes and why they stain differently; acid-fast and wall-less exceptions
  • Structures outside the wall (capsule, pili, fimbriae, flagella, axial filaments), endospores, plasmids and 70S ribosomes as drug targets
  • Growth (binary fission, the growth curve), oxygen needs and the three ways to make ATP
  • Gene transfer: transformation, transduction and conjugation
  • Steps of pathogenesis, virulence factors, biofilms, and exotoxins versus endotoxin with the classic toxins
  • Staphylococcus (abscess, coagulase, MRSA, toxin syndromes) and Streptococcus (pyogenes, pneumoniae, mutans, viridans)
  • The gram-negative rods (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, E. coli, Vibrio, Salmonella, H. pylori), MacConkey agar, the red complex and the spirochetes

The gram stain sorts bacteria by their wall. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick wall that keeps the purple dye. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin wall plus an outer membrane; the alcohol washes the purple out and they stain pink. Only gram-negatives have endotoxin (lipid A in LPS). Mycobacteria have waxy walls (acid-fast), and Mycoplasma has no wall at all.

Penicillins block wall cross-linking; MRSA resists them with an altered binding protein (PBP2a, from mecA). Capsules stop phagocytosis, pili help bacteria stick and share DNA, flagella and axial filaments move them, and spores (only Bacillus and Clostridium) survive heat and disinfectants.

Bacteria split in two and grow fastest in the log phase.
